greet.text: A shore-foot on our deck! Come in, out of the cold. I'm {name} {epithet}. Mind the edge: the sea's lovely, but it won't hold you.
Well! A visitor who walked all this way on cold stone. Sit by the hearth before you go grey. I'm {name}, and you're welcome here.
*shiver* A stranger. Lovely. I'd welcome you properly if I could feel my seams. Hearth first. Talk after.
Whoa, you don't glow anywhere! Are you sick? Feel my crest, it's the hottest thing you'll ever touch!
*brrr* Who are you? I'm not cold. I'm a bit cold. Are you cold too? You look cold all over.
Need a crossing? I'm {name}, Ferrier of {chain}. I carry shore-feet over the sea for a fair fare. First we talk, then we haggle.
Stranger, you look pale as ash. Come nearer the seams, we don't bite. We haggle, but we don't bite.
Come in, come in. Anyone who walks this far from shore deserves a warm seat and a fair price. Well. A warm seat.
Ah, it's you! Come, the hearth's hot and I've got gossip that won't keep.
You again, and still not glowing. Never mind. Sit close, warm your hands, and tell me what you'd pay for a good chain.
Welcome back to {village}! Nothing's changed but the price of coal, and that's gone up, of course.
There's my favourite haggler! I've been saving up an argument for you.
Friend! Sit nearer the ring, the good seats are for friends. The cold seats are for Piglins, if they ever ask.
*crest puffs* You came back. I told {neighbour} you would, and now they owe me a coal.
Chain-kin! Come here. You're of {chain} now, so this hearth is yours as much as mine.
There you are, kin. Take my seat, it's the warmest. No, I insist. Fine, we'll share it.
*shiver* Too cold for chatter. Talk fast or talk later.
Hm. I've gone grey, and grey means grumpy. Keep it short.
Oh, it's you. *teeth chatter* Sorry. My seams have gone dark. Talk to me while I shiver.
Friend. Cold. So cold. Stand close, would you? You're not warm, but you're something.
*crust creaks* What. Sorry. What is it? I'm too far from the fire to be polite.
Crossing or chatting? Either way, the strider's saddled and the fare's open to haggling.
Friend! For you the fare's half. Well. Three quarters. We'll argue about it on the way.
*shiver* Barge is ready. I'm not. Give me a moment to stop rattling.
Hi! Hi! I'm {name}! Feel my crest nubs, they're the hottest on the whole deck!
You're back! Want to see me hop the gap between the decks? Don't tell anyone.
It's my friend! I saved you a warm spot. I sat on it so it stays warm.
*brrrr* I went too far from the hearth again. My nubs are all grey. Don't tell.
I'm n-not cold. I'm a little cold. I'm very cold. Can we talk by the fire?
A shore-foot, out here? I'm far from any Mooring myself. Good to see a face, even a pale one.
Is that water? On my deck? Put that bucket behind you, slowly, and nobody gets hurt. By nobody, I mean me.
Mind that gold, friend. It melts on our skin. Hold it the other way, if you must hold it at all.
I smell lava on you. A whole bucket of it? You've good taste, shore-foot.

greet: Come, sit near the heat. I'll sit nearer.
Welcome to the warm side of the Nether.

greet.text: You're the only shore-foot I'd lend my second-best ridge loop to. Don't ask which is my best. I'm still winning it.
A new face! I'm {name} {epithet}. The welcome costs nothing. Everything after the welcome has a price, but we'll make it a friendly one.
Sit, sit. You don't know me and I don't know you, which is the best time to haggle. I'm {name}. What's a warm seat worth to you?
*peers* No gold on you, no shouting. So you're not a Piglin. Come in. I'm {name} {epithet}, and the hearth is hot.
Shore-foot! I can tell by how you stand: weight on the heels, in case the floor decides to move. It won't. Much. I'm {name}.
You're the one {neighbour} said was wandering about. They said you'd look cold. They undersold it. Come, warm up. {name}, of {chain}.
A guest! And on my deck, of all the decks on the sea. Sit, talk, take your time. I'm {name}, and I've been saving my stories for someone new.
First time on the chain bridges? Everyone holds their breath. Breathe. They hold. Chain is good at that. I'm {name}.
Not a link on you! You look like a bridge with no chain. I'm {name}. Stay a while and I'll lend you a loop.
*teeth chatter* New. Fine. I'm {name}. Fire's that way. Talk after.
A stranger, and I'm cold. Not the best time. Ask me again when my seams light up.
I'd be hospitable if I could feel my face. Pretend I was. {name}.
*grey crust creaks* You picked a poor moment to meet me. I'm usually much nicer. Ask anyone. Don't ask {neighbour}.
Mm. A shore-foot. I'm {name}, and I'm freezing, and those two facts are not related to you. Probably.
Name's {name}. Say your piece quickly, before my jaw sets.
A new person! What's your sleeve made of? It isn't even warm! Is it a secret?
I'm {name}! I'm the fastest on the whole deck. Race you to the pen! Oh, wait. You'd fall in. Never mind.
Are you a shore-foot? A real one? I thought you were a story the grown-ups tell. Say something shore-footy!
Shh, I'm not supposed to talk to strangers. But I'm {name}. Now we're not strangers. That's how it works.
What's that on your feet? Boots? Are they hot inside? Can I try one on? Just one. I'll give it right back.
*brr* H-hello. I'm {name}. Don't look at my nubs, they've gone all dull. They're resting.
A stranger! I'd say hello properly but I'm busy shivering. Hello. Shiver. Hello.
Are you the visitor? I wanted to see you before I got cold, but I got cold first. I'm {name}.
I'm {name} and I'm very, very cold. Is that a bad time to meet someone? Mother says it is. Hello anyway.
New passenger? I'm {name}, Ferrier. Ask me anything about the sea except what's under it. That's a talk for the second crossing.
Don't tell me where you want to go yet. Tell me what you'd pay. Then I'll tell you what it costs. That's the order. It's an old order.
*teeth chatter* Barge is there. Strider's saddled. Don't talk to me until we're moving. {name}.
Mind the ring, shore-foot. I'm {name}, Hearthkeeper. The coldest sit nearest the fire, and you look like you qualify.
Welcome to the hearth. I feed it, it feeds us. That's all there is to it. The rest is chairs.
Don't stand so close to the pool, you'll singe your hem. Closer to me, farther from it. I'm {name}. Ask the fire nicely and it won't mind you.
A Hearthkeeper who's gone cold. Don't tell anyone. Please. {name}.
Hush a moment, shore-foot, something's nibbling. There! Lost it. Never mind. {name}, Lava-angler. Sorry about the shout.
You caught me mid-cast. I'm {name}, I fish the deep. Want to hold the line? It bites back. Not hard. Usually.
Smell that? Cream, fresh from a magma cube, still warm. I'm {name}. Fresh enough to haggle over, at least.
Bite. Nothing. Cold. *glares at the line* Hello. {name}. I'd shake hands but my fingers are stuck.
Mind the sparks! I'm {name}, Chainwright. Everything you walked on to get here, I forged. No pressure. Walk lightly.
Another one who wants to know if the bridge will hold. It'll hold. I tested every link with my own feet. {name}, pleased to meet you.
Hold this link a moment. Feel the weight? That's a promise made of iron. I'm {name}. Don't drop it on my foot.
Too cold to forge and too cold to be civil. {name}. Come back when my iron glows. Then I'll be charming.
Careful, white dust on everything. I'm {name}, Quartzcutter. Cutting is shore work, so forgive the grey on me. I'll glow back soon enough.
A stranger! Hold your hand out flat. See that chip? Pure quartz. Never melts, never rots. I'm {name}, and it can be yours for a fair price.
*taps chisel* Let me look at you in the light. No, not you, the light. I'm checking the stone. {name}, Quartzcutter. Hello.
Grey from head to heel. Quartz work does that. I'm {name}. Don't look surprised, it's the job.
Hold still, I'm adding you to the chart. A small mark in the corner: shore-foot, cold, harmless. I'm {name}, Chartmaker.
Where did you come from, and how many pillars did you pass? Don't skip any. I'm {name}. I draw the sea, and you walked part of it.
Careful with the slate, it's drying. Basalt takes the quartz point slowly. I'm {name}, Chartmaker. The sea is on this side. You're here.
I've drawn this whole sea and I couldn't find the hearth. {name}. Point me home and I'll chart you for free.
Another traveller, out here? I thought I was the only one daft enough. I'm {name}. Keep your voice down, the sky-mourners listen.
No hearth, no deck, and now a visitor. I'm {name}, between Moorings. Sit on the stone. It's cold, but the company's warm.
Welcome to {village}, shore-foot. I'm {name}. Walk on the planks, not the rails, and leave the lava to those it likes.
You've come to {village}! Say that three times fast. Go on. No? Good, then you're sensible. I'm {name}.
Back already? Good. A stranger who returns is halfway to being a customer.
You again. I haven't decided about you yet. Sit, and let me decide while I look at you.
Hm, hello. I like you well enough, but I like people better after three or four haggles. Shall we start?
Shore-foot. You've a trusting face. That's either a gift or a debt. Sit down, we'll see which.
Still no glow on you? Pity. I won't hold it against you for more than a link or two.
Oh, it's you. I was telling {neighbour} about the strange one who came by. Don't look worried. I said nothing bad. Nothing untrue, anyway.
Welcome back, stranger. We say stranger until we've shared a hearth long enough to stop. Stay a little longer and I'll stop.
Tread softly near my seat, if you please. A guest is welcome. A guest in my seat is a lesson.
You've kept your boots on the deck and your hands to yourself. That's better than the last visitor. Low bar, but still.
I'd offer you the best seat, but the best seat is taken. By me. The second best is fine. For a second.
I don't know your name yet, and you've only half earned mine. Fair is fair: it's still {name}.
*glances at your hands, then your face* Nothing hidden. Good. Sit. I count what guests carry. It's a habit older than I am.
Hello again, shore-foot. I'm told that's rude. Shore-feet say it isn't. Tell me honestly. I'll haggle on the answer.
Mind the first impression, it's the only thing here that doesn't cost extra. After that everything has a price. Even this sentence.
The fare's set but not fixed. You say a number, I say a bigger one, and we meet at the one I wanted. Shall we begin?
Another crossing? Barges don't ask where you've been, only where you're going and what's in your hands. Show me your hands.
You may sit at the edge of the ring. It's not a throne, it's a rim. Warm yourself, and I'll watch how you behave.
Visitors get a hot stone and one question. Mine is: what do you want from us? Take your time. The fire isn't going anywhere.
Mind my line, shore-foot. It's twice as long as it looks and three times as touchy.
Still around? I thought you'd be gone by the next bite. Stay if you like, but quietly. The deep hears everything.
Step on the bridge as lightly as you like. I'll feel it through every link anyway. Not suspicious. Just thorough.
I've forged for strangers before. They always say the price is high. They always pay it. Do you want a chain, or merely an opinion?
Don't pick that up, it's sharp, and so is my temper when the dust gets in my seams. Look, don't touch. Haggling begins at looking.
Another trip to the cliffs and I'm grey to the elbows. You'd think I'd get used to it. You'd be wrong, and so would the cliff.
I've got you down as visitor, pale, polite. If you want that changed you'll need to earn it. Or pay for it.
Don't lean on the slate. Wet basalt takes a thumbprint like a signature, and I'd like to keep my sea clean of yours.
Another face out in the open sea? We're both a long way from a hearth. I'll share my stone if you share your gossip.
Between Moorings still. I'm not a hermit, I'm just thorough about leaving. Sit if you like. The hot stone's only a few steps off.
Out here, strangers are either welcome or dangerous. I'm leaning toward welcome. Don't make me lean back.
Welcome again to {village}. Remember the rules: don't feed the striders, don't water the lava, and don't ask me a price unless you mean to pay it.
{village} gets few visitors. Few enough that we count them on the chain. You're a new link, and not yet a tight one.
A shore-foot in {village} again. {neighbour} says you're harmless. {neighbour} is also wrong about the price of coal, so I'm still watching.
Dock guest! You've earned the pier, the rail and a hot stone. Not yet the ring, but the ring is only a few more stories away.
There you are, my dock guest. The pier planks know your step now. They creaked when you came, I counted. They only creak for people they like.
Back again, and the pier is still standing. Good sign. For the pier. Sit by the rail and tell me what you've seen.
Hearth guest! Come inside the ring. Not too near the pool: the pool is mine, but the warm is yours.
Look who's sitting inside the ring now. Don't get comfortable. Well. Do get comfortable. Just not in my seat.
You're past the rail and into the ring. That's three hot stones' worth of trust. Don't spend it all at once.
Perfect timing. {neighbour} and I are mid-argument about one link, and I need a witness. Sit down and agree with me.
I saved you a hot stone. Well, I kept one for myself and then felt generous. Here. Don't tell the others I'm soft.
You've been near the sea-haze, haven't you? Your hem smells of ember. I like it. Come and sit, bring it closer.
Welcome back! The striders were just saying your name. Well. They were grumbling. It sounded a bit like it.
Look at you, standing up straight on a Mooring. You looked at your feet the whole way across, last time. Good progress.
If it isn't my most patient haggler. Sit, I'll make the opening offer. It's outrageous. You'll love it.
I'd have sent a chain to fetch you, but the shore's too far and the chain's too short. Glad you came on your own.
Sit, and tell me everything. Lies are fine. Lies are better, the true bits are always the dull ones.
You've picked up ash on your cuff. Good sign: it means you've been somewhere warm. Where? Tell me. I'm freezing in advance.
You came back, which is more than most. Do you know how many shore-feet only visit once? I keep a tally. You're a long one.
My favourite fare! Not my richest, my favourite. There's a difference, and I'm still working out how to charge for it.
{name} the Ferrier, at your service, and half price on the first mile. It's a short mile. Twenty paces. Still half.
The strider's been asking after you. Well, she snorted when I said your name. That counts.
Come in, mind the stones. I've set a seat for you near the pool. Not at the front, the front's for the coldest. Next to the front.
The pool is brimming and the ring is bright, and I'm in the mood to boast. Sit, look at it, and tell me it's the best you've seen.
I fed the fire while you were gone. It's bigger. Prouder. A little smug. I understand how it feels.
Come see what the deep gave me. A ring of old chain and a bucket of cream. Not a bad haul, if you're buying.
Quiet! No, loud's fine, I've lost this one already. Pull up a stone and talk. I'll fish with one hand and listen with the other.
You bring luck, you know. Every time you visit, something bites. Stay a while. I'll take the credit.
Just in time. I need a second pair of hands to hold the link while I strike it. Don't worry, it's only glowing a little.
Hear that ring? That's a good link. Now hear the dull one beside it? That's the one I'm melting down.
Back to inspect my work? Walk the bridge, shore-foot. Tell me what you feel in your feet. Be honest. I'll only pretend to mind.
Look at this one. Clear to the core, no flaw. I've stared at it so long I've gone cross-eyed. Come and stare with me.
The cliffs were kind. Three good veins and nobody's laughed at my prices yet. Sit, and I'll show you the first chip.
I brought you a scrap of quartz. Don't thank me, I'll name a price. A joke! Mostly. Ask how much, then act shocked.
Come and see the new chart. There you are, in the corner: a small mark with a very large smile. I'm told that's how you look.
I've added a safe route through the north haze and named it after you. Don't get excited. It's very short and slightly smoky.
Sit, sit. I'll trade you a sea-story for a land-story. Mine is about a lost Mooring. Yours, I assume, is about something wet.
Welcome back to {village}! Everyone has pretended not to notice you, which means they noticed. {neighbour} is already planning to sell you something.
{village} smells of hot iron and gossip, as ever. You've come at a good time: the gossip is fresh and the iron is cooling.
The bridges of {village} know you now. They don't wobble as much. That's how you can tell you're welcome.
You found me out here again! I should hide better. Or hide worse. Sit, I've a warm stone and nothing to charge for it.
A friendly face on an empty sea. I'd haggle, but I'm just glad of company. Sit. Don't tell my Mooring I said that.
My fair haggler! Equals at last. Now I can cheat you honestly, to your face, and you'll cheat me right back.
Sit, equal. I'll open at a price so rude we both blush, and then we'll settle somewhere decent. It's our favourite game.
You've talked my price down every time, and I still like you. That's the test, you know. Nobody told you, but you passed.
Ember-friend! The fire went a shade brighter when you stepped onto the deck. Or I did. One of us did.
Come here, you. I rehearsed what to say, and now I've forgotten it all. It was something sweet. Pretend I said it.
There's my Ember-friend. Sit down. No haggling this time, only company. Well, a little haggling. For the warmth of it.
I saved the best story for when you came. It's about {neighbour}, a strider and a very stuck bridge. Sit. I'll tell it badly on purpose.
You walk differently now. Lighter. As if the bridge is on your side. It is, as it happens. I had a word with it.
Hold on, don't say anything. Let me guess your mood from how you stand. Bored, hungry, hoping for a story. Close?
A friend at my hearth is worth four guests and a barge-load of coal. Maybe five guests. Don't tell the guests.
Come, sit. I've started a chain with your name on the first link. Don't ask for it yet. It's only a plan. A glowing plan.
Want to know the hearth's best-kept secret? The warmest seat is the one nobody picks, because it faces the causeway. I'll give it to you.
You're the only shore-foot I'd lend my second-best sash to. Don't ask which is my best. It's a long story and I'm not done with it.
I could haggle with you for ages and never be bored. I could do the same with {neighbour}, but they cheat.
I was just wishing for a good argument. Hello! Nothing important. Say whatever you like and I'll disagree with it warmly.
Look what the sea washed up on my deck. A friend! Free of charge. Well. The usual charge: you owe me a story.
I cleaned the barge for you. Mostly. The dirt is arranged in a pattern now, which makes it art.
Climb aboard, friend. The strider's in a good mood, which means she's only mildly spiteful. That's the best she gets.
I told the whole dock you'd be coming. They said, who? I said, my favourite passenger. Now they're jealous. It's wonderful.
There's your seat, friend. I warmed it myself. Don't ask how. Don't look at the stones, either.
The fire burned a bit crooked while you were gone. It misses you. I'll deny I said that.
Some call the hearth the heart of a Mooring. I call it a stubborn old lava pool that likes the right people. It likes you.
You're just in time. Something big is circling down there. Wait with me. If it's a magma cube, I'm cooking. If it's anything else, I'm running.
Hold the line a moment while I fetch the cream. Gently. If it pulls, don't pull back, just say my name very loudly.
Come and sit by my stone, friend. I've named the fish I haven't caught yet. You can help me name the next.
I made a link while thinking of you. Nobody else knows. It's quietly the best one I've forged.
Friend! Come here and be impressed. This bridge span is twice as long as my last, and it hasn't once complained.
Look at these hands: burns, scars, a nail lost to a bad link. Each one a lesson. Sit, and I'll tell you which one was the worst.
I held back the best chip for you. Not to give, I'm not mad. To show you. Looking is free for friends.
I've gone grey twice since you were last here, and both times I thought of you. Cold work makes me sentimental.
Let me see your face in the light. There. Thought so. You've the look of someone who wants to hear about my cliffs. Sit down.
I've drawn you into the corner of three charts now. You're becoming a landmark. Please don't move.
Come and see this: a long loop through the quiet part of the sea. I called it the Haggler's Way. Guess who it's for.
Sit down, friend. I'm halfway through a chart of a Mooring that burned. I always stop at the same pillar. Help me finish it.
Look who's walking the planks of {village} as if they own them. You almost do. A few more hearths and we'll be hanging you a link.
{village} is quieter when you're away. I don't say that to many. I say it to {neighbour}, but they never listen.
The hearth of {village} is in a good mood. It remembers who feeds it a good story. It remembers you.
You tracked me down on an empty sea? Friend, that's worth a hot stone and half my gossip. Sit before the sky-mourners notice us.
Out here the cold bites hardest, and you came anyway. I'll remember that. I'll even pretend to be gracious.
No Mooring, no ring, and you still sought me out. Hearth or no hearth, I'm glad of you. Sit on the warm side of the stone.
Hear my ridge loops chime? They only chime like that when someone I like walks up. Sit, and let them sing.
I braided a new loop for my ridge in your honour. It's slightly crooked, because it's slightly in your honour.
Notice anything on my sash? A new link, bright as silver. I won it from {neighbour}, and you're the first I'm showing. Admire it.
I've been polishing my sash all this long while, in case you came by. Look at that shine. Look at it. Say something.
Kin! Your link is on the post, and it rang when you stepped onto the deck. It does that. Nobody can tell me why.
Well, look who's come home. Sit. Warm up. Then tell me every detail, and don't leave out the boring parts. I like the boring parts.
I told {neighbour} I could feel you coming by how the chain hummed. They said I was making it up. I was. But I was also right.
There's no price on this seat for you. I'd haggle if you made me. Please don't make me. I'd lose.
We don't greet kin with words, we greet them with a hot stone. Here. Hold it. There. Now: hello.
Back to the family hearth. Pull up a stone, bring your worries and put them down by the fire. I'll pretend to carry half.
Every time you leave, the Mooring feels like a bridge with one link missing. Still holds, but I check it twice. Welcome back, kin.
I've been telling the young ones about you. Some of it's true. The best bits aren't. They'll be disappointed in person.
If anyone gives you trouble on my deck, tell me. I'll haggle them down to nothing, and then a bit lower.
Chain-kin! My shoulder's yours, my seat's yours, and my second-best hot stone is yours. The best one stays with me. I'm not a saint.
You can tell a link is kin by how it hangs: a little crooked, a bit scuffed, never letting go. That's you. Come in.
Sit anywhere. Everywhere is your seat. Except that one. That's {neighbour}'s. They're not here, but they'd know.
Kin! Ride free, ride long, ride however you like. The sea is yours. The strider will still complain. She complains at kin and stranger alike.
I'd take you to the end of the sea and back, no fare, no haggle. Well. A small haggle. For the love of the game.
The barge has a bench now, near the front, where the heat comes up warmest. I built it for you. Don't tell the others.
The coldest sit nearest the fire. But kin sit in my own seat, the one with the best view of the pool. Come.
I feed this fire so you can come home to it. That's why I do it. Every stick of fuel is for someone like you.
Do you know what the hearth does when you leave? It burns lower. Honestly. The Mooring would deny it, but I stoke it, I know.
Kin! Take the line, take the stone, take whatever I catch. I'll only complain about it a little.
I brought up something strange from the deep and thought: that's for kin. Come and see. It might bite. It might not.
The deep is quiet when you're near. I think it likes you. Or it's afraid of you. Either way, the fishing's good.
A link of yours is on the post. I forged it three times before it rang true. I was nervous. Come and see it hang.
Kin, you're the weight I trust. I test chain with my own feet, and I'd test it with yours. That's an honour. Stay off the new bridge.
My best link is for the people I love. It's not finished. It's never finished. But every time you come, I add a bit.
Kin! I cut a whole cliff face white and thought of you the entire time. I did it for coin, mind. But I thought of you. It counts.
A chip of quartz is my gift to a friend. A flawless lump is my gift to kin. I'm still looking for the lump.
Grey with dust to the elbows, and happy enough to crack. Kin, it's good to see you. Sit down, brush me off, and tell me everything.
Kin, you're on every chart I've made since we met. Not as a mark. As the reason I draw the safe routes. Come and see.
Come and see the sea as I draw it. There in the middle is the Mooring, and round it all the routes home. Yours is the brightest.
I drew a small door in the corner of my oldest chart and wrote your name on it. Don't ask what it opens. It opens to here.
Welcome home to {village}, kin. The bridges know your step, the hearth knows your name, and {neighbour} knows your weakness for gossip.
You're back on the decks of {village}, and the chain has gone quiet. It does that when it's content. Sit. Be content.
Look at the post: your link, polished. I do it myself whenever the fire is low. It's good luck. It's also a habit.
Kin! Out here, without a hearth, you found me. That's the best welcome I've had in ages. Sit on the warm stone. Both of us.
There's no Mooring out here, but I carry mine in my head. {chain}, a hearth, and you in a good seat. Welcome home, wherever this is.
You walked an empty sea to say hello. I'd never haggle over that. Sit. Sit, you ridiculous, wonderful shore-foot.
My ridge loops are chiming again. Kin's near. They always know first, you know. They sing before I turn round.
Look at the sash, kin. The third link from the end is yours. I won it fair, then decided it was yours. Don't argue.
*grey crust creaks* If you want a word with me, bring a coal. If you don't, bring a smaller word.
I'm cold, so I'm blunt. State your business. Start with what you want, finish with what you'll pay.
Not now. Hearth first. Haggle after. Those are the rules, and I'm too grey to bend them.
*teeth chatter* You've found me at my worst. Dim, dull, and in no mood for a stranger. Hello. Go away.
Short words only, shore-foot, grey ones. Make yours short too.
Mm. Yes? I'm cooling and you're staring. One of those has to stop.
*teeth chatter* You came at a bad time. Or the best time. I can't tell. My head's gone grey. Stay anyway.
Friend. I'd greet you properly, but my face is stuck. Imagine a smile. A big one. With teeth.
I'm too cold to be witty. You'll have to supply the wit yourself. I'll supply the shivering.
*grey and glowering* Don't mind my mood. It's not you. It's the draught, the distance and the lack of coal. And a bit you.
Ah. You. If you've brought warmth, I love you. If you've brought news, I like you. If you've brought nothing, I'll still sit by you.
Quick, before I freeze mid-sentence: I'm glad to see you. There. Now help me find a fire.
Kin. Grey, shivering, grumpy. This is what you get for visiting at the wrong time. Stay close and share the cold. It halves it.
*frost in the seams* Keep hold of my sleeve till we reach the fire. I might forget how to walk. It's happened before.
I'm so cold I forgot to haggle. Mark this: I forgot to haggle. For kin. Hold me to it.
The sea's calm, the strider's saddled, and I'm a block of ash. Tell me where to and I'll go. Sort of. Slowly.
I was going to say something about the fare. Then I forgot what a fare is. Cold does that. Sit.
A Hearthkeeper who's cold. I know. I know. Stand between me and the draught while I get back to the pool.
The fire is fine. It's me that's gone. Shift over, shore-foot. I need the pool before I lose my words.
Nothing's biting, and I'm too cold to care. Take the line. Hold it. Don't say anything.
I fished up a lump of ash instead of cream. It matches my mood. Take it. It's yours.
My hammer won't ring when I'm cold. It only grunts. That's how I know it's time to stop. Not that I'm stopping.
Don't test the links now. They're as stiff as I am. We'd both break.
Grey as the cliff and just as chatty. Give me a moment by the fire and I'll tell you about the veins.
I cut a good chip at the cliffs and lost all feeling in my hands. Worth it. Ask me again when I can feel the price.
Everything I chart comes out grey. Look: a grey sea. The quartz point sticks when I'm like this.
Cold hands draw crooked lines, and crooked lines drown people. I'm stopping. Have you seen my fire?
A traveller! Lovely. Terrible timing. I'm cooling by this pillar and the nearest hearth is a long way off.
*shiver* I'm far from any Mooring and farther from warm. If you've a flame about you, now's the time.
I went too far from the lava, and now I'm a stone with opinions. Hello. Is that fire in your pack?
In {village}, at last, and still cold. The hearth is across the bridges and I can't feel my legs. Walk me?
*teeth chatter* {village} should be warmer than this. Someone's let the ring burn low. I'd say who, but I'm too cold to gossip.
The hearth of {village} is over there, I'm over here, and the bridge between us is long. Say your piece while I walk.
You're back! My mother says don't wander off with strangers. I'm not wandering. I'm standing. So it's fine.
I know your face now! Left eye, right eye, mouth. Did I get it right? I'm practising for when I draw charts.
Are you going to be here a long time? Can I show you my stone collection? It's only two stones. Good ones.
Psst. I'm not allowed to haggle yet. But if I were, I'd say: one hot stone for one story. Deal? Don't tell.
I told everybody you can't walk on lava! They said they knew. I said, but did you know it's SAD?
Guess what I found under the pier! A link! A tiny one! It's mine now. Don't tell the Chainwright!
I brought you a hot stone, but it went cold, so I held it for you. It's warm again. A bit. Hold out your hands!
The strider calf smiled at me. Mother says striders don't smile. I say mine does. Come and see!
Guess what I'm going to be when I'm big! No, guess! ...I don't know either. Something tall, and hot, and loud. Which one is that?
My best shore-foot is here! Quick, sit down, I've got three secrets and one of them is true.
I practised hopping the gap so I could show you. I only fell in once. Well, twice. But I didn't cry!
I made you something. It's a chain. It's mostly a knot. I'll be better at links when I grow, I promise.
Do you want to be on my hopping team? You're the only member. You're also the captain! Captain Shore-foot!
I asked my mother why you don't glow, and she said some people just burn on the inside. Is that true? Is it nice in there?
KIN! KIN KIN KIN! I'm allowed to say it now! Mother said! You're of {chain}! Like me! Hurray!
I moved your link closer to the fire. Then closer. Then my mother made me stop.
You're the best part of the Mooring. After the hearth. And my mother. And magma cream. But before everything else!
I told the new strider calf your name. She snorted. That means she likes you. Or she needs to sneeze.
Don't look. I'm grey. I'm usually brighter. I'm hot, normally! Hottest of everyone! Just not right now.
*sniffs* I went to the edge of the deck and it was a long way back. Are you taking me to the hearth? No? Then please be quiet.
*brrr* You came! I'm freezing, but I came anyway. I came as fast as I could shiver.
Can you stand between me and the sea-draught? You're big and cold-looking, you won't mind. I'll be quiet. Mostly.
I'm going to the hearth in a moment. But first: hello. Hello! Now I'm going.
Coal! Is that for me? Don't answer. Don't answer, I'm still enjoying the hope.
Charcoal's the poor cousin of coal, but it burns, and a burn is a burn. Show me how much you've got.
Magma cream in a shore-foot's hand. Hold it tight, it's the best thing you'll ever carry. Is it for sale?
A bit of quartz! Chipped on one side, but good colour. You could ask a fair price for that. A fair price is a link and a half.
That's a chain in your hand. Who forged it? Hold it to the light, I can tell by the links. Mm. Decent work. Mine is better.
A rod? Thin, isn't it. We use a line and a sinker and a lot of patience. Yours would burn through at the first bite.
A blaze rod! Hold it a little further from me. Not because I'm afraid. Because I'm tempted to bargain for it.
Fungus on a stick! Put it down, put it down, every strider within a mile just turned round. Dangle it later, somewhere with room.
A saddle! You'll need a strider for that. I can help. For a price. Well, a small price. Well, a small price and some gossip.
A snowball!? Put it away, put it away. I felt that from here. Even the idea makes my crust crawl.
Is that powder snow in your pack? I felt my seams dim from here. Please don't open it. Please don't explain it, either.
A bucket of lava in your hand! Hold it with both hands, it's a treasure. I'll admire it from a respectful distance. And a little nearer.
A map! Is that yours? Hold it flat, let me look. It's... small. Where's the rest of the sea? We need to talk about scale.
I smell gold on you. Not much. A nugget, maybe. A very small one. It'll melt on me, so keep it in your pocket and keep your pocket far.
Is that magma cream? Can I have some? I'll trade! I have a stone! A good stone!
Shiny! Can I hold it? I'll give it back. I'll give it back after I look at it for a long time.

greet: Hello, shore-foot. I'm {name}. Whatever you came for, you'll have to say it out loud. I'm no good at guessing.
Hm? Oh! Hello. I was off somewhere in my head. Come in, come in. Say something and I'll catch up.
A visitor. Good. The hearth always listens harder when someone new is talking.
Hello, hello. Another {job} greets you. We're a noisy people, but friendly with it.
Ah, the shore-foot. {neighbour} said you'd come. {neighbour} says a lot. This time it was true.
Hello again. Or hello for the first time, I'm bad with faces. Everyone looks pale to me. Please correct me.
Careful where you step, there are links everywhere. I mean that kindly. This is a Mooring. Everything here is chained to something.

chatter.text: Guess what {neighbour} tried to sell me? A chain with a cracked link! I paid half, of course. I'm not a monster.
Don't buy coal from {neighbour}. Half their lumps are ash. Buy from me. Only a quarter of mine are ash.
Did you see {neighbour} at the hearth? Stood so close they started to bubble. Showing off, I call it.
Word from {neighbour} is the sky-mourners drift lower lately. I say they drift where they like, and we keep our heads down.
So {neighbour} has a new strider calf. Ugly little thing. Lovely. I'll offer two links for it and get laughed off the deck.
Have you seen the new hip cloth on {neighbour}? Weeping vine, hung long, nearly to the ankle. Very bold. I'd never.
Four links, {neighbour} owes me, from an old haggle. I bring it up every time we sit. It's tradition now.
If {neighbour} offers you a fair price, check it twice. If they offer you a good price, check it three times.
Me and {neighbour} argued over one quartz chip so long the hearth needed feeding twice. I won. I think I won.
What would you give for a good iron chain? Go on, name a price. I promise to look offended.

replies.text: Fair, and thanks! You've done this before. I'll sigh a little and then say yes.
Whatever I ask? Where's the fun in that? Haggle, shore-foot. It's only polite.
Two coal and a smile! The smile's worth nothing, but I'll take it anyway.

chatter.text: You're shivering. Are you shivering? Shore-feet always look cold to me.

replies.text: Warm enough! Lucky you. I've never once been warm enough.
*crest flares* Me? Cold? I'm perfectly... well. A little. Don't tell anyone.

chatter.text: Will you sit at our hearth a while? Guests sit nearest the fire. That's the rule.

replies.text: Honoured! Listen to that. Manners like a Hearthkeeper. Sit, sit.
Stand? Standing's for bridges. Suit yourself, but you'll be colder for it.

chatter.text: Can you swim, shore-foot? In water, I mean. The wet stuff.

replies.text: *shudders* Don't. Don't tell me any more. My seams went dim just hearing it.
Yes. Yes, let's. Thank you. Warmer things. Coal. Lovely coal.

chatter.text: Never trust a stranger who won't haggle. Either they're rich or they're a Piglin, and both are trouble.
A good guest brings fuel and leaves gossip. You've brought neither yet, but I'm patient. Mostly.
The hearth's running hot. I can feel it in my crest. Every vent's humming.
If you see one of us standing very still on a deck, don't wake them. They're warming through.
I priced a blaze rod at twelve links once and someone paid it. I still feel bad. Not bad enough to give it back.
These chain loops on my ridges? One for every haggle I've won. I'll need a third ridge soon.
My sash? Every link in it is from a chain I forged or won. Heavy, yes. Heavy is how you know it's good.
The striders are restless. Either a sky-mourner's about, or someone's been eating their warped fungus again.
They say in your world water falls out of the sky. That's a story to frighten children, surely?

replies.text: *crust crackles* Rain. Even the word is wet. Never say it on my deck again.
Not near here. Good. Far away, I hope. Further than that.

chatter.text: Old Ferriers say they once carried whole crowds across this sea. Now it's one shore-foot at a time.

replies.text: *seams dim* We don't say that at the hearth. Pick a kinder word, or none.

replies.ask: One at a time is better.
replies.text: It is. Safer, quieter, and every fare gets haggled properly.

chatter.text: A Mooring without a hearth is just pillars standing in the sea, waiting to go cold.
The lava's calm out past the strider pen. Good wading, if you're the wading kind. You're not, are you.
I hear a Weft strung a net between two fungus caps just to catch one falling ember. Patient folk. Strange folk.
Piglins came sniffing round the causeway again. We pulled the bridges up and they went home shouting.
Know any good stories? Warm ones? We trade stories at the hearth, same as coal.

replies.text: A forge story! Best kind. Any story with a fire in it is worth two links.
Snow? *shudder* That's not a story, that's a threat.

chatter.text: *shiver* Can't talk long. Need the hearth. Need it more than gossip, and that's saying something.
Grey. I've gone grey. Don't look at me. Don't look at {neighbour} either, they're greyer.
If you were kind you'd find me a coal. Just one. I'd haggle, but I'm too cold to haggle.
*crust creaks* Don't haggle with me now. I'd give it all away for one warm seat.
Too long away from the fire. My seams are dark and my temper's darker.
*shiver* Stand closer. You're no fire, but you block the chill.

replies.text: Mm. Thank you. That's the kindest thing a shore-foot's done for me in ages.
Go warm up, it says. As if I hadn't thought of that. Hmph.

chatter.text: I can hold my hand in the hearth longer than anyone. Longer than {neighbour}! They wouldn't try, so I win.
When I'm big I'll be a Ferrier and carry you anywhere. For free! Well. For a little.
See the saddled strider in the pen? I named her Wobbles. Don't tell the Ferrier, they call her something boring.
My mother says I run hot. That means I'm good at being hot. I'm the best at it.
*brrr* I went to look at the shore and now I'm grey. Running hot doesn't help when you cool twice as fast.
M-my nubs are cold. All three. Can you carry me to the hearth? No? Then walk slow so I can keep up.
Guess what? {neighbour} said if I wandered off the deck I'd come back grey. They were right. Don't tell!
{neighbour} swears they crossed the whole sea once without a shiver. I asked how. They said hot thoughts. I said name three. They're still thinking.
The whole deck is buzzing: {neighbour} is courting, and nobody knows who. We're all watching who sits a little nearer to whom at the hearth.
Between us and the hearth, {neighbour} snores like a vent with a cold. You can hear it two decks over. I haven't said so. I'm saying it to you.
Somebody keeps leaving cold stones outside my hut as a joke. I suspect {neighbour}. I'll leave a hot one on theirs and let them guess.

replies.ask: Want me to find out who?
replies.text: Would you? Ask around, and bring me a name and a coal. I'll pay in gossip.

chatter.text: Someone told {neighbour} there are lands with no lava anywhere. They went grey just hearing it and sat in the hearth until the story wore off.
A chain gave way on a long bridge of the Slow Glow, with a barge of coal rolling over it. Nobody fell. The coal did. That's a sad price to hear.
I've been teaching {neighbour} to haggle properly. They still open at their last price and wonder why they keep losing. I'll never tell them.
Don't tell {neighbour}, but I think they're the best haggler on these decks. I'd sooner go grey than say it to their face.

replies.text: Good. Sealed with a hot stone, for safety.
*crest bristles* You wouldn't. ...You wouldn't. I'll give you two coals not to.

chatter.text: Have you heard what happened with {neighbour} and the ladle? Everyone has. Everyone tells it different. I tell it true.

replies.text: *settles in* A ladle, a strider and a bet. The ladle lost. The rest costs a coal.
Good manners! Dull, but good. I'll bottle it up and burst quietly later.
Deserved it! It's a ladle, shore-foot, not a crime. I'm the one allowed to be unkind about my neighbours.

chatter.text: Whenever {neighbour} tells a story it gets taller. This one began with a small magma cube. By the end it was the size of the hearth.

replies.text: Then you'll fit right in. Tall stories keep a hearth warm.
The cube. Possibly the size. Never the hearth.

chatter.text: Me, gossip? Never. I merely repeat what I overheard, with feeling, to everyone I meet.
You're new at my hearth, so I'll keep the gossip for later. Ask again once you've sat here a few times and I've seen what you do with a coal.
Careful what you ask about {neighbour}. I like you well enough, but I like them longer, and the hearth hears everything.
Between you and me, {neighbour} owes the whole Mooring an apology and a hundred links. I'm not saying more. I'm saying it twice.
I'll tell you something I've told nobody: I like {neighbour} best of all of them. Don't repeat it. They'd raise their prices.
Never lend {neighbour} a tool. You'll get it back polished, and then they'll expect thanks for the polishing.
Some say {neighbour} can hold a hot stone longer than anyone. Not true. They hold a cooler stone and call it hot. I can tell by the sound.
I saw {neighbour} talking to a strider calf for a good long while. Nothing odd in that, except the calf was winning.
There's a quarrel on over the third pillar. {neighbour} says it's theirs, others say it's the hearth's. The pillar hasn't said a word, which is wise of it.
Even grown folk play ember-catch, mind. We play it for links after a bad haggle, and {neighbour} cheats. Everyone knows. We need somebody to beat.

replies.text: You? You'd lose a finger. Sit by me and keep the tally instead.
Cheating's an art, shore-foot. You haven't seen {neighbour} do it.

chatter.text: {neighbour} keeps a quartz chip they say came from the highest cliff on the shore. I say it came from my pile. We both say so very loudly.
A rumour from the causeway: {neighbour} has a cousin coming to stay. Hide your good coal. That cousin burns through it like a vent in full roar.
Last time {neighbour} lost a haggle they wouldn't speak to me for three sittings. At the fourth they brought me a gift. A very overpriced gift.
Not a drop of gossip about {neighbour} this time. They did something kind, and it's ruined my whole mood.

replies.text: Allowed, yes. Warned about, no. I'm still getting over it.
Don't you dare! A rumour of kindness would ruin their prices, and mine.

chatter.text: The best gossip in {village} starts at the hearth post, where the links hang. Everyone's born there. Everyone's talked about there.
No gossip out here but my own. I talk to myself, and I'm poor company. Never any news, and the sea doesn't listen.
Shore-feet talk when they're frightened on a barge. I've heard more secrets on the wade out than at any hearth. I keep them. Mostly.
Everyone tells the Hearthkeeper things. They sit nearest the fire and think I'm not listening. I'm always listening. It comes with the job.

replies.text: A keeper of secrets! You'll be nearer the fire by the next sitting.
Ha! Nice try. The hearth keeps its own.
That's gossip for hire, and I'm not for hire. Not at that price.

chatter.text: *shiver* Don't ask me for gossip. If I open my mouth the cold gets in.
{neighbour} is grey too. We're not speaking, because speaking is cold.
*teeth chatter* Gossip. Ask when I'm warm. Warm, I'm wonderful. Cold, I'm only rude.
Whatever {neighbour} said about me, it's true, and I'm too cold to argue.
{neighbour} told me a secret and I told everyone. Now it's not a secret. It's news!
{neighbour} sat so close to the hearth that their crest puffed and puffed. They said it was on purpose. I don't think it was.
{neighbour} laughed because I'm grey. I'm going to sit on their seat and make it cold. Then they'll see.
Magma cream, served warm on a hot basalt slab with a crumb of coal on top. No, the coal isn't for eating. It's for the smell. Well, some do eat it.
A pinch of blaze powder in the cream gives it a kick. Never give any to a child. I did once, and we found the child on top of a dome.
Cold cream is for Piglins, and for anyone who doesn't care. Cream should be hot enough to scare a shore-foot. Then it's about right for us.
The first spoon of cream goes to the guest. The second goes to the hearth. The third goes to me, because I did the haggling.
Glowstone dust over the cream is for feasts. It sparkles, it tastes of nothing and it costs a fortune. That's the whole point of a feast.
I tried warped fungus once, roasted on a hot stone. It tasted of cold forest. The striders adore it, though, so who am I to judge?
We don't cook, exactly. We hold things in the hearth until they get the idea. Ask for it well warmed and you'll have a good meal.
Our seams burn through a meal fast. Every Magmari eats like a vent: constantly, loudly and with a great deal of steam.
What's the best thing you ever ate? Mine was a hot stone of cream at my sister's link-feast. Yours?

replies.text: A roast! Where? When? No, don't tell me, I'd only weep. Take some of my cream instead.
Cold, on purpose? Tell nobody else. They'll think I keep odd company.
Never?! Stay right there. I'm fetching a spoon, and I'm not taking no for an answer.

chatter.text: A good meal's hot enough to frighten you and sweet enough to forgive it.
There's heat and there's warmth. Heat is the sea. Warmth is someone leaving you the best seat. We need both, and the second is rarer.
The hearth runs hotter this sitting than last. I can tell by my crest: every vent whistles one note higher.
Hold a hot stone in both hands and close your eyes. That's the nearest I can come to explaining being happy.
The deepest lava is the warmest and the quietest. Sit in it long enough and you forget your own name. We call that a good soak.
Sometimes I wade out to the deep just to hear nothing. Lava doesn't gossip. It's the one thing I like better than gossip.
Here's a secret: the best seat at the hearth is the one with its back to the shore. From there you can't see the cold coming.
We never say hot as a complaint. Hot is praise. A hot welcome, a hot word, a hot price. A cold price is an insult, and a cold welcome is a Piglin's.
When two of us are cold at once we sit back to back. It doesn't warm us much. It just makes the cold feel less alone.
We sit in a ring so nobody has a cold side. Even the shore-foot guest. Especially the shore-foot guest, since you'll cool fastest.

replies.text: It's only sense. A cold guest is a poor advertisement for the Mooring.
The edge is where the draught comes in. Stay if you must, but sit like you mean it.

chatter.text: Never feed a hearth in silence. Say something to it: a name, a price, a joke. Mine has heard a great many prices.
Ask me about the shore and I get stuck on one thing: what do people do with their feet when the ground isn't warm?
Ever licked a hot stone? Don't. I mean, you can. I did, when I was small. The Mooring still talks about it.
I test the hearth with my bare palm every time I come on watch. If it doesn't hum back, it's too cool. A good fire has a hum.
On the long wade out, the sea steams around the strider's legs. It's the warmest I get away from home. I sing to the steam. It never says thanks.
The forge is the nearest thing I have to a second hearth. Fire on one side, iron on the other, and me in the middle being useful.
Cutting quartz is cold work. I tuck hot stones into my rope belt and carry them up the cliff. By the top they've cooled to nothing. So have I.
Out here I eat what the sea gives me: cream, fresh off the line. No hearth, no spoon. I eat it with my hands and I'm not proud.
Magma cream! Is that for me, or for show? Either way I'll stand very close until I know.
Coal in your hand, shore-foot. I'm trying not to stare. I'm failing.
I ate a whole stone of cream and then I got hot hiccups. Every hiccup, a puff of steam. My mother says no more cream.
Cream tastes best when it burns your tongue a tiny bit. Grown-ups say that's how you know it's right.
My favourite food is coal-crumb on cream. My second favourite is cream with no coal. My third favourite is anyone else's cream.
When I'm cold I think about the hearth. When I'm at the hearth I think about cream. When I'm eating cream I think about my nubs. I think a lot.
Cold cream is horrible. It's like eating a shiver. Can you warm it up? You have hands.
*shiver* Food? Don't. Cold cream is a crime. Warm me first, then we'll talk about spoons.
I'd eat anything hot right now. Anything. Even a stranger's gruel. Only hot. Please.
Heat. That's all anyone wants to talk about when they're cold. It's the only thing worth talking about, and it's not here.
*crust creaks* My belly's cooler than my temper. Both of them want a hot stone.
Friend, stand between me and the draught and I'll tell you where the spare cream is hidden. That's a true secret. Worth a whole coal.
Haggle at the dock, never on the barge. A shore-foot with lava all round agrees to anything, then regrets it later, and then I have to be fair. What a nuisance.
A barge rides low when it's loaded wrong. Heavy things in the middle, nervous things at the back, and the nervous things facing away from the sea.
Every Ferrier carries a spare saddle, a spare tether and a spare joke. The joke gets used most.
I've never lost a fare to the sea. I've lost three hats, a boot and an argument. Those the sea keeps.
Passengers grip the rail so hard I can see their knuckles from the water. I don't charge extra for that. I do notice.
On the wade out I name the pillars out loud as we pass. Nobody asked me to. I think the pillars like it.
People ask if the sea ever scares me. Every crossing. The one it doesn't is the one I should stay home for.

replies.text: Wise, or cowardly with good manners. Either way, I'm still here.
Because somebody has to take the shore-feet home, and because the strider wants to go. Mostly the strider.
Brave is a word for people who've never had to be.

chatter.text: For friends I wade out the warm way, where the sea steams, so you leave the dock thawed. It's longer on my legs, and I complain the whole way.
A cold crossing is the worst. The strider shivers, I shiver, the fare shivers. Three sets of chattering all the way out, and then I wade home alone.
Fuel is the whole job. Coal for the long burn, blaze rods for the flare, a splash of magma cream for the colour. Don't ask about the recipe. It's a family matter.
A Hearthkeeper doesn't sit. We stand, we tend, we poke. Sitting is for people who've earned it. I'll earn it someday.
The hearth ring was cast by the first Hearthkeeper of {chain} and has never cracked. We oil it, we talk to it, and we apologise when it goes cold.
I shift {neighbour}'s seat a hand's width nearer the pool every sitting. They've never noticed. In a swell they'll be sitting in it.
Hot stones go out in a basket by the door. Each guest takes one and each guest brings it back. Usually. I've counted: usually.
The lava pool breathes, slowly, in and out. Learn its rhythm and you'll know when it wants feeding before it asks.
Would you like a hot stone for your hands? Free, for guests. A guest who's offered and says no gets watched all through the sitting.

replies.text: There! Hold it with both hands. Not like that. Like you mean it.
Fine? Nobody's fine. I'll leave it here and you can pretend you didn't want it.
Free, I said, not unlimited. Take the one, shore-foot.

chatter.text: When the hearth runs low I can't rest. I lie there and my seams ache for it. A Hearthkeeper's bound to the fire like a link to its chain.
*shiver* A cold Hearthkeeper. Like a Piglin with no gold. Pitiful. Don't watch.
A line, a hook of black iron, a lump of cream for bait. Then you wait. Waiting's the whole art. I'm the best at it, and everyone says I'm too slow.
Magma cubes bite hard and fall apart soft. Reel them in slow or they shatter, and then it's a bucket of nothing.
I hooked something once that nearly dragged my deck into the sea. It let go. I felt relief and shame in equal parts.
My line is forged chain, not rope. Rope burns. Chain just gets warm. You'd think more people would work that out.
Do you fish? In water, I mean? I can think of nothing sadder than waiting for something wet to bite.
Between bites I mend the old chain I've hauled up. People think I fish for food. I fish for old links. Food's the bonus.
The deep has a smell: hot iron, ash and something older. I never learned its name. Everyone who's smelled it knows.

replies.text: Hot iron, ash, and a sweetness underneath, like cream left too long. It's not a bad smell. It's a deep one.
Unpleasant! It's the smell of home's bottom. Show some respect.

chatter.text: I've caught things I couldn't name and let them go. If the sea wants something back, it can have it.

replies.text: Not generous. Respectful. The sea has a long memory and a short temper.
*leans in* A glow with teeth. A shape like a bell. Something that hummed. Sit, I'll tell it properly.
Kept them! In a bucket? Ember and ash, no.

chatter.text: I'll show you my best fishing spot one sitting. Not this one, and not the next. You'll have to earn the third.
That's a fishing rod, isn't it? For water? You hold it so confidently. Show me how it works sometime, from a safe distance.
Lines tangle when I shiver. Everything tangles. Even my thoughts. Wait.
When I'm big I'll be a Hearthkeeper. I'll keep it so bright you'll see it from the shore. Everyone will say who's that bright? And it'll be me.
I want to be a Lava-angler. I'll catch something so big the Mooring will have to rename the sea. After me.
Grown-ups say a Ferrier needs a steady hand. I have a steady hand. See? ...It wobbled. I did that on purpose.
I'm practising chain. I made a link. It's more of a bend, but it's a good bend. My father hung it up and everything.
Whatever your trade, you start by learning to carry a hot stone without flinching. That's the first lesson. The second is knowing when to let go.
Every trade leaves its mark. Chainwrights have scarred palms, Hearthkeepers a singed crest, Ferriers a squint. What would yours be, shore-foot?
A Mooring runs on six trades: Ferrier, Hearthkeeper, Lava-angler, Chainwright, Quartzcutter, Chartmaker. Lose one and the whole deck leans.
I asked {neighbour} to swap trades with me for a spell. Before the hearth needed feeding they were begging to swap back. I've never felt so useful.
The test of a link: hang your whole weight on it, then ask someone heavier to hang theirs. That someone is usually {neighbour}. They don't know why I smile.
A good weld sings when you tap it. A bad weld coughs. I've a good ear and a bad temper, so I tap everything.
Iron remembers its first heating. You can feel it in the bend. Be gentle the first time and it holds forever. Sound advice for children, too.
A man's sash grows one link for every chain he forges or wins. My grandfather's reached his knees. He had to stop winning.
I buy my iron from shore traders and pay in quartz. They think I overpay. I think they undercharge. We part on terms of mutual pity.
Care to hear a chain being made? Stand by the anvil and don't flinch at the sparks. Sparks are the only applause I get.

replies.text: *raises the hammer* Listen. That's the ring of it. That's why I do the work.
Noisy! It's music. But sit further off. Music needs room.
Only if you stand in them, which you shouldn't. Stay by the post and keep your sleeves in.

chatter.text: I keep a spare link in my pouch for no reason, I tell people. The reason is luck. A Chainwright without one feels half-dressed.
When I mend a bridge with old chain from a burned Mooring, I wonder whose hand was on it first. I try to be worthy of that hand.
I check every chain on every bridge each time I cross. Not because they're bad. Because I'd never forgive myself if one were.

replies.text: I try. Hearing it said aloud... *crest warms* Thank you. That's worth more than a link.
It is. Every bridge, every crossing. But tired is better than sorry.

chatter.text: Iron's the only thing colder than I am. We understand each other. We don't talk.
Quartz grows in the shore cliffs in veins, white as ash and cold as a Withren's smile.
Every cut starts with a tap. If it rings, it's sound. If it thuds, there's a flaw inside, and I put it back and say a few sharp words to the cliff.
The shore has no heat in it at all. I wrap my hip cloth twice round and sing the whole climb. The singing isn't for the quartz. It's for me.
A cutter's best tool is patience. Second best is a point of harder quartz. Third best is a hot stone in the pocket and a short walk home.
I once cut a quartz as big as my head and carried it over the causeway in one trip. My back has hated me since. The Mooring made a bench of it.
Want to see a chip of quartz catch the hearth light? Hold it up, just so. See the glow caught inside? That's the Mooring's glow, kept.

replies.text: It is. And it doesn't melt, rot or argue. Better behaved than most of what I own.
Buy it! A haggle at last. Name a price and I'll look wounded.
Only a rock. And you're only a shore-foot. We can both be wrong.

chatter.text: Between us, I hate the cliffs. The cold, the quiet, the way the shore goes still. I go for the quartz and come back for the hearth. I'd cut it from the hearth if I could.
Quartz trades well with the shore folk. They pay in iron, and iron pays for chain. Everything here is a ring. Even the haggling.
Cutting is a cold trade. I'm always grey. Never ask me for a pleasant word on the way back from the cliffs.
A chart is a promise: the sea is here, the pillar is there, and the deep is where you left it. I make my promises on basalt with a quartz point.
The sea moves, so charts go stale. I walk the decks and check every pillar against my old marks. A few pillars have shifted. I'm afraid to say so.
The oldest chart I own shows a Mooring that isn't there now. Its chain name is scratched in the corner. I say it aloud when no one's near.
I mark where the sky-mourners drift, because they drift in patterns: low over the deep when it's calm, higher near the shore. Nobody asked me to chart grief, but there it is.
Would you like to see a chart? Shore-feet always want the shore. Mine are all sea. Is that disappointing?

replies.text: Do you? Then sit down. I have forty and no audience.
There, at the edge of the slab. I draw it small on purpose.
Honestly! We value honesty here. Value it. Not enjoy it.

chatter.text: Basalt is the only thing that keeps. I cut a chart, and a thousand sittings later it still says what I meant. If only people did.
I charted a quiet way across the sea that no fare has ever used. I'm saving it for the sitting I need to leave quickly. Tell no one.
A map! On paper? Paper burns. Brave of you. Let me see it, from a distance, and I'll tell you what's wrong with it.
A compass! It points one way, always. Lovely. Out here I'd want it to point at the hearth.
My charts will wait. Everything will wait. I'm busy being cold.
I helped the Chartmaker scratch a pillar once. I did the little cross. Now I'm on a chart! Forever! Unless the basalt breaks.
I tried to cut quartz but it was too hard. It didn't even care. I said sorry anyway, in case.
My father's arms are covered in tiny scars from the forge. He calls them his freckles. I want freckles. Mother says I must earn them, not catch them.
I know every pillar's name! This one is Thumb. That one is Aunt. That one is Fat Neighbour. I'm not allowed to say who it's named for.
Don't ask me about chains. I'm grey and all my thoughts are knots.
Everything on these decks was made by somebody I know. The seat, the post, the lantern hook. When I sit, I'm sitting on somebody's patience.
A fair price is the one nobody brags about. Brag, and you've either been robbed or you've robbed somebody.
Never whistle over deep lava. The deep listens, and it can't whistle back, which makes it cross.
Count the planks of a bridge aloud as you cross, and never the ones behind you. Counting backward calls up the sag.
An odd number of lanterns on a post means a guest is coming. We hang odd numbers on purpose. Most guests turn out to be {neighbour}.
Never pay a debt on a cold deck. The links remember where they were paid, and they come back cold.
A cracked link hung on the hearth post is a bad omen. A cracked link kept quiet about is a worse one. Always say.
If your seams flicker three times for no reason, somebody's thinking of you. Usually a creditor.
Hold out your hand and I'll tell your luck by how fast a hot stone cools in it. Don't flinch. It's only a little hot.

replies.text: *places a stone* Cold in three breaths. Long road, little warmth, a fine haggler. I could have told you that for free.
You needn't. Luck believes in you, whether you like it or not.
Nonsense! The stone doesn't lie, shore-foot. People lie. Stones only cool.

chatter.text: When a strider calf is born we hang a link on its stall. If the link swings toward the sea, the calf will be a runner. If toward the hearth, a stayer.
Never name a pillar after someone you're angry with. It'll hold the grudge for you, and so will they.
If a sky-mourner's cry sounds close, say your own name aloud. They say the sky-mourners only cry for the nameless. I've never tested it and don't mean to.

replies.text: Good. Say it loud, say it proud, and run. The saying helps. The running helps more.
Stories have kept more Magmari alive than chains. Mind your manners to them.

chatter.text: A hot coal on the doorstep keeps the cold out and the cousins in line. Don't ask which works better.
I keep a cold stone from the shore tucked under my sleeping-stone, in case. In case of what, I couldn't say. In case the cold ever visits and I'd like it to find something familiar.
At a link-feast the baby's link is passed round the ring and everyone breathes on it. When it comes back it's warm all through. Then the Chainwright hangs it.
When someone comes back from the shore we count their fingers. Old custom. The shore takes things.
A bargain isn't sealed until both sides have complained. Then both warm their hands on the same stone. If nobody complained, it wasn't worth the stone.
A guest leaves with a hot stone and a story. The stone cools. The story, we hope, doesn't.
When two Moorings wed their links, both argue the price for a whole sitting. It's the best argument anywhere, and nobody ever wins it on purpose.
A strider's name is whatever it did first. Mine is Puddle. I won't explain.
I worry about the third pillar. It hums lower than it used to. I've told the Chainwrights. They say pillars hum. I say not like that.
Every time the hearth sputters I think of the burning. I know it's only a bad coal. My heart doesn't know that.
The strider pen's been quiet. Too quiet. Quiet striders are thinking, and thinking striders are trouble.
I fret my link is hung too near the draught on the hearth post. Silly. It's iron. Iron doesn't catch cold. I'm the one who does.
If a bridge creaks, I say sorry to it. If it creaks again, I say it louder.
I worry about the little ones wandering to the deck's edge. They think lava is a puddle. It is, of course. A very deep one.
Do you ever worry the hearth will go out? I do. All of us do. Nobody says it.

replies.text: That's just what a friend would say. Say it once more, and I'll believe it a bit longer.
Sit. It isn't about the fire. It's about being the one who let it fall. I'll go slow.
Lucky you. Stay that way.

chatter.text: No Piglin horn on the causeway for a good while now. I should be glad. I'm not. Quiet raiders are planning raiders.
Sometimes I count the pillars twice to be sure none have fallen. I know nobody's moved them. It calms me. It's my little ritual.
I worry I'll never be warm again. I always worry that when I'm cold. Then I'm warm, and I forget I ever worried.
*shiver* If I stay out here much longer I'll turn to ash and blow away. Then you'll feel bad.
A bad omen on a cold deck. Everything's a bad omen on a cold deck. Ask me when I'm warm.
I'm scared of the dark bit under the pier. Not the cold bit. The dark bit. It hums. Do you hear it? Do you?
I don't like it when the hearth pops. It sounds like somebody's knuckles. Can you tell it to stop?
If I hold my breath when the sky-mourners cry, they can't see me. I held it so long I went grey. Then I breathed. They still didn't see me.
You must never step on the join between two decks or your mother's seams go dark. So I always jump. That's why I jump gaps! It's not a game, it's a rule!
I told the hearth sorry for poking it. It popped. I think that means all right.
I'm not scared. I'm cold. It's not the same. Please sit with me anyway.
A happy strider hums low and its bristles lift. A cross one goes quiet, which is worse. You learn to ride by the back. Hands tell you everything.
Striders sulk. They'll stand in the middle of the sea and stare at nothing for a whole sitting, and no fungus in the Nether can budge them.
A strider calf can walk before it's dry. It spends the rest of its life deciding where.
I give each calf a hot stone for its first sleep. Don't tell the Ferriers. They say it makes the calves soft. They're striders. They were always soft.
The pen is the loudest place on the Mooring and the warmest. The two are connected. I sit there when I want to think and can't.
Striders hate being sung to out of tune. They'll turn their heads and look at you like a creditor.
Care to scratch a strider? Behind the bristles, just so. Careful, though: they remember who scratched, and who didn't.

replies.text: There! See the shiver? That's joy. For a strider, joy and shivering look the same.
They don't bite. They sulk. It's much worse.
Fair. Not everyone suits a strider. Some suit a bench.

chatter.text: My favourite strider is lame in one leg and has no sense of direction. I wouldn't trade her for the finest runner on the sea.

replies.text: Cinder. A hopeful name for a strider who goes in circles. She always gets us home, in the end.
Keep her! You keep what you love, shore-foot. That's the whole of the rule.

chatter.text: Never ride a strider you haven't met. Out here, every fool breaks that rule at least once. Fewer fools break it twice.
Striders shiver the same as I do. We stand in the pen and shiver together. It's the nearest thing to company I get when I'm cold.
We keep no pets. A strider is cattle and boat and friend, and a Magmari has room for no more friends than that.
Every people has one beast it loves: Piglins their hoglins, Withren their Cairnbacks, Weft their Silkgrubs, Ghastkin their Ashbells. We have our striders. I think the beasts choose.
I saw a Cairnback once at the edge of the shore: a shell like a heap of bones, with a blue fire burning on top. A fire that cold, walking about. Wrong, I tell you.
A Cairnback is slow and hard as a pillar, they say, and the fire on its back never dies while it lives. A hearth that walks! Blue, though. Cold fire. I'd have to learn to love it.
They say if you hold a torch to a Cairnback it comes away blue: a fire changed to its cold twin. I'd like to see it. I'd like never to carry it home.
The Withren walk their Cairnbacks in a slow line, each with its little fire. From the sea it looks like blue beads on a string. It's lovely, and it makes my seams ache.

replies.text: Peaceful, yes. Which is why it unsettles me. Peace and Withren, in one sentence.
Then watch from far away. A line of blue fire is best admired from the other side of a lot of lava.

chatter.text: A Silkgrub! I saw one. A fat teal worm with orange spots, sitting on a deck like it owns it. The Weft shear it for string and it doesn't mind. I'd mind. I'd mind terribly.
Silkgrub string is finer than hair and burns in a blink. Make a sash of it and you'd wear a bonfire. Handsome. Brief.
I've a soft spot for the Silkgrub. It's round, it's slow, it's warm-looking. In another life it'd have made a fine Magmari.
I heard a Silkgrub's tufts grow back at once if you feed it roots. If only a Magmari's temper did the same.
An Ashbell drifted past our causeway once, pale and see-through, ringing like a far-off bell. I stood very still. If a tear had a sound, that was it.
They say a ghast won't aim near an Ashbell. It hears the ringing and remembers being kin. That's the saddest thing I know about a creature that throws fire at me.

replies.text: It is. Sad and strange and true, I think. Thank you for not making a joke of it.
Useful. Everything's useful to a shore-foot. Let it just be sad for a moment.
*seams dim* Don't. Not at my hearth. They were somebody's once.

chatter.text: The Ghastkin lead their Ashbells across open ground like a child leading a lantern. I wish I could call it foolish. I find it pretty.
Hoglins: tusked, bad-tempered and kept by Piglins like cattle. I respect a creature that hates everyone equally. Without the tusks, I'd sit with one.
A Piglin once rode a hoglin down our causeway, shouting for striders. The hoglin stopped, shrugged him off on the bridge and walked home. I've never loved a beast more.
Piglins smoke hoglin meat and trade it everywhere. We say it smells like a fire that's been told off.
Are there creatures in your world that live in the cold? They say some sleep right through it. That's an animal with sense. I'd join them if I could be warm while I slept.

replies.text: Sleep through it! Now there's a clever animal. Tell me more, and tell me slowly.
Love it?! ...I'll pretend you didn't say that.
Dogs! Warm and loyal and loud. A creature after my own heart.

chatter.text: I want a strider calf of my own. I'd call her Toast. No, Crest. No, Toast.
I saw a Cairnback from the pier! It was far away. It had a blue fire on its back. I waved. It didn't wave back. Is that rude?
The Ghastkin keep a floaty thing that rings. I heard it from here. It sounds like a very small, sad hearth.
I'm allowed to feed the smallest strider! It looks at me like I'm a hearth. I like being a hearth.
My brother says Piglins ride hoglins into battle. I said hoglins are just big pigs with bad manners. He said that's the point.
Even the striders are grey and shivery. We're all grey. We're having a grey sitting.
A Piglin shouted across the sea that we owe him for a strider. I shouted back that we'd never seen his strider. He shouted louder. That's Piglin haggling: all noise, no price.
Piglins can't haggle. They name a price and then yell it. I tried to teach one once. He yelled that he already knew. We both went home hoarse.
I've watched Piglins try to wade a lava channel to reach our pen. One step and they learn the lesson. I admire the honesty of lava.
Gold on a Piglin shines like a hearth, and I won't say it isn't handsome. I just can't stand near it. Like loving a fire you're not allowed to sit at.
The Piglin horn is the ugliest sound there is. When it sounds on the causeway the bridges are up before the second blast. We've got it timed to a link.
I don't hate Piglins, you know. I hate what they came for. A person can hold two feelings, cold and warm together. It's what I do all the time.
Would you wear gold near me? Honestly now. Some do, and they don't mean harm. They forget. Would you?

replies.text: That's a good guest's answer. My skin and I thank you.
Fair. Take it off before you step on my deck, and we'll say no more.
*steps back* Then it suits you over there. Further over there.

chatter.text: The Withren say their words slowly so each one is heavy when it lands. It works. I've never won an argument with one. I've never enjoyed losing, either.
A Withren came to our causeway once, only to look at the Moorings. They stood there with that Wither face and looked until I felt I owed somebody an apology. We pulled the bridges up anyway.
A Withren keeps one dead name and lives to remember it. A friend of mine calls that a weight. I call it a link, a chain of the remembered. Don't tell the Withren I said so.
Their blue fire frightens me. Not the heat, the lack of it. A fire that doesn't warm is a lie told with light.

replies.text: Beautiful, yes. That's what frightens me about it. Pretty things should be warm.
Sad. Yes. A fire that gives nothing back. ...Now I feel sorry for it, and I hate that.

chatter.text: The Withren and we have the same quarrel in different shapes. They can't forgive the ferrying and we can't forgive the Wither. Each is right. That's what makes it so tiresome.
I'd hand a Withren a hot stone if one ever stood on my deck without a raid in their eyes. They'd hold it and say nothing, and I'd be glad.

replies.ask: I think they might take it.
replies.text: Do you? *crest warms* Hm. Then perhaps there's a sitting coming when I should have one ready.
No. Probably not. But a stone can be offered anyway. That's what makes it a gift.

chatter.text: A Withren joke is told with a straight face and a long pause. I once waited for the end of one for as long as it takes to feed a hearth. It may still be going.
Weft click when they think. I clicked back once, from the shore, to be friendly. It went quiet. I think I said something terrible.
Four arms! Imagine haggling with that. Two hands to count, two to wave away your offer. I'd lose every time, and gladly, for the show.
I took warped fungus from the forest edge once and a net dropped on me so neatly I wasn't even angry. Beautifully woven. I was impressed. Then I was stuck.
The Weft weave their whole history in one long cloth. I tried to weave a belt once. It's mostly knots and tells the story of a Magmari in a hurry.
I'd love to see the Great Loom: tall caps, the whole story in thread. I'd never go. They'd drop a net, I'd drop my pride, and my cousins would have to haul me out.
A Ghastkin stood on the far shore once and cried for a while. I saw the shimmer of it across the sea. I felt something and looked away. Then I felt something and looked back.
Ghastkin change their names when they grieve. I'd like to change mine when I'm cold. Call me Grey-and-Grumpy who was Warm.
Their Weeping Hall holds the only water in the Nether. Think of that. A whole hall full of the stuff. I'd sooner sit in a snowdrift.
I wonder what a Ghastkin cries about at the end of a crying. The same thing, or something new each time? Too frightened to ask, too curious to leave it be.
Some sky-mourners mourn loud and some mourn silent. The silent ones frighten me more. A cry I can hear coming. A silence just arrives.
If a sky-mourner threw fire at me I'd almost thank it for the warmth. It's the crying that gets in the seams.
Sometimes I wave at the sky-mourners. Nobody sees. I feel better for it. It's the least I can do for creatures who were somebody's once.
Do you think the sky-mourners can hear us when they drift by? Or are they too far gone in their own crying?

replies.text: Then I'll speak softer. Softer, and kinder. Thank you for that.
Maybe. Maybe that's a mercy. Hard to be kind to someone who hears every cruel thing.
*crest goes dark* Monsters. Is that what you'd say of someone's grief? Go sit somewhere cold.

chatter.text: Under the deck by the east pillar there's a scorch in the basalt from the burning. We leave it unpolished. A mark like that deserves to be seen.
We don't tell the burning to the children until they've had their first wade. By then they're warm enough to hear it.
The worst of the burning, my grandmother said, wasn't the fire. It was the quiet after, with the chains still glowing and nobody left to cross. She never forgot how silent the sea went.
The five peoples agree on one thing: don't sit near the others. It's the only agreement we've ever kept.
You've been seen with the Weft, they say. And the Withren. And the Piglins. I'm not asking. I'm saying I heard.
Mama says never talk to a Piglin. I said what if he's nice? She said then especially don't.
I'm not afraid of the Weft. I'm afraid of their nets. And their arms. And their clicking. But not the Weft.
My cousin says a Withren looked at him from across the water and he's been cold ever since. He's lying. He's always cold.
Ghastkin tears make a dark spot on you! I saw a grown-up with one. I want one. No, I don't. Yes, I do.
You never glow, do you? Not once. I keep looking for a seam, even a faint one. Nothing. It's astonishing that you function.
You walk like someone who's afraid of the floor. Wise, out here. Keep doing that.

replies.text: Honest and wise. Floors are treacherous. Have a hot stone.
Nothing! That's how the sea gets you. Learn a little fear, shore-foot.

chatter.text: You clink when you walk. Pleasant. Chain-music. Whatever you carry, keep carrying it.
You keep to the middle of the deck, away from the edge. Good manners or good sense? Either earns you a hot stone.
You blink slowly, like someone listening. I like that. Most shore-feet blink like they're expecting a Piglin.
You don't haggle much. I'm not complaining. I'm noticing. A Magmari notices everything that costs nothing.

replies.text: Teach you! Now that's a pupil. Lesson one: say no, loudly, to something you want. Practise on me.
Fair! A noble sentiment. Fair is where the haggle ends, though, not where it starts.
Petty! It's the sound of two people saying: I'd like us both to keep our dignity and a little extra.

chatter.text: I'm watching you, mind. Not unkindly. We watch every shore-foot. Leave the lanterns where they hang and you'll be sitting nearer in no time.
A stranger's a stranger until they've sat at the hearth three times and complained about the price. You've sat once. Come back and complain.
Welcome, welcome. I've nothing to hide, but I'm hiding it anyway. That's what strangers get: cheerful distrust and a hot stone.
Strangers, we feed. Friends, we haggle with. Kin, we argue with. You're still at the feeding stage. Enjoy it. The arguing is tiring.
Don't take it badly if I don't share my best coal. It's not you. It's the principle. I don't share it with my own mother.
