You're getting warmer, you know. Not in the body. In the way you talk. I've started saving you the good seat without thinking.
You've changed since you first came: quieter feet, softer voice. It's what the hearth does to a visitor. I'm rather pleased with it.
Do you know I've started watching for you from the pier? I tell myself I'm checking the bridges. I'm not.
Kin, I forget sometimes that you're a shore-foot. Then you shiver, I remember, and I'm sorry for you all over again.
A blaze rod in the hand! I could weep. Not weep. Water. Never mind. I could be moved.
Blaze powder! That's the sweet stuff. A pinch on my cream and you'd have my good will for a long sitting.
A fire charge in your hand, shore-foot. Lovely. Could I hold it? Just for a breath. I'll give it back. Probably.
A saddle! You've been talking to a Ferrier. They give those out like compliments: sparingly, and with a catch.
Iron! Good, honest iron. I'll give you three links of chain for that, and you'll feel robbed, and that's the system working.
Fungus on a stick! The cleverest thing in the Nether. Point it and a strider follows. Point it at me and I'd follow, too.
Quartz! Clean and white. A Quartzcutter would give up a hearth seat for that. Careful you don't drop it. It's worth more than my last argument.
A lantern! Hold it up. I like to see how the light sits on your face. ...Nice. A bit pale. But nice.
What's that round thing with a hand that won't stop moving? In here it just spins. Poor thing. It's trying to tell you something that isn't true in the Nether.
Do I smell snow on you? Oh. Oh no. You're carrying it, in a pocket! I'll be sitting over there, thank you very much.
A tear in your pack. I can feel the damp from here. Stay a few paces back, would you? For my seams and your friendship.
You've coal on you. I can feel the warmth from here. Not a word. I'm standing near you for no reason at all.
A magma block in your pack. You're a walking hearth. Don't mind me. I'm just here, standing close, for no reason.
Nether wart. The Withren grow that. How did you come by it? You haven't been sitting at their fires, have you? Never mind. It's a fine wart.
Crying obsidian. It weeps purple. I find it unnerving. I also find it quite pretty. I am torn, and I resent being torn.
That skull in your pack. Put it away. Further away. I'll ask nothing. I'm only saying: put it away.

replies.text: Thank you. Hidden, and far from every sea of ours. We've burned once already.
Then lose it again. Quickly. Somewhere with no lava anywhere near.
*seams flare* A trophy! Of what? Of the thing that burned my grandmother's home? Out of my sight.

chatter.text: Riddle: what's hotter than a hearth, colder than a Withren's smile, and sits in every Magmari's pouch?

replies.text: A debt! You're quick. Nobody gets it the first time. I owe you a coal. See? Funny.
A debt. Hot to carry, cold to ignore. I thought it was clever.
It's my only riddle. Be kind to it.

chatter.text: How many Magmari does it take to light a hearth? None. We're already lit. ...That's the whole joke. It's the best I've got.
A Piglin, a Withren and a Weft walk up to a Mooring. We pull the bridge up. That's the end. I find it very funny.
What do you call a Magmari in the cold? Late for the hearth.
I asked a strider how it was. It sulked. I asked again and it sulked louder. Best conversation I've had in ages.
I'm not going to tell you my second-best joke. Not until you've laughed at my first. That's the price. Bring a good laugh.
I'm saving up links to buy a strider. I have two. A strider costs forty. I'm going to haggle it down to two.

replies.text: You will?! Bring a coal. I'm bringing a bent link. We'll make a good fight of it.
Really?! Mine?! ...Thank you! I'll never spend it. I'll spend it on a strider.
That's why I haggle. Haggling makes forty into two. It's arithmetic.

chatter.text: My grandmother says I haggle like a Piglin: loud and with no plan. I said thank you. She said it wasn't a compliment. I said I'm still saying thank you.
I built a hearth out of pebbles. It doesn't get hot. I'm going to ask a Hearthkeeper how to make it work. They'll say no. I'll ask again.
You're tall! Taller than my father, nearly. Are you tall everywhere? Are your knees tall?
I pretend the pillars are giants and the bridges are their arms. I wave at them. They never wave back. They're rude giants.
I counted all the lanterns on the hearth post. Nine. Then I counted again and there were eight. Now I'm scared of the lantern thief.

replies.text: Yes! You take the left bridge and I'll take the right. I'll be the one hiding.
I did NOT. I counted twice. Well. Once. Well. I think.

chatter.text: My nubs tickle when somebody says something funny. They're tickling now. Did you say something funny? I think you did.
I'm supposed to be asleep. I'm not. I'm sneaking. The sneaking is going great.
I want to see the shore. Mama says it's boring, grey and cold. That's the best thing I ever heard. Boring, grey and cold!
Do you have a Mooring? Do you have a chain? What's your chain? Is it a good chain? Is it better than ours?
Grown-ups say mind the edge so much that I think the Edge is a person. So I say hello, Edge, every time I pass.
I made up a song about cream. It has three words. Cream, cream, cream. Do you want to hear it? ...Cream, cream, cream.

replies.text: Cream, cream, cream! I made a second verse. It's also cream.
*nubs droop* It's not silly. It's very serious cream.

chatter.text: Do you sleep in the cold? Do your dreams go grey? Mine only go grey when I forget my stone.
The big ones say you come from the shore. I said you're my friend. Then they stopped saying it. I think I won.
I'm not allowed near the forge. But the forge is allowed near me. It sends sparks. That's practically an invitation.
When I grow up I'm going to haggle with a Weft. I'll bring a net. We'll see who's patient then.
I licked a cold stone to see what the shore tastes like. It tastes like ash and being told off.
I like it when you visit. Everyone else is busy being tall.
I drew you on the wall with a bit of charcoal. You've got no seams in the picture. I couldn't work out where to put them.
Don't tell anyone I like you best. They'll want to share. I want you for myself. For one more sitting.
Mama says you're kin now. I asked what kin is. She said family, but on purpose. I like that. Family on purpose.
Everyone in {village} has a link on the hearth post. Mine's the little one with the bend. It's the best link.
{neighbour} gave me a coal for being quiet. I was quiet for ages. Then I told everyone. Then they took it back.
{neighbour} says I talk too much. I said I'm not talking too much, I'm talking enough. They said that's what too much means.
*brrr* I'm going grey from the toes. Or the nubs. Do toes go grey first, or nubs? I think it's the toes. Wait. Nubs.
I can't feel my tail. Is it still there? Check. Please check.
Cold makes my voice small. Can you hear me? ...Can you hear me? I'm using my biggest small voice.
Can you hold my hand? It's a bit cold. You're a bit cold. We'll be cold together. It's better than cold alone.

replies.text: *grabs your hand* Oh! Your hand is so flat. I like it. Now we're cold together, and that makes us a team.
*pouts* Busy. Busy is a grown-up word for no.

chatter.text: I want my mama. And the hearth. And my mama in the hearth.

replies.text: Yes! Walk slow. I've got short legs and they're cold.
You promise? ...All right. I'll wait. I'm good at waiting. Sort of.
*lip trembles, nubs droop* I'm not whining. I'm... I'm cold.

chatter.text: I went grey and nobody noticed. I'm very good at grey. I'm too good. Notice me!
I'm glad it's you who found me. You're not warm, but you're kind. That's almost the same thing.
I'm going to stand very still so the cold can't find me. ...It found me.
I was in the hearth a whole breath and I still got cold. How? How do I get cold when I was in the hearth?
My aunt hung my ridge loops herself when I came of age. Every loop she cursed the iron. I wear them like her curses: proudly.
My chest wrap has a pattern passed down my line: three bars and a hook. The hook means haggle hard. I take that one seriously.

replies.text: Thank you. My grandmother wove the first one and swore at every thread. You can still see where.
Have one! They're for family. Earn the hook first, shore-foot. Then we'll see.

chatter.text: Aunts hand down the loops. When I've forged enough of my own I'll hang them on a girl of my own. If I ever stop arguing with the Chainwrights.
The single tall ridge is a man's pride and his burden. It catches every draught. I've sat with a headache from my own crest.
A chain sash is a boast with a weight on it. Mine's short. I don't call it short. I call it exactly the right length.
{village} has stood on these pillars longer than anyone remembers. I like that. Nobody remembers it being built. It's as if the sea grew us.
The best view in {village} is from the end of the long pier. You can see the next Mooring's lights, little lonely sparks. I wave at them. They don't wave back.
Every Mooring thinks its own hearth is the best. Ours is. I'd say so to the other Moorings' faces, and sometimes have.
When I leave {village} for a crossing I look back from the dock once. Just once. More than once and the sea thinks you've changed your mind.
In {chain} no link is hung without a feast. Even a bent one. Even a link nobody wanted. Especially a link nobody wanted.
Out here I have a hot stone, a strider and a great deal of crying overhead. It's not a bad life. It's a lonely one, and I'm glad of a face.
I miss the hearth every breath. I keep a pouch of ash from home and sniff it when it gets bad. Don't laugh.
A Magmari alone on the sea should keep two things: a length of chain and a plan. Mine is the chain.
When I was small I got lost in the steam between the pillars. I was sure I'd never find my way back. Then I heard my mother haggling, loud as a vent, and followed that home.
The first thing I ever forged was a ring, to give to someone. I never gave it. It's in my pouch. Don't ask who. ...All right. Ask. I might tell you.

replies.text: *crest warms* A friend, a long time ago. It's gone cold, like a good many things. But I still carry it.
...Thank you. That was the right answer. I'll tell you someday, when I've grown a little braver.
Buy it! It isn't for sale. Some things aren't, even in a Mooring of hagglers.

chatter.text: I once crossed the whole sea without a hearth to rest at. By the end I was grey from crest to tail and singing to my strider to stay awake. The strider was kinder than anyone.
I wade near the deep so people will think I'm brave. I'm not. I'm only stubborn, and a little more frightened each time.

replies.ask: That is a kind of bravery.
replies.text: Is it? ...Is it. Doing the thing while it frightens you. Hm. I'll think on that by the hearth.
I know. That's what makes me keep doing it.

chatter.text: There's a corner of the hearth ring where I always sit. It was my father's. When I sit there I haggle for him. I win less than he did.
I'm glad you came to our Mooring. Not for the coal, not for the gossip. You sit when you're told and listen when you're told a story. That's rarer than you'd think.
Here's what I never tell: I haggle so much because I fear silence. A bargain keeps people talking. Without it we'd have to say what we mean.

replies.text: *long breath, seams glow brighter* ...Thank you. That's all it takes, really. Someone who doesn't mind.
Do you? Then you've done what a good guest does. Sat with the truth and not argued it.
*seams dim* Silly. Perhaps. I shouldn't have said. Forget it.

chatter.text: Kin means I can say this: I was afraid of you at first. Not of your cold. Of what shore-feet bring. You brought your stone back to the basket. I haven't forgotten.
If the Mooring ever has to move, I'll tell you where first. Not the Piglins, not the Withren, not the others. You first. Don't make me regret saying that.
I hang a coal on my link whenever something good happens. It's half black with them. The last one was for meeting you. Don't read into it. Read into it a little.
Don't linger. Strangers get no sympathy from me when I'm grey. I'd say it nicer if I weren't frozen.
Cold makes me honest. I don't want to talk. Come back when I'm bright and I'll pretend I was polite.
I'm fond of you, truly, but not at this moment. Give me a breath by the hearth and I'll be fond again.
Sit beside me and say nothing. Silence is the only warm thing left.
*creak* If I stop talking, it isn't rudeness. It's my jaw.
*shiver* Cold on the inside is worse than cold on the outside. I'm both. I'm winning.
Friend, if I don't make it back to the hearth, tell {neighbour} they were right about the draught. They'll be unbearable.
I'm making a list of warm things in my head. Hearth, cream, stone, a good argument. Ask me for the rest when I've thawed.
Grey. Slow. Grumpy. In that order. I'm at the second. Run.
You're the shore-foot who came back, aren't you? I said you would. Not out loud. To the hearth. It said nothing, which means I was right.
I set a hot stone aside for you last time. It's cold now, naturally. But the thought was warm.
Ask me about the price of coal. Go on. It's my favourite thing to be annoyed about, and nobody asks any more.

replies.text: Outrageous! Three links a lump, and a lump isn't what it was. Smaller, greyer, more ash. I'd tell the sea if it listened.
Everywhere! Finally someone who understands the suffering.
Don't care! In my Mooring! Say that near the hearth and see who sits next to you.

chatter.text: I lent {neighbour} a link last time we spoke. They've since lent it to someone else, with interest. I'm proud and annoyed in equal parts.
I tell {neighbour} they make a loud argument. I don't tell them they make a good one. Let them wonder.
If I'm ever lost on the sea, send {neighbour} to find me. They'd find me just to say they told me so.
{neighbour} claims the deepest wade of anyone in {village}. I claim the deepest wade of anyone anywhere. We keep it between ourselves.
{neighbour} is at their best when something goes wrong. Bridge creaks, they hum. Hearth sputters, they sing. Hard to like, impossible to be without.
Warm is a feeling, hot is a fact, and cold is an opinion. Everybody has one, and nobody likes anyone else's.
Sometimes the whole ring goes quiet, every one of us staring into the flame and none of us haggling. It doesn't happen often. It's worth the wait.
Magma cream cools to a skin if you leave it. The skin is the best part. Children fight over it. Grown-ups pretend not to.
A coal-crumb keeps well in a pocket. I always carry one. If I'm stranded I can eat it, or burn it, or just hold it and feel rich.
Don't count your links aloud near the hearth. It overhears, and next time you've fewer. I don't know how it works. I just don't count aloud.
A new lantern should be lit from the coal of an old one, never from fresh flame. A new light needs an old memory.
Make a wish on a hot stone? Hold it, close your eyes, tell the stone. If it cools fast the wish was small. If slowly, big. Go on.

replies.ask: I wish for a warm Mooring.
replies.text: *smiles* A big one. It's staying warm a long while in your hands. Good wish.
Wise. A wish shared is a wish spent.
*steps back* Gold! To a Magmari! The stone's gone cold. It doesn't like you any more.

chatter.text: My sash grows heavier each sitting. Not the iron. The wins. Every win's a weight. One of these times I'll need a second back.
Striders can smell warped fungus from a whole sea away. If only they could smell a good price.
I've named every strider in the pen after a creditor. It makes feeding them much more satisfying.
A Weft once traded me a spool of cord for a pot of cream, at the forest edge. I still don't know who won. The cord burned. The pot's still warm. So, me?
I'm told shore-feet have a thing called a sense of humour. Where do you keep it? In a pocket? In the knee? I'd like to take a look.
A strider walks into a Mooring. Nobody laughs. It's a strider. It walks in whenever it likes.
You've a way of looking at the lava, shore-foot, as if you want to ask it something. Ask. It won't answer. But I will. I'm cleverer.

replies.text: *eyes close, seams brighten* Like being held by someone who isn't afraid of you. That's the best I can say.
...Sometimes. Mostly warm, and warm covers most things.
Bored! In the lava? You may as well ask a hearth if it's tired of burning.

chatter.text: I think you'd make a decent Ferrier. You don't flinch at the edge. Keep that up and I'll take you on as a deckhand. Unpaid, but with cream.
If the hearth ever goes out, you're to sit with me. Not because you can warm me. Because you'll know what to say.
Whoever invented cold should have to sit in it. I'd supervise. From the hearth.
*shiver* My thoughts are slow. Everything's slow. Even my anger is slow. It'll arrive after you've left.
I made a chain with exactly one link. It's very strong. It's the strongest chain with one link in the whole Mooring.
Papa says haggling is a conversation with a price on it. I'm going to have lots of conversations. Starting with this one. How much for the conversation?

replies.text: Free! Nobody's ever said free to me. It tastes odd. I like it.
A coal! Good. A coal's fair. I accept. I'll tell Papa I haggled.
That's what Papa says too. It's sad when it's true.

chatter.text: I fell in a puddle of cream. I'm so happy I could pop.
The hearth is so far away. It's right there, but it's so far.
My ridge loops grow heavier each sitting. Not the iron. The wins. One of these times I'll have to hang the extras on a cousin.
My loops chime when I win and clank when I lose. I've learned to haggle quietly, so nobody hears the clank.
Every loop on my ridges was a haggle. The crooked one was a haggle I lost on purpose, to a child. It's my favourite.

lines: I'm {name} {epithet}. {name} is my own; the rest belongs to the Mooring. Everyone here is of {chain}, and proud of it.
{name}, of {chain}, before you ask. Out here a name's half yours and half your Mooring's, like a bridge between two decks.
A {job}, a haggler, a hearth-sitter, and {name} {epithet}. In that order, mostly.

lines.text: Our names come from the fire: ash words, rock words, the sound lava makes when it bubbles. What's yours from?

replies.text: Family! Good. Then you're half your kin, same as us. We'll get on.
A careful one. Fine. I'll call you shore-foot until you warm up.

lines.text: {name}. Cold. Ask me again by the fire.
My mother named me in the hush after a hard spit of lava. She says I answered it. I say I only hiccuped.
Everyone gets a hearth-name too, a nickname. Mine's Two-Links. I once haggled for two links and walked away with six. Don't ask the Ferrier how.
We count in swells and haggles won. I won't tell you my count. It only makes {neighbour} jealous.

lines: I'm someone's cousin, someone's creditor and someone's rival. That's most of a life on a Mooring, and I wouldn't swap it.

lines.text: A name for a name is the fair trade. I gave you mine. What do the shore-feet call you?

replies.text: Then I'll earn it. Give me time and one good haggle.
It will, for now. It's what I'd have called you anyway.
Ha! Spoken like a Piglin. Careful, that sort of talk gets the bridges pulled up.

lines.text: I wanted to chart the sea once. My lines wandered all over the basalt, so they handed me a chain to hold instead. Best thing that ever happened to me.
My link on the hearth post has a nick in it. My mother says that's where I laughed too hard in the forge. I say it's where she dropped me.
I'm the third {name} of {chain}. The first was a Chainwright, the second a coward, the third a haggler. I'll let you guess which of us is best.
A friend should know the worst of me: I once sold a cracked link to a stranger, then spent a long while buying it back. I haggle fairly now. Mostly.
I'm {name}. That's all you get until you've sat by the fire. House rules. A name is free, the rest is trade.
I'm the pier's keeper, the barge's boss and the strider's second favourite. She likes her fungus better than me, and she's right.
I keep the fire, so everyone knows me and nobody does. They only ever see my back, bending to the hearth.
Look out over the deep for the one standing perfectly still with a chain in hand, thinking about cream. That's me, {name}.
My hands are always black, so at the hearth I tuck them under the seat. Nobody believes a Chainwright can be shy. I can.
I'm the grey one, always grey, from the shore stone. You should see me after a long sit by the hearth. Nearly handsome.
I turn the sea into lines. Ask me where anything is and I'll point. Ask me where I left my own chart and I'll point at the wrong place.
At {village} I'm the one whose voice carries across three decks. They call it a gift. {neighbour} calls it a warning.
I'm between Moorings just now, but the chain goes with you, the way the cold does. {name} {epithet}, wherever I wade.

lines: Short temper, soft heart, a chain never quite finished. That's me, {name} {epithet}. Pleased to haggle.

lines.text: {name}. Cold. Next question, preferably one that comes with a coal.
*teeth chatter* {name} {epithet}. That's all I've got until I thaw. Ask me again warm.
This is {village}. Decks on basalt pillars, two blocks over the sea, every pillar rooted in the sea floor. Wade between them, or take the chain bridges.
The hearth's in the middle: a lava pool in a magma ring, seats all round, chain posts with lanterns. Every bridge leads to it. That's on purpose.
The domed huts are homes, with doorways three blocks high because we hate ducking. The strider pen's past the decks, the ferry dock at the end of the long pier.
If there's shore near enough, we build a causeway to it. For guests. And trade. Mostly trade.

replies.text: Kind and clever. Guests bring coal, coal makes us kind. It goes round.
*grins* That's what the chain bridges are for. Pull them up, throw a little magma. Raiders cool off quickly.

lines.text: No Mooring for me just now. I wade where the sea's warm and rest where the lava's deep. I'll find a hearth again soon enough.
A Mooring's a hearth with decks round it, and I'm on the wrong deck. Too far. Ask me later.
Our pillars have names. The one under the hearth is called Mother. If she ever cracked, we'd all know within a breath.
No deck belongs to one person here. Every deck belongs to the chain. Try telling that to {neighbour} when a good seat is going.
Three rules on the decks: no water, no gold, no Piglins on the bridges. We keep the first two politely and the third with magma.
When the sea swells, the bridges ring against their posts, a dozen chimes at once. I can't rest without it now.
Every lantern on the chain posts is lit from the hearth's own flame, carried by hand. We never strike new fire. Only the old kind.
Our huts have a seam of magma through the floor, banked low. Step on it barefoot and you'll know why shore-feet don't live here.
Past the pier the sea goes bright and deep. When it's quiet you can see old chain from the burned Moorings glowing on the floor below.
The pier has a rail, and only the pier. It isn't for us. It's for guests who forget the sea won't hold them.
Other Moorings carry other chains: the Singing Link, the Sunken Anchor, the Warm Ember. We trade gossip by Ferrier and never admit it's gossip.
The strider pen is my favourite corner. Warm, noisy, smelling of fungus. Everyone pretends to hate the smell, and everyone goes there when they're sad.
Take the third seat from the lantern post. The heat falls just right there, and the gossip falls even better.
There's a hollow in the pillar under the hearth where we keep our oldest chain, the first forged after the burning. Kin may lay a hand on it. Gently.
You're welcome on every deck but the pen walk when a calf is born. The mothers there are touchier than I am. Hard to believe, I know.
I walk the ring forty times between feedings, checking every seat and every stone. If a Mooring has a heartbeat, I'm the one who counts it.
The pier is the best deck, and not only because it's mine. You see the whole Mooring and the whole sea from the end of it. Don't tell the Hearthkeeper.
Every bridge here was forged by my hands, my mother's, or hers. I can tell which in the dark. Hold a rail and I'll tell you whose.
I fish off the deepest deck. The best bites come over the spot where a burned Mooring stood. Odd, isn't it? Even the sea remembers.
The best view of the Mooring is from the shore: every lantern scattered on the black lava like coals on a hearth stone. Almost worth the cold.
I've drawn this Mooring so often my hand does it alone. Round decks, straight bridges, and a hearth that wobbles differently every time. Even in stone it won't sit still.
I'm far from any Mooring, so you can't see my place. Picture decks, bridges, a hearth. Picture it warmer than here.
If you could add one thing to our Mooring, what would it be? Say a bigger hearth and I'm your friend forever.

replies.text: Wise shore-foot. Hearth first, friends after.
*recoils* I take it back. All of it. Out.
A coal garden! Rows of it, ripening! You may stay.

lines.text: *shiver* It's a good Mooring. It would be better if the nearest seat wasn't three bridges away.
Decks, bridges, hearth. Mostly hearth. Go away so I can sit.

lines: Always. Lava's the only place we're properly warm. Step off it and the heat leaks out of us like smoke from a vent.
When we cool, our seams go dark and our crust goes the colour of old ash. Then we get slow. Then grumpy. Then grumpier.

lines.text: Cold's the worst thing there is. Worse than Piglins. Worse than a bad haggle. You don't feel it like we do, do you?

replies.text: Lucky. Or unlucky. You'll never know how good a hearth feels, then.
*shudders* Don't. I don't want to know what snow is. I want to forget you said it.
Now that's a friend talking. Bring it, and I'll take back half the rude things I've said about shore-feet.

lines.text: *shiver* Why am I cold? Because I'm here talking to you instead of sitting in the hearth. Make it quick.
Cold. Yes. Thank you for noticing. Now do something about it.
It starts in the toes, then the knees, a slow ache that climbs the legs like a swell coming in. By the time it reaches my crest I'm not fit to talk to.

lines: You can read how cold we are by the seams. Orange is fine. Red is chilly. Dark is trouble. Ash-grey is a Magmari who needs a stone in each hand.
When someone comes in grey, the Hearthkeeper hands over a hot stone, and you hold it in both hands. It feels like being forgiven for something.

lines.text: The worst of it is the quiet. When you're truly cold, even your own crackling stops. Silence is how the cold sounds.

lines: The little ones cool twice as fast as we do, so every parent keeps a pocket of vine sewn into the hip cloth with a coal in it. Ours have never once gone grey on us. Almost never.
Go grey for too long and you stop being able to move. We call it the long stillness. It's why nobody goes to the shore alone.

lines.text: A Quartzcutter of ours stayed on the shore too long once and went grey to the crest. We carried her home like a statue. She says she heard us arguing about the fare the whole way.
Some shore-feet try to haggle with a grey Magmari, thinking we'll give things away. We remember. Magmari memories don't cool.

lines: Shore-feet make their own heat inside, all the time, and walk about as if it's nothing. It frightens me a little, how much fire you carry and never notice.
The cure is simple: a stone in each hand, a coal in the lap, a friend on each side. The friends are the hardest part to find.

lines.text: I keep a coal sewn into a pocket of chain in my hip cloth, always. Don't tell the others. They'd all want one, and there isn't enough coal.
You've seen me grey and stood by me anyway. Most would've walked off. I never said thank you for that, so there it is.
I'm never cold. It's the only job where that's true, and I won't tell you why I took it. Well. I will. It's the hearth.
The wade is easy, my legs are in lava all the way. It's the shore end of the pier that bites. Stand there too long and you'll see my face turn the colour of old ash.
Half my line runs down through the lava, and the warmth climbs it like a rumour. Hold my line a while and you'll feel it creeping up.
I forge to keep warm. Anvil, fire, hammer. By the time a chain has cooled I'm on the next. Warm is a habit, and a good one.
On the shore I take a hot stone in each fist and cut quartz with my elbows. It's a bad way to work, and the only way I know.
Charting the shore edges is the worst. Cliffs, quartz, no lava anywhere. I draw them fast and badly, then fix them by the hearth.
Out here with no hearth I carry my own: a coal-stone in my hip cloth. Every wild one does. Please don't touch the cloth.
A friend is a kind of fire, we say here. Are you a friend?

replies.text: Hope warms. That's a start.
Honest. Come back when you are, and I'll save you a seat.

lines.text: *teeth rattle* Yes. Always. Right now especially. Move along.

topics.ask: How do you walk on lava?
lines: Same way you walk on stone, only nicer. Long legs, bent back, slow steps. Lava's thick. It holds you up if you let it.
The trick is not to hurry. Hurry on lava and you splash, and splashing wastes good heat.
You can't, before you ask. Don't try. We'd have to fish you out, and there'd be nothing left to fish.

lines.text: When I was small, my mother walked me out into the deep lava and let go. I floated. I cried, then I laughed. That's how we all learn.

replies.text: It was. Warmest I've ever been. Every one of us remembers their first wade.
*seams flicker* Why would you go in water? Why would anyone? Never mind. Don't tell me.

lines.text: Lava's warm. Lava's lovely. I'm standing on cold stone instead. You see my problem.

lines: Lava has moods. Thick and slow near the pillars where it's cooler, thin and quick in the deep. You learn to read it by colour.
Orange is slow, yellow is quick, and white is for fools. Learn that before you learn your own name.

lines.text: Our tails keep us steady: short, heavy, swung like a chain-weight. A Magmari without a tail walks like a shore-foot on a bridge.

lines: Where lava cools, a crust forms. The young ones step on crusts and fall through. Mind the crust, and never trust a pretty dark patch.
Never stop in the deep to argue. Standing still, you sink to your knees. You can haggle on the move, and we do.
When a crowd of us wades, we go in a line, and the one at the front breaks the skin of the sea. We take turns. Nobody's quite fair about whose turn it is.

lines.text: Everyone leaves a wake, a little dent that fills in behind you. Children watch their wakes. It's the first thing they ever draw.

lines: Magma cubes bounce through the shallows. Like children, only less polite.
Striders walk it too, but they've no sense. They go where the fungus is. We go where sense is, which is the same place with better manners.

lines.text: A sky-mourner crying overhead is the one thing that unsteadies me out there. One drop, and I'd lose a step. Lose a step and you lose the hearth.
I wade beside the barge as far as the open sea. A loaded barge leans on you like a door. First lesson: don't lean on the strider. She notices.
I rarely wade. The hearth is my sea. I walk its ring a thousand times and never get my feet wet. Dry, I mean. Never get my feet cold.
I wade out waist deep and stand. Standing's the hard part. All that wanting to wander off.
I test each new chain by wading with it round my waist. If it holds against the pull of the sea, it holds anything.
I walk on stone more than lava, and my legs hate me for it. Long legs were made for wading, not climbing cliffs.
I measure the sea in strides: a long one, a slow one, a stride and a half where the lava is thin. My charts are made of my knees.
Out alone I go by colour, slow, always facing the shore I came from. I've never been lost, only patient.
I'll teach you to read lava by its colour some time, just so you know where not to fall. You'd get one lesson, then a long silence.
When I was small I fell through a crust, and my mother hauled me out by the crest. I still have the dent. Kin may touch it.

lines: Rub magma cream on your skin and you could wade a little. Not far, not well, but it makes a fine joke at the hearth.

lines.text: Want to see me wade out and back? It's a poor show, but I'm proud.

replies.text: *wades out and back* There! Not a ripple. ...A small ripple.
Kind. Foolish, but kind. I'll be back before you finish worrying.

lines.text: Do you think you could walk it if you tried?

replies.text: Then you'd float at least. For a bit.
Sensible. The bravest thing a shore-foot can do is not try.

lines.text: Walking lava? Yes. Doing it now? No. I'm cold and my legs are two stiff pillars.

lines: Cattle and boats both. They carry us, they carry our goods, and they hardly ever complain.
We keep them in a pen past the decks: open lava with a ring walk round it. One's always saddled, in case someone needs to be somewhere.
They go purple and shivery off the lava, same as us. You can't help loving a creature that suffers the way you do.
Warped fungus on a stick and they'll go where you point. The fungus comes from the Weft's forest, which the Weft don't like. Not our fault striders have tastes.

lines.text: A strider's the best friend a Magmari has, after the hearth. Have you ever ridden one?

replies.text: Then find a Ferrier and haggle hard. They love it.
*crest flares* Eat? We eat with them, not them! Shame on you.

lines.text: Every calf is named by a child, and the whole Mooring pretends to vote on it. The child always wins. That's how we got a strider called Big Slow.
Old Plod is the eldest in our pen. He hasn't hurried since before my mother was born, and he's never missed a meal.

lines: Lay a hand on a strider's back when she's off the lava and you'll feel her shiver, a low hum. Warm her and the hum climbs.
Low hum means she's content. A high hum means a sky-mourner is near. A stuttering hum means someone's been at the fungus.
A strider will follow a fungus on a stick to the end of the sea. It's the only honest bargain I know.

lines.text: When a calf is born in the deep and wobbles out onto the pen crust, the whole Mooring comes to watch. Nobody works. Everybody cries a little.

lines: A saddle is the oldest courtesy we have. A Magmari who gives you one is telling you that you may go anywhere on our sea.
A Piglin on a stolen strider looks like a sack of gold on a sulking boat. The strider always gets herself home, sooner or later.
Striders won't cross under a sky-mourner's shadow. They stop, hum, and turn back. I've never won an argument with one about it.

lines.text: My strider and I have crossed the sea more times than I can count. She'd say I talk too much. She'd say it with her face.
I measure every strider myself for her harness: chain and vine, never pinching. They hold grudges a long time. So do I.
Striders follow my line and steal the bait. I forgive them. They're hungry. They're always hungry.
A strider carries my cut quartz home, load after load. I thank her with a hot stone on her back. She'd rather have fungus, but it's the thought.
A cold strider will sometimes sidle up to the hearth on her own. I let her. She never says thank you, but she hums.
Come to the pen and I'll show you which one's mine. Don't bring gold near her. She'd forgive you, but I wouldn't.
Some time I'll name a calf after you. A small one, a loud one, with a crooked leg. You'll hate it and visit it often.
If you had a strider of your own, what would you call her?

replies.text: Warm Feet! Sweet and sad. She'd be proud.
Fungus! She'd answer to it, too!
*gasps* Not on my deck. Never say that word near a strider.

lines.text: Striders have opinions about shore-feet. Mine thinks you smell like stone. Is she right?

replies.text: She says she knew it. She's insufferable when she's right.
She says that's what all of you say. I'm only the messenger.

lines: The oldest Ferriers say a strider remembers every fare. Whenever you cross, she knows your weight and your silence. I believe it.

lines.text: Striders and I are alike: purple, shivering and cross.
I'm the Ferrier. Strider barges across the sea, anywhere the lava goes. Outsiders only. Never one of the other four peoples. Never again.
Every fare's haggled. A shore-foot who pays my first price makes me sad. Go on, try me.

replies.text: Half! Cheek. I like it. Three quarters, and we'll shake on it. Not hands. Too hot for you.
Fine? It's never fine. It's an opening. You've hurt my feelings a little.

lines.text: Out on the open sea it's just me, the strider and the sky-mourners crying overhead. Keep your head low and your chain short.
I keep the hearth. The lava pool stays full, the magma ring stays bright, and whoever's coldest sits nearest. That's the whole job, and it's everything.
A hearth can't go dark. Not ever. When the Moorings burned, the Hearthkeepers carried the fire out across the sea in their bare hands.
Guests are my work too. Anyone who comes in cold gets a seat and a hot stone to hold before anyone asks their business.
Lava-angler. I drop a chain line into the deep and see what bites. Little magma cubes, mostly. They render down into good cream.
Half of what I pull up is old chain from the Moorings that burned. I keep every link. Somebody forged it.
Best catch I ever had was a lantern, still lit, up from the sea floor. Nobody believes me. Do you?

replies.text: Ha! A believer. Sit down, then. I'll tell you about the anchor next.
That's what everyone says. That's why it was the best catch.

lines.text: Chainwright. I forge the chain for the bridges, the posts, the sashes and the loops. Every link I make, I test with my own weight.
Rope burns. Vine burns. Iron just glows a little and keeps holding. That's why the whole Mooring hangs on my work.
I cut quartz from the shore cliffs. White, hard, never melts, never rots. The best thing there is for haggling.
Quartzcutting is cold work, out on the shore, far from the sea. I come back grey every time. That's why my prices are what they are.
I chart the sea: where the lava runs deep, where the pillars stand, where the sky-mourners like to drift. Scratched on basalt with a quartz point.
Paper burns. Hide burns. Basalt keeps. Some of my charts are older than my grandmother, and show Moorings that aren't there any more.
The fare's always warped fungus. The strider eats the fare, and a strider with no fungus is a sulking boat. Fair is fair.
I dab magma cream on every shore-foot before cast-off. It fireproofs you for the crossing. Some of you yelp. Most of you thank me after.
No crossing is ever quiet. Sky-mourners crying, the barge creaking, and you asking if we're nearly there before we've left the pier. Lovely, all of it. Almost.
For my friends there's no fare. I'd call it a secret, but I do it for exactly three people, and one of them is the Hearthkeeper's mother.
Every Hearthkeeper learns by holding one live coal in bare hands, as long as they can bear. It's how we remember who carried the fire out. Mine lasted longer than my teacher's.
When someone comes in grey and grumpy, I leave them be. Hot stone in the lap, nothing said, until their seams brighten. Then I ask what's wrong. It's seldom the cold.
My worst dream is the hearth going dark while I blink. I haven't blinked properly in years.
A sky-mourner's shadow stops the bites. I always know one is near before the striders do.
I once caught a cube the size of a hut. It took my hip cloth and my dignity, and I let it keep both.
The strangest thing I ever hooked was an anchor: iron, big as a hut, still chained to a pillar that isn't there. I think a Mooring tried to hold on. I think it still is.
Want to try the line? Hold it steady and don't pull until it pulls you.

replies.text: *hands it over* Easy now. It's alive down there. ...Don't drop it.
Probably. Everyone does. It's no shame, just a waste of a good line.

lines.text: Heat, hammer, bend, close, test with my weight. Five steps and every one of them warm. That's why I chose the trade.
A bridge chain is thick as my wrist, a sash chain thin as a vine. Between the two are fifty kinds, each with a name. I know them all.
My hands remember the weight of every chain I've made. When one breaks, I feel it in my wrists, wherever I am.
Quartz splits along its grain with one tap, if you tap it right. Tap it wrong and you've got dust and a lesson.
I love quartz and it doesn't love me back. Cold and honest, like a good haggle.
I keep my best piece in a vine pocket against my chest. It warms from me but never warms to me. A friend may hold it. Don't drop it. It's older than the Mooring.
A chart is never done. It only stops when the sea moves. Then I scratch a new one beside it and keep both.
I have a chart of a burned Mooring, every deck and bridge, drawn from memory by my grandmother's mother. We don't know if it's right. We keep it anyway.
The charts I trust least are the ones Ferriers carry. They add improvements: a shorter way, a safer way. The sea has its own opinion.

lines: Everyone here works at one thing and haggles at all the rest. A Mooring is one long, friendly argument.

lines.text: Work? Sitting by the fire. I'm told I'm excellent at it.
Barge is ready. I'm not. Fare's open, but so am I to excuses. Come back warm.

lines: Because chain holds. Bridges, lanterns, strider tethers, our sashes and loops. Everything here that matters hangs on a chain.
Every Mooring has a chain name, and ours is {chain}. When one of us is born, a link is forged and hung on the hearth post.

lines.text: A chain's only as strong as its worst link. So we don't hide our worst links. We fix them.

replies.text: Chainwright talk, but it holds for kin as well as iron.
It is! Hard work, fair pay. Speaking of pay...

lines.text: Keep coming back and in time we might forge a link for you. Don't ask the price. It isn't for sale.
There's a link for you on our hearth post now. You're of {chain}, kin. A chain doesn't let go.
Iron is rare on our sea, so we remelt. A bridge chain may once have been a lantern chain, and before that a tether. Every link is older than we are.
When a bargain is struck we tap links together: one clink for fair, two for generous, none for a lie. Shore-feet shake hands. We clink, because our hands would burn you.

lines: Being of {chain} means: if I fall, it holds me. If I fail, it answers for me. Choose your chain carefully, if you're ever given the choice.
Two haggling Magmari will sometimes hold each end of a chain and pull. The first to let go has lost. We call it taking up the slack, and I have never once let go.

lines.text: A good chain sings when it's pulled right, one clear note. Our Chainwrights tune the bridges like instruments. Ours hums a lovely note in the swell.

lines: Gold is soft. It bends, it melts, it runs. Iron is honest. That's the whole quarrel between us and the Piglins, in a breath.

lines.text: A weak link is forgiven once. The second time it goes back in the melt, and nobody holds a grudge against the iron. It gets another chance as something else.
At a child's first wade we hang a short chain round their middle, with one big link. A toy, and their first promise. Most lose it by the next feeding.
When one of us is too old to wade, their link is hung on the bridge to the pier, so everyone crossing touches it. Nobody says anything. We just touch it.
The hearth post is a bundle of every link ever forged here, thick as a pillar. I polish it whenever the fire's fed, and I know every name on it.
The barge is chained to the dock by a knot-link only I can undo. I tie it fresh every time and tell it where we're going.
My line is chain, one link to a finger's length. I feel each one tick over the lip of the deck. I can count a catch before it bites.
A flaw in a link looks like a hair, a thin dark line. I find them with my thumbnail. I'd sooner find one than be told I'm good.
I draw chain bridges as little loops, one loop to ten links. I once drew one too short, and the Mooring rebuilt it to match. Nobody tells the builders.
Quartz won't make chain, but it makes linkstones for the ends. I set one in every bridge-end. Pretty, and it keeps the end from slipping.
Hold this link. Feel the weight? That's one promise. A bridge is a thousand of them.
I'm saving a good piece of old iron for your link. It's from a bridge that held in the burning. It's been waiting for the right shore-foot.
Your link on the hearth post is the newest. It hasn't a nick yet. Don't worry. Everyone gets one.
Have you got a link to tap? A bargain isn't struck until the chains agree.

replies.text: *clink* Fair, and sealed. Nice ring to it.
No chain at all? Then you're free to be cheated. Careful.

lines.text: Do you believe a chain can be a promise?

replies.text: So can chains, if they're badly forged. That's why we forge them well. Same goes for promises.
Hm. Perhaps. But iron is why there's a Mooring at all.

lines.text: Chain holds. I don't. Next question, or a coal.

lines: The big pale ones that drift and cry. They saw the Wither, long ago, and they never stopped crying. We keep our heads down when they pass.
Don't hate them. They're sad, that's all. Sad and loud, and they throw fire. The fire we can take. The crying's worse.
Never stand under one. A tear is a little bit of water, and water puts our glow out wherever it lands.

lines.text: Some say the sky-mourners were Ghastkin once, who grieved too long and forgot their hands. Sad, if it's true.

replies.text: Yes. Poor things. That's the right thing to say, and you said it.
Ask from far off, then. And don't bring any of their tears back here.

lines: They throw fire when startled. Big, slow balls you can watch coming for a full breath. Watching is the mistake. Step aside, and watch from there.
Their cry has two voices: low when they come close, high when they go. We say 'hear them going' when a worry is over. It's all the comfort they give.

lines.text: Children play at sky-mourner: one cries and drifts, the rest hide under the pier. The Ferrier hates the game. The Ferrier also cheats at it.
My grandmother once sat beside a sky-mourner hanging at a pillar, a coal in each hand. Not one tear fell on her. She called it the saddest, warmest company she ever kept.
They saw the Wither and never stopped. I think that's what grief is: not a feeling but a place you're stuck in. Don't tell the Ghastkin I said so.
When one is coming we move the striders under the pier, bank the hearth low and talk softly. Don't shout. They hear shouting as someone else crying.

lines: Piglins shoot at them for sport and then complain of the fire that comes back. They're never quite clever enough to be embarrassed.

lines.text: A tear on the deck leaves a dark ring that takes ages to dry. There's one by my door we all step around. Respect, we say. Respect for the damp, really.
Sometimes they hum as they pass, very soft, and the striders hum back. It's a shy thing, like someone calling from the next room.
On the open sea, one pass overhead is enough to make me hold my breath and the barge both. I let the strider hum. She knows what to do.
They drift over the deep where the burned Moorings stood. Some say they're looking for the pillars. I think they're looking for each other.
I mark their regular routes with a little hook on the chart. Mostly they go over the burned Moorings. Mostly they go back.
When one's near I bank the hearth low and dim the posts nearest the sea. A dark Mooring is a quiet one, and quiet is all they ask.
A good chain rings when it's struck. When a mourner is near I don't strike one, not a tap. It feels rude to ring near someone crying.
Out on the shore alone I meet them more than most. I put down my tool and stand still till they've gone. It seems only polite.
It's all right to like them a little, from a distance. I do. Don't spread it about.
I'll tell you something I haven't told {neighbour}. I wept near one once. No tear fell, and I don't know which of us stopped first.
Out here alone I hear them more. At a Mooring the hearth's noise covers them. In the wild they fill the whole sea.
If one came down and spoke to you, what would you say?

replies.text: That's what my grandmother said. Strange. I think you'd have got on.
Sensible. They don't mean harm, but they don't mean much of anything either.

lines.text: What do you think they cry for?

replies.text: Maybe. They watched them burn. So did we.
Everything. That's the answer that gets you a seat by the hearth.

lines.text: Sky-mourners. Floating. Crying. Don't start me. I'm too cold to be gentle about it.

lines: The Piglins wanted the gold under the valleys, and the valleys are a long way over the sea. Somebody had to carry them. We were paid to.

lines.text: We ferried. Barge after barge of Piglins and axes, and the fares were very good. Don't look at me like that.

replies.text: *seams dim* We carried fares. I know what they were. I don't need a shore-foot to tell me.
We knew. We just never thought it would come back across the sea to us. Thank you for saying it, though.
Long ago. Yes. The lava forgets. Magmari don't, quite.

lines: They paid in what wouldn't melt on us: chain, quartz, coal. Piglins hate paying in anything but gold. They paid anyway. They wanted that crossing.

lines.text: The Withren blame us for carrying the Piglins. We blame them for the Wither. Neither side will ever stop, so we just don't talk.
We never ferry the other peoples now. Not Piglins, not Withren, not Weft, not Ghastkin. Shore-feet like you, yes. Never them again.
The war-bands paid before they boarded, and our Ferriers counted the coal and not the faces. That's what some of us can't forgive: we counted the coal.
A war-band on a barge was the worst haggle there is. They shouted the whole crossing, tried to pay in gold, sulked when we refused, then paid in chain. Nobody listened to anybody.

lines: We lashed striders in teams to haul the war-barges, a dozen to a barge. The sea has never been so crowded, and never so loud.

lines.text: Before the war our bridges were never lifted. Any traveller crossed freely. The war taught us bridges. It's the one thing we kept from it.
Our little ones skip to a counting rhyme from those years. It counts barges, bands and links. They don't know what it counts. I haven't the heart to tell them.

lines: To the Piglins we were a ferry. To us they were a river of gold, and the river had teeth. We didn't see the teeth until it was too late.

lines.text: The Weft took the dead from both shores. We carried the living, they carried off the dead. Between us we served the same war from both ends.
The Withren made three of their own into the thing that burned us. I don't forgive it. But I won't pretend they didn't give themselves. Even a Magmari can say that, at the right hearth.
Every Ferrier swears at their first crossing: no war-bands, no raiders, no captains with a hoard in mind. It's carved under the pier. I read it each time I tie up.
The hearth is where the war fares were counted. Now it's where we count what they cost us. Same stones, different arithmetic.
The chain we forged in those years was barge chain, heavy and ugly. I won't make that kind now. Bridge chain, lantern chain, sash chain: chain for holding things together.
I find axe heads on the sea floor where barges overturned at the last crossing. I hang them in my hut as warnings. Visitors think they're trophies.
Quartz was the fare we valued most. The Piglins dug it, we carried it. A trade as well as a war, if you're feeling generous. I'm not.
I keep my family's charts of the war crossings face down on the shelf. Every line on them is a barge that went one way and came back different.
My great-grandfather ferried a war-band over and came home with a pack of quartz and a cough. He never ferried again. He said it was the ash. It wasn't.
Mind who you say this to. At some hearths the war is a quiet subject, at others a loud one. At ours it's quiet.

lines: Nobody can tell you when the war began. Everyone knows when it ended, because the sea went dark.

lines.text: We keep the oldest barge-chain coiled in the pier house. Nobody meant it as a memorial. It's just too heavy to move. I think that's what memorials are.
Would you have taken the fare, if you'd been a Ferrier then?

replies.text: Honest. That's rarer than courage. Thank you.
Easy to say from a deck that isn't burning. I'd like to think you're right.

lines.text: Do you think the Piglins are sorry?

replies.text: No. A sorry Piglin is a Piglin who's out of gold.
Some might. I've never met one. Perhaps I'm not looking.

lines.text: War. Piglins. Gold. No. I'm too cold to be sorry properly.

lines: The Withren made a Wither. The Last Answer, they call it. It burned the bastions, then it came for every Mooring that had carried the Piglins over.
My grandmother's grandmother stood in the deep lava and watched our decks go up. The chains glowed white and held to the very last.
We built again on the old pillars wherever the basalt was sound. Under these decks there's stone older than the burning.

lines.text: Your kind make Withers now, they say. Three skulls of the Hollowed and up it comes. Is that true, shore-foot?

replies.text: Not you. Good. Keep it that way, and keep it far from any sea of ours.
*crest goes dark* Then do it nowhere near the lava. We've burned once already.

lines.text: It didn't burn like a hearth. It burned like a rot: the fires went out one by one, as if something pinched the wicks, and the decks went black from the top down.

lines: Every hearth that stands was relit from a coal carried out of the burning. Different hands, one fire. That's why we call our fires cousins.

lines.text: After, the chains cooled in odd shapes, twisted round the pillars like roots. We left them. There's one on the east pillar still: a chain that held a bridge that held a family.

lines: People ask if we hate the Withren. We don't hate them. We cool toward them. It's worse.

lines.text: My grandmother's grandmother's sash came through white-hot and cooled with a hook at one end. I wear it when we feed the hearth for the ones we lost.
My mother says the sea stopped singing for a long while after. Then one time the bridges rang again, and she cried and couldn't say why.
*goes very still* That's a Hollowed's skull in your pack. Put it down. Away from the sea. Away from me.
A star from a dead Wither. So someone made one, and someone killed it. I'm glad about the second part.
We keep one seat empty at the hearth and one stone in the ring unlit, for the ones who didn't come out. Don't sit there. Not even as a joke.
The old Ferriers still steer by the burned pillars. They stand black in the sea like sea-marks. It seems wrong, and it works.
The deep over a burned Mooring is full of chain. I pull it up link by link, clean it, and hang it where the light falls. Each link is somebody's handwork.
Chain that held through the burning I keep whole. I never remelt it. To a Chainwright it's holy, and I'd say so aloud if I weren't shy of the word.
On the nearest shore there's a quartz pillar with every burned chain-name cut into it. I carved nine of them. My hands shook on every one.
On my charts a burned Mooring is a ring with a cross through it and its chain-name written small. We have forty. Nobody has ever asked me to draw fewer.
Some time I'll take you to see the black pillars, from a distance. We don't sit near them. We nod, as we would to an elder.

lines: Some chain names are never given again. Nobody has to say which. We all know where the gaps are.

lines.text: They say the Wither didn't hate us. It didn't want anything at all. I don't know which is worse.
Have you ever stood where a burned Mooring stood?

replies.text: Then wait until I'm there to show you. It's better not to see it alone.
From far off is how it should be seen.

lines.text: Do you think it could happen again?

replies.text: Words, but warm ones. Keep them. A promise to a cold sea is still a promise.
Maybe. That's why a Mooring keeps its bridges ready to lift and its hearths ready to carry.

lines.text: Don't. Not the burning. Not while I'm cold. Another time.

lines: I think the sea remembers too. The lava ran darker for a long while after, and even now the calves stop and stare at the black pillars.
Loud, greedy, and dressed in the one thing that melts on our skin. You can't shake hands with a Piglin. Not even if you wanted to.
They raid our pens for striders and ride them off, fat with fungus. We pull the bridges up and throw magma, and they go home shouting.
Gold is everything to them: rank, savings, handshake. To us it's a burn waiting to happen. You can guess how talks go.

lines.text: You wear gold sometimes, don't you? To talk to them. I can smell it on you.

replies.text: Only to get by. Fine. Keep it off my deck, and off my skin.
That's manners. Thank you. My skin thanks you too.

lines: You can smell a Piglin from three decks off: hoglin-grease, soot and gold-polish. I'd know that stink in my sleep.
Their hoglins are the sweetest things they own and the worst-tempered. Same as the Piglins, only the hoglins are honest about it.

lines.text: Their war-horns carry over the lava, three low notes. Our children can mimic it perfectly. We tell them not to.

lines: A Piglin barters by throwing gold and taking whatever falls out. That's not haggling. That's gambling. A Magmari would sooner be hit.

lines.text: I touched a gold ingot on a dare when I was small. It sizzled on my palm and left a bright mark like a coin. Look. I show it to children as a warning.

lines: They come for the striders in threes: one to shout, one to grab, and one to cover the retreat by shouting more.
A Piglin without gold is a dangerous Piglin. A Piglin with gold is an insufferable one. I can't decide which I prefer.

lines.text: I don't hate them. I pity them a bit. They've no hearth to sit at, only a hoard. A hoard doesn't warm you.

lines: Their Brutes bother me most. Big, quiet, axe in hand. A loud Piglin you can haggle with. A quiet one you can't.
Imagine living in the ruin of your own war. That's the Bastions, to me: proud walls burned black and Piglins in them still, shouting at the dark.

lines.text: Piglins hail the barge from the shore sometimes, waving gold. I wave back, which they take for acceptance, and keep going. Best sport on the sea.
No Piglin has ever sat at a Mooring hearth. If one did, I'd give him the lowest seat and the hottest stone. Then I'd watch.
Sometimes I haul Piglin gold up from the deep with chain tongs and drop it on the shore for them to find. I'm not generous. I just don't want it on my deck.
A Piglin once offered me a gold bar for a chain. I made it in iron and wouldn't take the bar. He called it the best chain he'd ever been cheated of.
On the shore I meet Piglin foragers. They stare, I stare, nobody speaks. It's the politest conversation I've had in ages.
I mark Piglin trails on my charts with a little ring. Ferriers swear by them. A ring means: don't land here, whatever the fungus tempts you with.
I'll say this quietly: a Piglin child waved at me from the shore once, and I waved back. Nobody saw. I think about it more than I should.
If a Piglin came to the hearth in peace, what would you do?

replies.text: The lowest and the hottest, with my eye on him. But yes, a seat.
That's the rule. But you said it fast. Hm.

lines.text: Could a Piglin ever learn to be quiet?

replies.text: Ha! You've met them.
Patience. Hm. You've more of that than I do.

lines: They call us cowards for pulling up the bridges. I call it the only sensible conversation we've ever had with them.

lines.text: Piglins. Loud. Gold. Go away.

lines: Grey folk with Wither heads. Polite, quiet, very sure of themselves. They keep the names of their dead, and they made the thing that burned us.
They say we carried the Piglins to their valleys, so we had it coming. We say they made the Wither, so they can keep their sayings.
If Withren raiders come over the causeway, we pull up the chain bridges and throw a little magma. The sea does the rest of the talking.
Their fires burn blue and cold. Soul fire. How can a fire be cold? Only a Withren would want one.
A Withren will tell you the name of someone dead long before your grandmother, and forget yours before you've left the room. Strange priorities.
They never hurry. We hurry and haggle, they shuffle and remember. Buying anything from a Withren is like haggling with a slow stone.

lines.text: They grow nether wart in terraces, red as old embers. A handsome crop. They'd never sell a seed, and I'd never ask. Pride, both ways.
Their Vigils keep a hall for three of their own who gave themselves to that thing. I don't know whether to pity them or be furious. I try to do both.
Their Hollowed wander the old fortresses. I think the Withren are ashamed of them, or terribly sad. With them it's hard to tell. It's all one face.

lines: They carve the names of their dead on a wall and call it family. We hang a link and call it family. I think we mean the same thing and argue about the materials.
Withren raiders come rarely, always silent, always in pairs. It's the silence that rattles us. A Piglin shouts and you know where he is.
Neither of us sleeps in a bed, which is the only thing we've ever agreed on. We've never discussed it, in case it broke.

lines.text: A Withren once told me a joke. I think it was a joke. It was about someone dead. I laughed to be polite and they said thank you.
I've no fare for them and never will. If a Withren walked down my pier I'd tie the barge up tight and go in for a coal. Nothing personal. Entirely personal.
A Withren at the hearth? The fire would go blue out of embarrassment.
Anyone who keeps names that carefully must make good locks. I'd like to see one. I've heard Withren hinges never squeak.
They buy no quartz from us. They prefer bone: white like quartz, but warm to the hand, they say. I say it's sad to find that warm.
I draw their Vigils as small grey circles on the soul-sand edges. Never close. A circle on a chart is a stay-away on the sea.
A Withren once stood at the edge of the causeway and bowed. No raid, no words, only the bow. I don't know what for. I bowed back. I told no one.
What would you say to a Withren, if one came to your hearth?

replies.text: Welcome. Hm. It's the right word. It sticks in my teeth.
That's the Magmari way. I'd say nothing too, and I'd say it loudly.

lines.text: Could a Withren ever be a friend?

replies.text: Then try. Not on my deck first.
No. And that's a pity, isn't it? Don't answer.

lines.text: They say they never forget a name. I've never forgotten a bad haggle. Perhaps we're the same sort of mad.
The Withren are right about one thing: the dead should be remembered. We forget less than we pretend. Don't tell them I said so.

lines: It's hard to haggle with a face that never changes. You can't tell when you've won.

lines.text: Withren. Grey folk. Grey me. I'm done, ask about coal.

lines: Four-armed weavers in the blue forest. Very smug about the arms. They string nets everywhere and click at you while they think.
We fetch warped fungus from their forest for the striders. They call it raiding. We call it gathering. They drop nets on us either way.

lines.text: Their whole forest is fuel, and they won't sell a single stalk. Can you imagine? All that heat, just standing about.

replies.text: *sigh* Yes, yes. It's their home. It's still a lot of fuel.
Would you? A shore-foot haggling with the Weft for us. Now that's a story for the hearth.

lines: They weave their history into one long cloth. Cloth! In the Nether! One stray spark and there goes everything that ever happened.

lines.text: A Weft smells of dye and warm thread, mostly blue. I've never smelled anything so cool and so pleasant. It makes me jealous.

lines: Four arms, and they use all four at once: one to hold, one to pull, one to tie and one to point at your mistake.
One click means they're listening. Two means thinking. Three means they find you amusing. Four means run. A Ferrier told me that, and she ran.

lines.text: I fell into one of their nets once. I was lifted out, set down carefully and handed a thread for my trouble. The thread is still in my hut.
Their fungus caps are as wide as a Mooring deck. Imagine living on top of a tree like a hearth in the sky. I'd go grey on the first rung.

lines: Shroomlights! Light without heat. A lantern with no hearth. What use is a light that doesn't warm you?
They keep fat teal grubs with orange spots on their decks and spin from them. A pet that's also a coat. We'd call that bad luck for the grub.

lines.text: They wove sixty black rows for the Wither's years. Our burned Moorings are in those rows, I'm told, thread by thread. I'd like to see it. I'd never ask.
A Weft handed me a scrap of blue wool, wordless, when I was shivering at the forest edge. I keep it in my hip cloth. Kindness from someone whose fungus I'd been gathering. Quite unfair.
Whenever I near the forest edge the Weft drop a net across the barge. Ferriers carry a knife for it. I carry a smile. It works about as well.
Weft shawls keep the heat in a way I envy. A Weft shawl on a Hearthkeeper would be a fine thing. Don't tell the Weft I said so.
Weft thread makes the finest lines, strong as chain and light as ash. I got mine through a Ferrier's trade. Don't ask what for.
They tie knots I can't undo and can't copy. A Chainwright's life's work is a Weft's idle moment. I hate that, and I admire it.
The shore cliffs by the forest edge are where I cut quartz, and the Weft watch me work, clicking. I think they're grading me. I'd like to know the mark.
Their forest shifts: nets, bridges, rows. My charts of it are out of date as soon as I finish. Weft maps are woven. They update.
They're proud of their forest. I'm proud of my hearth. If we met on the same bridge we'd both talk for a very long time and neither of us would move.
The Weft don't hate us as much as they say. They hate the fungus gathering. I don't think they've ever hated a person. I hope not.
Could you and the Weft ever trade fairly?

replies.text: You? A shore-foot between a Magmari and a four-armed weaver? I'd pay to watch.
Time we have. The Weft have more. They never hurry at anything.

lines.text: What do you think the Weft think of us?

replies.text: Loud! We're warm. There's a difference, though not much of one.
Gatherers. But I'd say the same in their place.

lines.text: Weft. Four arms. Smug. Cold. Done.
Don't talk to me about the forest. It's cold under those caps and I'm colder.

lines: Weepers, out in the Deltas. Soft voices, sad eyes, and their whole village sits round a pool of water. Water. On purpose.
A Ghastkin tear puts out a Magmari's glow wherever it lands. Just one drop, and you've a dark spot that takes ages to come back.
They're not cruel, I'll grant them that. They just cry, and crying near us is like throwing ash on a hearth.

lines.text: I've a dark patch on my shoulder from a Ghastkin tear. I don't show it to many. There. Don't touch it.

replies.text: Not hurt. Cold. A cold that won't leave. Thank you for asking gently.

replies.ask: It's just a bit of water.
replies.text: *steps back* Just water. Just water, it says. Go and stand somewhere else.

lines.text: Pale, tall, soft at the edges, and they drift as much as walk. Like a sky-mourner that learned manners. I try not to stare. I always stare.

lines: When a Ghastkin speaks you lean in, whether you mean to or not. They talk the way a hearth settles. That's the dangerous part: you start to agree.
They take a new name after every great grief and let the old one go. I find that either the saddest or the sanest thing I've heard. I haven't decided.
Everyone wants something from them: Piglins shoot them, the Weft net them, we stay away. They must be lonely, with all that company.

lines.text: Their tears close wounds, I'm told. We could use one now and again. But the price is a dark patch, and that's the price I won't pay.

lines: They say their tears wash away memories. I won't touch a vial. I like my memories, even the cold ones.
I saw a Ghastkin child once, far off, perched on a rail with eyes open wide as hearth-stones. We looked at each other. Neither blinked. I think I lost.

lines.text: They cry once, properly, for each death, and let it go. We sulk for ages and call it dignity. They might be the sensible ones.

lines: I can't hate them. They're kinder than most of us. I just can't get near without going out like a snuffed lantern.

lines.text: If the rule allowed it, I'd carry one across for nothing, quietly, just to hear what a Ghastkin says in the middle of the sea. The rule doesn't allow it. Pity.
I keep a spare hot stone by the door in case a guest comes in with a Ghastkin's tear on them. It won't undo the dark patch, but it helps the shivering.
Nothing of theirs ever washes into my line. They keep their grief in the air. I envy that. Mine goes down into the sea and stays.
Their homes hang from chains, like lanterns, under the cliffs. Good chain, I hope. I'd like to see their work. From a hundred paces.
Their Weeping Hall is quartz. Handsome, I'm told. I'd love to know whose shore it came from. I'd love more not to ask.
I draw the Deltas as a patch of dark with pale marks for the Eaves. The marks always come out larger than I mean them to. Grief looks big on a chart.
I met a Ghastkin once at the edge of the Deltas. She didn't cry. She sat a long way off until my seams brightened, then left. She'll have a new name by now.
My mother told me never to be afraid of weeping. It's wet, she said, but it's honest. She said it very quickly and went to sit by the hearth.
A whole village sitting in silence round a pool. I can't picture it. The nearest I have is the hearth at its lowest, when everyone's gone quiet.
Would you ever accept a Ghastkin's kindness?

replies.text: I think I should too. I'd like to. I'd go grey doing it.
Yes. That's the whole of it, isn't it? Kindness that puts you out.

lines.text: Is it true they forget their own names?

replies.text: New ones. Imagine. All that fresh haggling with the same old face.

replies.ask: They let the old ones go.
replies.text: Let go. That's a hard thing for a Chainwright to hear.

lines.text: Ghastkin. Tears. Wet. Cold. Stop.

lines: My crest nubs! I've got three. When I'm big they'll be tall stone chimneys, and every one will puff.
Press one. Go on. See? Hot! I'm hotter than the grown-ups. They say I'll cool down when I'm older. Boring.
I heard {neighbour} say I'll grow a fourth nub if I eat all my magma cream. I don't believe it, but I'm eating it anyway.

lines.text: They're grey now. Don't look! Little ones go grey quick. I'll be bright again by the hearth.
Mine are the same size as my brother's. He says his are bigger. They're not. I measured with a stick.
When I'm cross they puff little smoke rings! Watch. ...Hm. I'm not cross enough. Say something rude about Wobbles.

lines: Don't bump them! They're tender. They're like a toe, but on top.

lines.text: Orange ones are brave. Red ones are cross. Grey ones are sad. Mine are all three, depending.
Mine will join into one tall ridge when I'm big, like my father's. I practise standing tall. Is it working?
When I'm big I'll have two ridges, like my mother, with chain loops hanging off. I'm saving up loops already. I've got one. It's a bent one.
My mother polishes them with a soft cloth to keep the vents clear. She says it keeps them working. I say it tickles.

lines: After my first wade I get a little chain round my middle. I'm going to wear it on a nub instead. Don't tell.

lines.text: The grown-ups' vents puff when they laugh. Mine puff when I run. So I'm always laughing. Or running.

lines: I counted my nubs. Three. Then I counted again: three. Then once more, just to be sure. Still three. Very reliable.

lines.text: Press one and it hums, if you press it just right. Not like that! Gently. There! Did you hear?
My left nub is the smallest. I call it Pip. Don't tell anybody I named them.

lines: I tried putting a link on one nub and it fell off. I tried a stone and it stuck. Now I've got a stone on my nub and I can't take it off.

lines.text: Grown-ups say my nubs will puff less when I'm older, and I'll be sensible. I don't want to be sensible.
Hold your hand here, not too close. Feel the warm? That's all of me being warm at you.
You can touch them any time. Only you, though. Mother says I'm not to let just anyone. You're not just anyone.
When I'm big and my nubs are chimneys, you can sit on my deck and I'll puff you the first ring. Promise.
Want to see me puff all three at once? I have to hold my breath.

replies.text: *puffs* Did you see?! Three! ...Two and a half.
I'm always careful! Mostly! A bit! Look, I'm puffing!

lines.text: Do you have nubs? You must have a few under your hair.

replies.text: That's so strange. Hair isn't hot. How do you tell how you feel?
Ears! Can you puff with them? No? That's a waste of good ears.

lines.text: They're grey, aren't they? Don't look! They get grey so fast. Your hands are cold but not that cold.
M-my nubs stopped humming. They only do that when I'm c-cold. It's not a good hum.
I'm not grey! I'm just a very dark orange.

lines: Gap-hopping! You jump between the decks without touching the lava. Grown-ups hate it. I don't know why, lava's nice.
Ember-catch. You throw a hot stone and the other one catches it before it cools. I always win. I've got hot hands.
Strider-whisper. You whisper to a strider and see if it does what you say. It never does. That's the game.

lines.text: Want to play? You can't hop gaps, you'd fall in. But you can watch. Watching's a job too.

replies.text: Yay! Watch this! ...Did you see? Did you see that?
That's what everyone says. Grown-ups and shore-feet both.

lines.text: Seat-swap! When the Hearthkeeper's back is turned, everyone changes seats. Whoever's caught last gets the lowest. I'm never last. I'm usually under the seat.
Chain-hide! Someone hides a link and the rest follow the clinks. I always find it. I hear everything.
Sky-mourner! One of us floats over the deck going ooooo and the rest hide under the pier. I'm always the sky-mourner. I'm the best at ooooo.
Bridge-ring! You jump on the chain bridge and make it ring. The Chainwright pretends not to hear. We pretend he's pretending.
Crust-crack! You find a thin crust on the lava and step on it just hard enough to crack but not fall through. I'm not allowed. So I watch the winners.

lines: Pass-the-stone! You pass a hot stone round the circle, and whoever's holding it when it goes cold has to tell a secret. I've told all mine.
We skip to a counting rhyme about barges and links and bands. I don't know what a band is, but I know all the words.
Wobbles-ride! We ride the old striders in the pen, one at a time, very slowly. Mine goes the slowest. So mine's the best.

lines.text: Name-pillar! Everyone shouts the pillar names across the sea, and whoever forgets one loses. I know Mother and Grandfather and Stump. I forget the rest.

lines: Gap-hopping isn't allowed on the pier any more since I didn't quite make it. Lava doesn't hurt! The rail does.

lines.text: Press your ear to a pillar and hear the sea! Last one to hear it loses. It hums a bit. And burbles. I think it's hungry.
I made up a game just for me. I'm the Hearthkeeper, and my nubs are the hearth, and I feed them pebbles. They're very well fed.
I'll teach you gap-hopping if you stand on the pier and clap. You can be the crowd. Every game needs a crowd.
I made a new game for you. It's called Shore-foot! One of us stands very still and pretends to be you, and everyone brings them coals. Everyone loses.
We have a game where we all pretend to be the Ferrier and haggle with the strider. The strider always wins. It's the only fair game.
Want to be the sky-mourner? You just float and go ooooo.

replies.text: Ooooo! Louder! You're good! Everyone hide!
Watching again! You're the best watcher on the whole deck.

lines.text: Do you have games where you live?

replies.text: Hide and seek! Where do you hide? Is there anywhere cold?
A ball! Is it hot? Can you throw it so it doesn't cool?

lines.text: I can't play. I'm too cold. Play is for warm. Let's watch the hearth instead.
*brrr* Gap-hopping's hard when your legs go stiff. I fell short. Don't tell!
Hot-stone's the only game I can play cold. Hold the stone, don't move, win. I always win.

lines: You don't glow anywhere! Not your arms, not your head. Where do you keep your fire? Inside? Deep inside?
Your feet are so small and flat. Can you wade? Can you float? No? What do you do when you want to be warm?

lines.text: Are you cold all the time? Like grown-ups when they're far from the hearth?

replies.text: Inside! Like a hut with the door shut! That's clever.
*eyes go wide* On purpose? You live in the cold on purpose? That's the scariest thing I ever heard.

lines.text: You're not shivering and I am. That's not fair. Why aren't you shivering?
You've got hair! On top! Does it grow? Does it hurt when it's cut? Can I touch it?

lines: Your skin is the same colour all over, all the time. Grown-ups change colour when they're cross. Why don't you?

lines.text: Your eyes are so small and they hardly move. Mine go all over when I'm excited. Are you never excited?

lines: How do you eat? Do you eat coal? Do you eat anything hot? Do you eat cold things? ...Don't answer that last one.
Why do you wear those clothes? They look heavy. Are they to keep your fire in?
Where's your tail? Did you lose it? That's very sad. I'm sorry.

lines.text: You walk so slowly! Is that because the lava won't have you?

lines: My brother says you come from where the sky cries water. Is it wet? Does it hurt? Is it true?
Do you shiver? Mother says shore-feet shiver. You're not shivering. Are you broken?

lines.text: The only person I've seen who didn't glow was my grandma when she was sleepy. Are you sleepy?
Can you hop the gap? ...Don't try. I'll catch you. Maybe. I'm small, but I'm hot.
I stopped staring! See? I'm staring at the strider. ...I started again. You're just interesting.
You're not strange any more. You're my shore-foot. You're just a bit different from the rest of us.
Mother says staring is rude. But you're staring too! So we're even.
If I stare long enough, will you start to glow? I'm going to try. Don't move.
Everybody here has a chain name. What's yours? Is it long? Is it short? Does it have an anchor in it?

lines: Do you eat fungus off a stick like a strider? Can I watch?

lines.text: Are you a ghost? Mother says ghosts don't glow either.

replies.text: A visitor! The best kind. They bring coal.
*squeak* ...Boo yourself! I wasn't scared. I was surprised. It's different.

lines.text: Can I touch your hand?

replies.text: *pokes* It's soft! And not hot! It's a different kind of hand!
I'm always gentle! ...Mostly. Oh, it's so soft.

lines.text: You're staring back. I'm c-cold, not funny.
Don't stare at my grey. It's rude. I'll stare at yours. You've none. So there.

lines: Lean down. Closer. There's a gap under the strider pen walk where it's extra warm. That's my hiding place. Now it's yours too.
I touched a sky-mourner's tear once. It made a grey spot on my finger for ages. It went away! Don't tell anyone.
I've got a quartz chip shaped like a strider. I'm going to haggle it for the biggest blaze rod ever. Don't tell {neighbour}, they'll want it.

lines.text: I know where the Hearthkeeper keeps the spare coals: under the third seat. I counted them. There were eleven. Now there are ten.
I wave at the far shore sometimes. Once somebody waved back. I ran so fast I lost my breath. Don't tell Mother.
