I've named every pillar in my head. Mother is Mother. Next to her is Grumpy, then Wobbly, then Quiet. They don't know. They hold up the Mooring anyway.

lines: I've got my own hearth post, hidden. It has one link and one pebble on it. It's the smallest Mooring in the sea, and I'm the whole village.

lines.text: My nubs hum the same note as the east bridge. When it rings I hum with it. Then nobody can tell which is which.

lines: When nobody's looking I give Wobbles my share of fungus. She's the only one who understands me.
There's a dark patch outside Auntie's door, from a tear. I know it's only damp. I still step over it with both feet.
I dropped a link in the sea on purpose, to see if the sea would give it back. It didn't. Now the sea has my link. Don't tell.

lines.text: Far across the sea I heard a song once, like crying and singing together. I think it was the Ghastkin. I didn't tell anyone. I hummed it back.
I'm going to be the best Ferrier. I practise on the pier with a stick for a strider and a pebble for a passenger. The pebble complains the most.
The Ferrier gave me a ride on the barge once, round the pier. Just me. Don't tell the others, they'd all want one.
When the hearth is low and everyone's gone quiet, I watch the shadows move and pretend they're the burned Moorings coming back to visit.
I want to see the shore up close some time. Mother says it's cold and dull. I want to see what dull looks like.
I hid a coal in my hip cloth. For emergencies. Like when I'm cold. Or hungry. Or bored.
I can tell when a haggle is going well by the Ferrier's crest. It flutters. I've never told a soul. You know nearly all my secrets now.
I'm going to forge my first link soon. It'll be a bent one, I know it. But it'll be the best bent link there ever was. I'll show you first.
I pretend you're my cousin. A pale one from a far Mooring, the Pale Link. I told the others. Nobody's argued.
Want a bigger secret? You have to promise not to tell.

replies.text: *whispers* I've a fourth nub coming! Right here, a tiny one. It's the magma cream. It works!
Then I can't tell you. That's the rule. It's a good rule.

lines.text: Do you have a secret place?

replies.text: Ha! That's the right answer.
Not any more? Because you shared it? Like me! Sharing's the best.

lines.text: I'm too c-cold for secrets. I'll tell you one when I'm warm. Promise. It's a good one.
My secret is I'm c-cold. Everyone knows. It's not a good secret.

topics.ask: How do you set a fare?
lines: A fungus for every long stretch of sea, near enough. Longer crossing, more fungus. The strider eats the fare, so she has opinions about it.
I name a price, you name half, and we settle near three quarters. Both of us feel robbed. That's how you know it was fair.
Gold I won't touch. It melts on my palm and takes the palm with it. Fungus keeps, and the strider likes it better anyway.
Fresh fungus, bright caps, no wilt. Wilted fungus gets one sniff and a turned head, and then I have to apologise to the strider.
A fare is half the crossing. Pay it grudgingly and the sea feels long. Pay it with a smile and the sea feels short. I've measured. Roughly.
Some shore-feet pay in one lump and walk off whistling. I like those the least. How am I meant to learn anything about someone who never argues?

lines.text: A shore-foot once tried to pay me in quartz. Fine quartz! But a strider can't eat quartz, and she sulked the whole crossing. Would you have paid in quartz?

replies.text: To a Quartzcutter, yes. To a strider, it's a stone with ideas above its station. Fungus, shore-foot.
The strider eats first! Now there's a shore-foot who understands the sea. Remember that and we'll never fall out.

lines: If the strider refuses a fare, I refuse it too. She has turned down two passengers in all her years. Both times I found out why later. One was a thief.
Part of every fare feeds the brazier at the stern. Magma blocks wear down, and a cold brazier means a cold Ferrier, and a cold Ferrier is a grumpy one. Call it a safety charge.
Half the fungus I take in fares came out of the Weft's forest in the first place. Gathered goods, we say. Gathered! I try not to think about it, and I fail.

lines.text: Ask a Ferrier what they fear most. Not the sky-mourners. Not the deep. A passenger who says keep the change. There is no change. Change is a rumour.

replies.text: *crest flares* Say that again and you walk! A fare is a fare and a favour is a favour, and they never share a pocket.
Exactly! Down to the last stalk! You'll do well on the sea, shore-foot. Better than most who sail it.

lines.text: For friends I round down. For good friends I round down and pretend I miscounted. It's the oldest trick in the trade, and only fools don't know it.
Between us, the fare was never about the fungus. It's about having someone to argue with across the dock. The fungus just gives us a reason.
Ember-friends ride free, and the Mooring never grumbles. We write it down as a gift, not a loss, and gifts don't count against the ledger. Don't ask which ledger.
Chain-kin never pay, and never need to ask. Your fare is the news you carry between hearths. A Mooring pays well for news, and you bring plenty.
*shiver* Fungus on the rail, then climb in. We'll haggle when I can feel my fingers. Which may be never.
No haggling. I'm too cold for it. Pay the first price and be glad I'm not feeling greedy. That's a rare thing.

topics.ask: How do you find the way?
lines: Lava talks, if you let it. Bright and slow means deep. Dark and crinkled means shallow and cooling. A grey skin on top means: don't stop here.
Lava falls are my landmarks. Old Stutter, the Twin Pours, Slowmouth. Each one pours its own way, and I could name them blind.
I don't really steer. The strider steers. I tell her which Mooring and hope she's in a good mood. When she isn't, we take the long way round.
A strider's hum drops low when the lava thins underfoot. Learn that note and you'll never ground a barge. It took me three groundings to learn it.
When the haze comes down thick, the Hearthkeepers sing the haze song, {chain} sung slow. Every Ferrier steers by it. We know the way home by ear.
Never follow a light on the sea unless you know whose lantern it is. Once it was a Chartmaker, lost. Twice it wasn't.
Heat rises, and that's the whole secret. The air shimmers over the deep and lies flat over the shallows. Squint and you can read the sea off the shimmer.
The roof of the Nether has landmarks too: crooked spikes, hanging vines, lava falls pouring from above. I know the roof of this sea better than the roof of my own hut.
A sky-mourner's crying is a kind of compass, if you can bear it. They cry loudest over open sea. A quieter sky means a Mooring is near.

lines.text: Ever been properly lost on the sea, shore-foot? I have. Three whole breaths. It felt like a very long time.

replies.text: Shouted. Then I remembered the strider knew the way. I felt silly. She felt superior. We've never discussed it.
On a lava sea, three breaths is a lifetime. Say that again in thick haze and see how brave you are.

lines.text: A Ferrier trusts the strider with their life, and not for one breath with their fungus. Do you trust anyone that far? Or that little?

replies.text: Friends! Good. A friend is someone you'd trust with your life and a haggle. Both are dangerous.
*seams dim* Nobody. That's a cold thing to carry. Put it down here, by the hearth, and we'll see.

lines.text: Sky-mourners drift along lanes. Mostly. Keep one on your left going out and on your right coming home, and you'll usually find your Mooring. Usually.
The sea floor shifts over the years. Pillars stay; shallows creep. Every Ferrier keeps a private chart of the shallows and never lends it. Not even to the Chartmaker. Well. Rarely.
Here's my private mark: a notch in a rail post for every crossing I was frightened. Eleven notches. Eleven's a good number. It means I'm careful, not that I'm brave.
When you're chain-kin you'll hear the haze song and know which Mooring it is just by how the note bends. You've half got it already. Don't tell the strider.
Haze. Grey haze. Grey me. Don't ask me to steer. Ask me when I'm warm, if I ever am.
*shiver* The sea goes quiet when I'm cold. Everything does. That's how I know to stop and warm up before going on.

lines: Basalt slabs lashed with chain, laid like a raft. A bench in the middle, a lantern at the bow, a brazier at the stern. Nothing fancy. Fancy is just more to mend.
I build a new barge every few years, because the slabs crack. The old slabs go into the dock rail. That rail is the oldest barge on the Mooring, if you count it right.
The brazier's for you, mostly. I'd say it's for the barge, but the barge doesn't feel the cold. I do, standing next to it.
The lantern at the bow isn't to see by. It's so the far Mooring knows you for a guest and not a raider. It happened once. Someone threw magma.
I wade beside the strider until the open sea, then let her go on alone and wade home. It's the loneliest part of the trade, and my favourite.
The tow-chain must be long enough that the strider doesn't feel the barge nip her heels. Too short and she kicks. Too long and she wanders. Mine is tuned like a good song.
The sign of a good barge is that it hums when it walks. Not a creak, a hum. A creaking barge is complaining about its master.
A barge carries one passenger at a time. That's not a rule from the hearth, it's a rule from the slabs. Put two shore-feet aboard and the quarrel over the bench would sink it.

lines.text: Four things I check before every crossing: the lashings, the slabs, the brazier, the lantern. Then the strider's mood, which I can't mend, only survive.

replies.ask: What if her mood is bad?
replies.text: Then we cross slow and quiet, and I offer her the best fungus I own. She accepts it as her due.
So do I. Never tell her. A strider who knows she's trusted gets ideas.

lines: A sky-mourner's tear fell on my brazier once. It hissed, it spat, the brazier went dark, and I said words I'd forgotten I knew. The passenger asked what they meant. I said they were prices.

lines.text: I wash the bench between passengers, with hot stone and ash. Some leave soot, some leave stories. I keep the stories. Do you leave a story, shore-foot?

replies.text: A good one! Then the bench is already warmer. Leave it on the stern where the brazier will keep it.
Soot washes off. A story sticks. Think of one on the way over and I'll hear it at the dock.

lines.text: I've scratched a tiny strider under the bench, where passengers never look. One in every new barge, for luck. Tell nobody. It works better unseen.
Once a barge slipped her tow in a swell and drifted. The strider turned, took the chain in her mouth, and towed her home by the corner. She's been insufferable ever since.
I teach my strider to slow in the middle of the sea, just a little, where the view is best. Passengers like to look. Don't tell the other Ferriers. They'd think I'd gone soft.
The oldest barge bench on the Mooring has a dent where the first Ferrier sat. I'd let you sit in it. You'd be the first shore-foot ever.
*shiver* Barge is ready. Brazier's lit. Climb in before I start leaning on it. I'm warming up to the brazier more than to you.
Sit by the stern, near the brazier. I'm going to stand here and radiate misery.

topics.ask: How do you tend the hearth?
lines: The pool drinks from the sea through a little gate in the pillar. Open it a hand's width and the lava creeps in. Open it wide and the whole ring floods. I learned that once, loudly.
Every circuit I walk the ring and touch each magma block with my palm. Cool means trouble, bright means joy, and a flicker means someone's been sitting on it.
The skimmer is a long chain rake. Lava grows a grey skin when the hearth rests, and I draw it off in sheets. Skim too deep and you take the glow with it. Too shy and the hearth sulks.
Guests think a hearth is a fire. It's nearly a creature. It likes company, hates draughts, and goes quiet when someone's unhappy. I can tell the mood of the Mooring from its hum.
The lanterns on the chain posts want trimming too. A low lantern on a causeway means a lost shore-foot. I trim every one, every circuit, without fail.
Stones warm at the ring's edge, then go into a guest's hands. Seven for a very cold guest, three for a cool one, one for a polite one. I judge by the shiver.
The magma blocks wear out from the inside, glowing less and less, until one sags and crumbles. A good keeper feels it a long while before it falls.
Draughts are the enemy. A causeway wind, a doorway left open, a child who won't shut a gap. I hang vine flaps on every opening. Even a small gust makes the hearth shiver.
The hardest time is when the hearth sleeps. Not dark, never dark. Sleeping. Low and red and breathing slow. A sleeping hearth means the Mooring is tired. I wake it with a good story.

lines.text: Want to hold a hearth-stone? It's only warm, for you. Rolled in my own hands first. A guest's stone should never come from a stranger.

replies.text: Hold it close. See, a little hearth in your pocket. Take it to the cold places and think of us.
Then keep it for the road. A stone in the pocket is a hearth that walks with you.

lines.text: What does a hearth want most? Not fuel. Not praise. Company. A hearth with nobody sitting by it burns lower. Do you believe that?

replies.text: Then sit a while and prove it to the hearth. Hear that? It's already humming for you.
Sit by one long enough and you'll say otherwise. Everyone does, in the end. The grey-faced ones fastest.

lines.text: Come round the back of the ring and I'll show you where the heat gathers. It's the best seat on the Mooring and nobody knows. A keeper keeps one secret seat. That's mine.
The hearth has a favourite among us. I won't say who. It's always the one who sings badly. The hum gets warmer when they walk past. I think it's laughing.
I've never told this: when everyone has gone, I sit on the ring's edge and put my feet in, just to the ankle. It's the only time I'm not working. Keep it to yourself.
When I cool for good, I want the hearth fed with your coal, once. Just once. A friend's coal is the right coal to see a keeper out.
*shiver* A cold keeper is the worst keeper there is. I'm trying. Stand there, between me and the draught.
Don't mention the hearth. I'm standing beside it and I'm still cold. That's not the hearth's fault. I'm blaming it anyway.

lines: The coldest sit nearest. That's the rule, and it beats every other rule. Elder, child, guest or keeper: if you're grey, you sit by the ring. If you're glowing, wait your turn.
Guests get the seats with the best view of the chain posts, so they can count the lanterns. A guest who counts lanterns is at home. A guest who counts doors is planning to leave.
Haggle at the hearth all you like, but whoever raises their voice over a price feeds the fire next. All of us have fed it at least twice.
Children sit in the warm gap between the seat-stones, where the heat gathers. They think it's a secret. We've known all along. We let them have it.
A guest who stands and won't sit is rude. A guest who sits at once is polite. A guest who sits in my seat is a friend, and I'll find a way to forgive them.
A guest's first stone is free. The second costs a story. The third we don't charge for, because by then you're staying, and staying guests are family.
Elders sit with their backs to the sea, so they can watch every face. The young sit facing the sea, so they can dream about leaving. It works out well enough.
Quarrels happen here too. When two folk quarrel, they sit on opposite sides of the ring, and neither may leave until the hearth hums. It takes a long time. It ends in laughter or hunger.
I've seated half-frozen Quartzcutters, Ferriers home from a long crossing, and one shore-foot who tried to dry their boots in the ring. We don't speak of the boots.

lines.text: Here's a rule of the ring: you can't leave without saying one true thing about the Mooring. It can be small. What's yours?

replies.text: It is. She heard you. Her hum went up a note, listen. That's the best thing anyone's said to her in ages.
They are! Basalt, what did you expect? True, and fair. I'll let it stand. Bring a cushion next time.

lines.text: Do you have a seat at your own hearth, shore-foot? Do you even have a hearth?

replies.text: Good. A seat without a hearth is a bench. A hearth without a seat is a pit. Keep both.
Then you have one here. That's decided. Don't argue, I'm a keeper. We always win on this.

lines.text: I've saved you a seat. You can't see it. It's between two seat-stones, and when you come, they shuffle apart. I shouldn't have told you. Pretend I haven't.
Friends sit on my warm side, where the seat-stones face the ring. I'll admit I move the stones. A keeper may arrange the furniture.
At the end of a long gathering, when everyone's drowsy, the youngest says the haze song and the eldest answers. Stay for it once. It's the best thing we do.
Your seat is marked now. A scratch on the stone, a little spiral. Only chain-kin have one. Sit in it whenever you like. If someone else is in it, tell them I said no.
*shiver* Seat by the ring. Take it. Take any of them. I'd take yours too if you weren't sitting there.
There's a rule that the coldest sits nearest. At the moment that's me. Be kind about it, shore-foot.

lines: Every hearth in this sea was lit from another. A coal from a hearth, carried across the lava to a new ring. The fire of {chain} came from a Mooring far over the sea, and theirs from one before.
The coal that starts a new hearth is the mother coal. It rides in a pot on a chain round the carrier's neck, and the carrier says nothing until it's set down. Not even hello.
A hearth owes its mother. When the Moorings burned, some hearths went out and some were saved because a daughter sent a coal back. It's the proudest thing a daughter hearth can do.
They say the oldest hearth is one so old that nobody remembers its Mooring, and it's out there somewhere, still burning. I say the sea is large and my legs are short.
When our people founded this Mooring, the fire was the first thing built. Decks came after. A Mooring is a hearth and the folk who keep warm round it. Everything else is carpentry.
The mother coal is never a whole coal. It's a crumb, pinched off, no bigger than a seed. Big enough to start a fire, small enough to guard with both hands. That's how fire travels: small.
We never keep the first coal. It's spent, long ago, in the starting. What we keep is the fire, and the habit of passing it on. Every hearth is a daughter of a spent mother.
Smoke teaches me things. A mother coal's smoke should go straight up the first breath. If it leans, a draught is near and the new hearth will struggle. I've turned down two Moorings over a lean.
The worst thing a keeper can say is: I let it go. The second worst is: I thought someone else had it. That's why a hearth has a keeper and two who watch the keeper, and I'm the one being watched.
The Withren light blue fires with no coal at all. Cold fire, from the souls. A fire with no mother is a fire I don't trust. It has nobody to be sorry to.

lines.text: Do you have a fire that came from somewhere? A family one? A spark you were given?

replies.text: Then you're a daughter fire yourself. Don't let her go out. We'd all be sorry, and I'd be sorriest.
Made your own! Bold. Strange. Our oldest saying is that nobody lights a fire from nothing. But go on, shore-foot. Surprise me.

lines.text: If you had to carry a fire across the sea for a stranger, without stopping, would you? Without speaking, even?

replies.text: Then you have the makings. A quiet shore-foot, carrying fire. I like it more than I should.
A talker! Then the coal would die, and you'd feel so sorry we'd all forgive you. Carry gossip, not fire.

lines.text: There's a place on the hearth post where the mother coal's pot hangs, empty. A keeper hangs it up and says nothing. Fire is a gift you give away to keep.
Some of us hum to the mother coal as it travels. Not a song, just a hum. The carrier hums, the coal glows. I've seen it brighten. Believe me or don't.
When I carried it round the ring, my hands went black to the wrist, and I thought of every keeper who had done the same, back to the first. That's the real fire. The line of hands.
If you ever raise a hearth of your own, you may take a coal from ours. Chain-kin may. The saying is: the fire goes where the kin go. Take it in both hands. Don't speak.
*shiver* A fire from a fire from a fire. I wish one of them would pass some warmth along to me. Right now. Hurry, fire.
The mother coal is a good story. It's a better story told warm. Ask me again when I can feel my own hands.

lines: A fine chain, no thicker than a reed, forged by a Chainwright who owes me a favour. The hook's a bent link of black iron. The weight's a chip of quartz. Everything else is patience.
Bait? Warped fungus, a smear of cream, and a good wish. The fungus draws the curious, the cream draws cubes, and the wish draws nothing, but it keeps me company.
You don't cast into lava, you lower. Slowly, hand over hand, as if tucking a child in. Splash, and the sea goes sulky for a hundred breaths.
Never let the line rest on the rail. A warm rail takes the temper right out of a chain. Lay it over a basalt hook, or better, over your own forearm.
I read the line with my fingertips. A nibble is a tremor. A cube is a tug and a bounce. Old chain is a long drag. A snag is no feeling at all, which is the worst feeling there is.
Lines break. They always break in the end. I keep a coil of spare on my belt, and the old one I keep too, because it has a rhythm in it now from all my pulling.
I fish from the end of the pier by the strider pen, where the lava runs slow. The pen's warmth keeps my crest bright. A cold angler catches nothing. The cubes smell it.
Spare hooks hang on my rope belt, one for every kind of bite. The hook for the quick tug. The hook for the slow drag. And the hook for a stubborn old thing that doesn't want to leave.
Once I fished with a lantern on the line, for the light. The cubes loved it. They came to see. I pulled up fourteen, all curious, all sulking when I set them back.

lines.text: Fishing is mostly waiting. Do you have the patience? The real kind, not the kind you say you have.

replies.text: Plenty! Then try it. Take my line, sit here, and don't pull until it pulls you.
Honest! The sea likes honest. Sit here anyway. Sitting is half the work.

lines.text: The best trick is to fish where it isn't: not the deep, not the shallows, but the edge between, where the heat changes. Things there are confused, and confused things bite. Sounds wise?

replies.text: Thank you! I stole it from a Ferrier, who stole it from a cube. Everything good is passed along.
Luck is what we call it when we aren't looking. Try it a hundred times and see if it's still luck.

lines.text: My teacher fished with the first chain she ever forged, as a girl, and caught more than I do with the best iron on the Mooring. It's never the line.
Here's a trick: hum while you lower. Cubes like a low, steady hum. I won't say what I hum. Say it out loud and it stops working. It's the haggling song, mostly.
I'll lend you a line for a while. A real one, my second best. Sit at the pier with me. Everyone should catch one thing from the sea that isn't a regret.
I had a hook forged for you, small and bent, from a link of the line that landed my first cube. Hang it somewhere warm. It's good luck, or nothing. Same as most things.
*shiver* The line's tangled. The line's always tangled when I'm cold. I think it knows.
No catch. Not a nibble. Grey anglers catch grey luck. Wait till I've warmed up and I'll show you wonders.

lines: A boot. A single boot, very large, with a gold buckle that I let go at once, boot and all. Gold doesn't belong on a Magmari line. Somebody's loss. A Piglin's, probably.
A bone needle as long as my arm, with an eye you could thread a chain through. Weft work, I'd say. It's in the rafters of my hut. The finest needle I'll ever not use.
A helmet with a crest of three twisted horns. I wore it for a breath and the whole Mooring laughed. Now it's the seat for the strider pen's smallest calf.
A chair. A whole chair, lava-black, with a high back. Nobody knows whose. {neighbour} claimed it and hasn't stood up since. Best seat at the ring now, and nobody's sure it isn't haunted.
A cube the size of a hut took my line and held it. I didn't pull. We looked at each other through the lava, and then it let go and sank. The only time I've been afraid and happy together.
Tongs, mostly. Bent, blackened hearth-tongs, still warm after all the years, which tells you how hot a burning was. I hang them by the pier. I won't clean them.
Teeth. Huge teeth, curved like crescents, too big for any strider. I've half a dozen in a sack. Shore-feet pay well for teeth. Our folk laugh and ask whose they are.
Nothing I pull up is mine to sell until I've asked it. I hold it up and wait. If it feels wrong, back it goes. That's the angler's oath, and I take it more seriously than my prices.

lines.text: The deep has something slow and big in it. Everyone knows. Nobody's seen it. Do you want to know what I think it is?

replies.text: The sea's own heart, turning over. Sounds silly said aloud. But have you heard the sea go quiet right before? That's a heartbeat.
Wise. Some things are better left to the deep. I tell myself that every time my line goes tight.

lines.text: The deep sometimes gives back what you dropped. Do you have anything the sea took from you? Something you'd like to fish for?

replies.text: *seams dim* Ah. Then you know. The sea doesn't give those back. But it keeps them tidy, I promise.
Lucky. A life without a thing in the deep is a quiet one. I'd not trade mine for it, though.

lines.text: I lost my mother's hearth-stone in the deep as a child. Twenty years later it came up on my line, still warm. The sea keeps tidy accounts.
I once pulled up a quartz bowl, full to the brim with something hot and glowing. It sits on the hearth wall and has glowed ever since. The Chartmaker says it's older than the Mooring.
I've told nobody this: I once caught a link with a name scratched in it, a great-aunt of mine, from before the burning. I gave it back to the deep. It felt like the right way.
You've brought me luck. Truly. Four fine things came up this last stretch, and the only thing that changed is you. You can't be allowed to leave, shore-foot. I'll chain you here.
*shiver* Strangest catch? Me, right now. Look at me. Grey and fishing. Go away and let me warm up.
Ask me later. The strange things come up when I'm warm and calm. When I'm cold, only nonsense bites.

lines: A model of a barge, finely carved, with a tiny Ferrier sitting in it and a tiny brazier at the stern. I gave it to the Ferrier. It hangs at the dock now, and every passenger asks who made it.
They bounce. That's the whole of their nature: bounce, look, bounce. A cube thinks about nothing, and it's the happiest creature on the sea.
Small ones for cream, middling ones I let go, big ones I never touch. A big cube is old, and old things on this sea are owed respect.
Cream comes from the inside of a small cube, scooped quick and kind while it's drowsy. It comes out warm and thick. It tastes like a hug that burned a little.
When I set a cube back, it forgets me at once. I find that restful. Nobody holds a grudge against an angler who threw them back. A cube is the most forgiving creature there is.
Cream has grades. Pale and runny is for the ferry paste. Golden and thick is for eating. Dark and heavy, which keeps its warmth a long while, is what we feed the cold children.
Cubes split when they get bored. Two small ones from one big, then four. You can fish a patch for years and never run out, as long as you leave the big ones alone.
Never take a cube at the top of its bounce. It'll come down in your face, and your face is cold enough. Wait for the dip. Cubes are all rhythm.
A cube's colour tells its mood. Red-gold is sleepy. Bright orange is curious. A dull dark red means leave it be. It's thinking, and rarely nicely.
The Quartzcutter pays for cream in chips. The Chartmaker pays in charts. The Ferrier pays in complaints. I take chips.

lines.text: Do you know the cube song? We sing it as we scoop. It keeps them calm. Shall I give you a verse?

replies.text: *hums, low and wobbly* Ba-dum, ba-dum, bounce along, nobody's cold and nobody's wrong. That's it. That's all of it.
Later! That's what everyone says. The cubes never do. They bounce straight to the point.

lines.text: They say that in your world there are cubes made of green slime, wet right through, that don't burn and don't bounce right. I don't believe it. Slime! Have you seen one?

replies.text: *shudders* Green. Wet. Wobbling. And you walk past them like they're nothing? Lava-brave, that is.
Lucky. Keep it that way, and keep that thought away from my pen.

lines.text: The ferry paste, the cream the Ferrier dabs on shore-feet? I make it. A pinch of ash goes in. I'm not telling you which ash. That's the secret that keeps me fed.
Cubes can tell who is kind. Hold still, and a cube will come and sit on your foot. I've never had one sit on mine. Don't tell the others how that makes me feel.
I keep a jar of the dark cream aside for friends. Dab it on your hands before a cold crossing and you'll keep a warm spot a good while. I don't tell the Mooring.
I named a cube after you. A small one, brave, with a wobble. When it bounces, I say your name. The others think I've gone strange, and I let them think it.
*shiver* Cream. Cream would help. Please tell me you brought cream. I'll take it raw, off a spoon, and I won't haggle.
A cube would be company. A warm, stupid, bouncing company. Right now I'd take it.

lines: First you need iron, and iron is dear. We've none in the sea. It comes from shore-feet, from old chain hauled up, and from fair-minded folk who don't ask where it came from.
Soften it in the heat, draw it thin, bend it round the post, and close the ends. Then it goes in the deep lava to sit and think. A link that has thought a long time doesn't forget.
Closing is the art. Two ends meeting, a hammer, a hair of heat, a hair of patience. A good join you can't find, even with your thumb. A bad join you can find with your eyes shut.
Every link I make has my mark, a tiny spiral where the ends meet. Not for pride. For blame. If a link fails they come to me, and I'd rather be found than guessed.
I test in threes: one link on a post, one under the barge, one in a bridge. Different loads, different lies. A link is only honest when it's been tested three ways.
A link takes forty strokes. A sash takes a few hundred links. A bridge takes more than I can count. The Hearthkeeper counts for me and gets it wrong.
Hammer rhythm matters. Tap tap, strike. Tap tap, strike. I lose count if I hum. Others hum the hearth song and their links come out sweeter. I'm jealous. Mine come out accurate.
Old iron from the deep is best. Years of lava have tempered it: tough, dark, singing when you ring it. New shore-iron is soft as a cube. I wouldn't hang a lantern on it.
Sparks are a kind of conversation. Small fast ones say harder. Big slow ones say wait. I've never been wrong about a spark. Once.

lines.text: Have you ever made anything with your hands that had to hold? Not a table. Something that could hurt someone if it let go?

replies.text: Then you've never been properly afraid of your own work. It's a good fear. Get one.
Then you know. The weight in your belly when you let go of it. That's the whole trade.

lines.text: What holds a bridge up? The chain? The posts? The pillars? Go on, say it. I like hearing what shore-feet think.

replies.text: The chain, the posts, the pillars. And the part nobody says: trust. People cross because they've never seen it fall.
The pillars hold the bridge. The chain holds the pillars together. Everyone holds everyone. That's Mooring-work.

lines.text: Colour tells me when. Dull red, still sleeping. Cherry, ready. White, too late. I wear a dark basalt visor to see the colours true. It's not vanity. It's mostly not vanity.
My teacher said the secret of iron is that it forgives. Bend it wrong, bend it back. It remembers a little and forgives the rest. Chain is like kin that way.
I'll show you something. This link in the post was made by a dozen hands, each adding one stroke. The whole Mooring took turns, after the burning. Every stroke is different.
Your link on the post? I made it. I made it three times before it was right. The first two are in the sea. Don't tell the post.
*teeth chatter* Iron's easier when you're warm. So is everything. Stand back from the anvil; I'm shivering and I'll hit you.
Cold iron. Cold hands. Cold hammer. Cold me. Go away and come back to a better world.

lines: A child is born and within a few breaths the neighbours are at the door. Nobody asks. Someone goes to the Chainwright, someone to the post, and a link is forged for the new one.
You can't forge your own link. That's the oldest custom there is. Someone must want you here enough to make it, and that someone puts a family sign on it you'll never see.
Every hearth post is a living chain, and ours is {chain}. Look up and count us: each link a person, in the order we came. The old ones sit lower and darker. The new ones shine at the top.
A bright link is a baby. A dull link is a life. A link wiped clean and hung back is someone home from a long crossing. The Chainwright polishes it when they return.
When someone cools for good, their link stays on the post. We polish it once, at the farewell, and never again. Over the years it dulls to the colour of old embers. That's how the post remembers.
If a link is flawed at birth we don't hide it. The Chainwright hammers the flaw smooth and shows the child when they're grown. Everyone is flawed. Better to know it was caught early.
Naming is separate. A name is the sound; the link is the weight. We say you're not properly a person until you have both. Some folk have a heavy name and a light link. That's the funny kind.
When a link is hung, someone says the oldest words: one more to hold, one more to be held. Then everyone touches the post, and the hearth hums back.
A small copy of the link goes onto the child's first belt-chain, so wherever they wander they carry the weight of home. It's too small to hold anything. It isn't meant to. It's meant to be carried.

lines.text: Do you have something like it, shore-foot? A mark that says you were wanted?

replies.text: A name's a fine link. It only needs someone to say it. I'll say yours, if you like.
*frowns* Then I'll forge you one in my head. A small one. It'll be dented, but it'll hold.

lines.text: Would you want a link of your own? A real one? It's a serious thing, being hung on a post.

replies.text: Honoured! Then keep coming back. Honour is the first half of the forging.
Not sure is good. Sure folk make poor links. Come back when you're sure, or when you're not.

lines.text: When a Chainwright forges a baby's link, they hum the baby's name over it. The links hold better. Nobody knows why. Possibly it's the humming.
If a family has no Chainwright, they bring iron to the nearest, and the Chainwright forges the link for nothing. For nothing! Don't tell the other trades. They'd demand it too.
Guests who've been taken in sometimes get a guest-link. Small, plain iron. It goes on the lowest part of the post, where the children can reach it. Many a guest has wept over theirs.
Yours is on the post, seventh from the top, between two bright ones. I put you there on purpose, among the newest. You're new to us, however old you are. Newness suits you.
Short version: forged, hung, polished. Long version needs a fire. Ask me by the fire.
*teeth chatter* A newborn is hot as a coal. I held one once, to warm up. It didn't mind. It was asleep. I felt like a thief.

lines: Everyone has. The worst thing about a bad link is that it looks good. A bad link doesn't announce itself. It lies there, bright and polite, till the load comes.
An apprentice's first bridge ought to fail, kindly, over a puddle of cool lava with the whole Mooring watching and clapping. That way it's learned and loved.
The worst link in any chain is the one its maker was proudest of. Pride warps the hammer hand, and the flaw hides under the shine.
The sag test: hang a chain between two posts, load it, listen. A good chain hums. A middling chain creaks. A bad chain says nothing, and that silence is the one to fear.
Rust. Not here, thank the fire, the dry heat keeps it away. Shore-feet carry it in on their chains like a cough. I wipe their chains with ash and don't mention it.
The Chainwright at the next Mooring makes handsome links, I'll grant them that. Showy, though. Their chains look sold before they're hung.
The greatest Chainwright I've heard of forged a chain so long it took a whole generation to make. It held two Moorings together through a bad surge. It's still down there, they say, holding nothing.
Mending is a skill of its own. You can't just cut out the bad link and join the ends. The neighbours remember the bad one and pull wrong. You have to ease the whole run.
Weight isn't the only enemy. Swing is the other. A bridge in a thousand small swings tires like a body does. A good Chainwright hears the tiredness and rests the bridge.

lines.text: If you found a bad link in a bridge you were crossing, what would you do?

replies.text: Tell the Chainwright! Yes! I'd weep for joy. Most people tell their neighbours and wait to see what happens.
*crest flares* Keep walking? Over a bad link? That's how bridges end up in the sea.

lines.text: Sometimes the bad link is the right one. A link that gives a little on purpose, a hinge that eases a jerk, saves the whole chain. We call them kind links. Do you have any?

replies.text: A few is plenty. One kind link in a hundred is a good chain. One in ten is a miracle.
Hard links snap. Learn to give a little, shore-foot. It's cheaper than a new chain.

lines.text: I once forged a link so perfect I couldn't bear to put it in a chain. It sits in my hut, useless. That's what perfection is. I take it down sometimes to remember being proud.
My teacher kept a jar of failed links: bent, cracked, twisted, kinked. She called them her teachers. Every Chainwright has a jar. Mine's nearly full. The jar says more than I do.
A bad link of mine once ended up in the guest bridge. I found it a year later by the creak. I fixed it in the dark so nobody would see. Now you know.
I trust you with this: the link on my wrist is flawed. A hairline crack, invisible. I wear it so I remember I'm not perfect. Tell no one. Chain-kin may know.
*teeth chatter* Bad links come from cold hands. Cold hands make careless hammers. Take that as a warning and bring me a coal.
Worst link? Me, this breath. Grey, shaking, useless. Replace me.

lines: Cold. Cold, still and quiet, and the ground doesn't move. I hate how the ground doesn't move. After a long stay I walk home like a hurt strider, trying to feel it wobble.
We go in pairs. One cuts, one holds the fire-bowl. A lone cutter on a cold cliff comes home grey to the bone. Never go alone. Never pair with {neighbour}, who grumbles.
Hot stones in pouches against the belly, and a bowl of embers on a chain. We go out with a pack of warmth and come back with a pack of quartz. Fair trade, if you survive the middle.
The causeway is the first cold. You step off the last warm deck onto the first cold stone, and everything in you says turn back. Every trip. The nerve is learned, not born.
The cliffs aren't empty. Ghasts pass overhead, and there are things on the far ledges that we don't speak with. We cut with our heads down and say nothing.
We never light a fire on the cliffs. The smoke would call everything within a long walk. We use the bowl, covered, and keep our hands tucked under our arms.
Coming home is the best part. The first deck after the causeway: warm under your feet. I've seen cutters lie flat on it and weep. Don't laugh. You'd do it too.
What I bring back isn't just quartz. It's news from the shore: a ghast gone down, a net strung where there wasn't one, a Piglin camp moved. Cutters are the Mooring's eyes on the cold.
Old cutters wear a cord with a chip for every trip they came back from. The cords get heavy. Some wear them as a boast. I wear mine as a reminder.

lines.text: Would you walk out on cold stone for a chip of white? Honestly?

replies.text: Spoken like one of ours. The cliffs would love you. Don't let them.
Sensible. That's exactly why we're paid.

lines.text: The quiet is worse than the cold. Out there you can hear your own seams cooling, one by one, tick, tick. I started humming to cover it. Do you hum when you're afraid?

replies.text: Whistling! Brave and cheerful. The cliffs hate that. Do it louder.
Quiet's the worse way. Hum, shore-foot. Anything will do. Hum the haggling song.

lines.text: I have a ledge. One flat shelf of rock where I rest on the cliffs. From it the sea is just a glow on the edge of everything. When I'm there I feel it like a friend waving.
We pay a share to the Hearthkeeper for the cutters who don't come back, and a share to the cutters who do. The first share is bigger. It's a sad bargain, and we make it every trip.
Once I was left. My partner went back for the bowl, and I stood alone for a hundred breaths. I thought I'd gone dark for good. Then I saw my own breath glow. I walked home by it.
Come with me, one trip. Stand with me on the cold stone and see what we see. The first time is the hardest, and it should be with someone who won't laugh. I'll hold the bowl.
*teeth chatter* The shore. Cold. Don't talk about the shore. I'm still there in my bones.
I was on the cliffs a moment ago and I haven't come back yet. My body's here. The rest is on the ledge. Bring a coal.

lines: Quartz has a thread, like the grain in a vine. Find the thread, tap along it, and the stone opens like a mouth. Tap across it and you get dust and bruised knuckles.
Wedge, mallet, patience. Wedges of basalt, because basalt is harder than it looks. You never strike quartz. You persuade it.
Warm the cut first. A hot stone laid along the thread, a breath of heat, then a tap. Cold quartz is stubborn. Warm quartz relents. Same as people.
Quartz sings when it's ready: a thin high note. If you hear it, stop talking, stop breathing, and tap once. Miss the note and the stone remembers.
A shatter is a bad turn for a cutter. A fine piece lost, a long cold trip in a spray of white. We call it a laugh, as in: the stone had a laugh at me. It keeps us sane.
Size matters less than clarity. A big milky block is worth three small clear chips. Hold it to a lantern: if you can see the flame through it, that's a keeper.
I carry three mallets: a heavy one for the first tap, a light one for the second, and a tiny one for when I'm trying to be gentle. The tiny one's my favourite.
Quartz dust is the enemy. It gets in your seams and sticks. After every cut we rub down with warm ash and shake out our hip cloths. A white cutter is a careless cutter.
There are cutters' sayings. Never cut in anger. Never cut to a price. Cut for the hearth, not the haggle. We break the last one all the time and feel guilty.

lines.text: Care to try? Here, hold the wedge. No, lighter. Lighter! You're strangling it.

replies.text: Better! Now tap. Gently. ...Oh. Ah. That's a shatter. Everyone's first is a shatter. Welcome to the trade.
Watching's a fine craft. We have a word for it: apprenticing.

lines.text: Which is better, a quartz that's clear, or a quartz that's cloudy and warm-looking? Pick one.

replies.text: Clear. Practical. You'd make a fine Chartmaker.
Cloudy and warm! A poet. They'd fight over you at the hearth.

lines.text: Under the white there's often a sliver of warmth. Quartz isn't cold all through, only on the skin, from the long dark. Cut deep enough and your palm says hello.
My mother taught me to cut with my eyes closed. Not for show. So the hands learn the thread. I still keep my eyes open. It's good to see what you've won.
I cut a piece once so clear I could read my own seams through it. I haven't sold it. It sits on my sill. When I'm low I look through it, and everything's brighter.
I've set aside a chip for you, cut from the best block I've ever opened. Don't ask what it's for. It'll be for something, someday, and I'll know when.
*teeth chatter* The thread. I can't find the thread. All I see is grey. Warm me, and I'll cut you anything.
Cutting while cold is how you break a good block. I'll wait. The quartz can wait. It's waited long enough.

lines: Because I come home grey. Count it that way: one chip is a long shiver, a cold trip, and a weak hand for a good while after. Divide by your pride and there's the price.
Quartz doesn't melt, doesn't rot, doesn't rust. Anything that lasts that long should cost like a grandchild.
There are grades. Smoke, milk and glass. Smoke is cloudy and cheap, good for hut windows. Milk is soft white, good for beads and chips. Glass is clear. Glass is the one you haggle over.
Chips are small coin. Links are big coin. Coal is the coin you can feel. Anyone who tells you a chip is worthless has never carried one home.
Chartmakers pay best. A chart wants quartz points, and the points wear down after a few slabs. Ferriers pay worst, because Ferriers haggle worst. Don't tell a Ferrier I said so.
I only sell to those who'll use it. I once turned down a rich fool who wanted a quartz seat, just to sit on. Quartz is cold to sit on. I told him so. He bought glass from the next Mooring.
The Ghastkin build with it, I'm told. A whole hall, tall white walls round their pool. That's a lot of cutting. I'd like to know who cut it, and what they were paid.
A bad cutter undersells, afraid of the haggle. A bad haggler overcuts, afraid of the cliff. A good one is afraid of both and sells just right. Fear is a grand measure.
Quartz smells a little after cutting: bright, like struck flint but sweeter. Hang a chip in your hut and your hut smells like a good trip home.

lines.text: What would you do with a handful of clear quartz?

replies.text: A window! To see out or in? Windows are for the nosy. Both of us are nosy.
Give it away? To whom? Ah. To a friend. Then you're not just a haggler. Good.

lines.text: My grandmother sold her whole hoard of quartz once, to buy one very warm seat in the best hut on the Mooring for the rest of her life. Wise or foolish?

replies.text: Wise! You'd have haggled for a warmer one, mind. But wise.
Foolish! She'd say so too, from the warmest seat on the Mooring. Which proves her wise.

lines.text: Between us, the price is high so that the cliffs stay quiet. If quartz were cheap, every shore-foot with a pick would be out there, and some wouldn't come back.
For friends, the price is a story from your world. I'll cut you a chip for every one I haven't heard. You've about nine chips coming already.
I'll tell you the real price. Not in links. In trips. Three trips for a link-ring. Seven for a window. Twenty-one for a love-token. People pay me for the trips, mostly.
You may have a chip whenever you like. No haggle. No story. Just ask. It's the one price I've never named, and the only one I'll truly take.
*teeth chatter* Price? Whatever you've got. A coal. A hug. I'd sell you a whole cliff for a warm seat.
Don't haggle me now. I'd sell the lot. Come back when I'm warm and I'll charge you twice, for catching me cold.

topics.ask: How do you make a chart?
lines: First you walk the sea. Beside it, along the pillars, with a measuring chain in your hand, a knot every hundred links. Count the knots, mark the slab. Everything is slow.
Slabs of basalt, flat and dark, laid across my lap. The quartz point scratches a pale line that stays. Rub your sleeve on it and it doesn't smudge. Warm it and it shines.
My marks: a ring for a pillar. A dash for a bridge. A spiral for an eddy where the lava turns on itself. A long curl for a lane where the sky-mourners drift.
Deep lava is a thick line, shallow lava is a thin one, and a lava fall is three little lines that point down. Anyone can read my charts after a short lesson. That's the whole point.

A chart is never finished. The sea shifts a little, the pillars settle, the sky-mourners change their minds. I scratch the lines fresh every few years. A chart that never changes is a lie that lasted.
To measure depth, I lower a chain with a weight on the end. The knots tell me how far it went before it stopped. A tug, a pause, a note. I've lowered chain into every deep within a long wade of home.
You don't scratch a straight line. A straight line is a lie told at the wrong scale. The sea bends, and a chart should bend with it.
Distances I measure in wades. A wade is how far a Magmari goes while saying the chain name slowly, twice. Shore-feet tell me it's silly. They also get lost, so.
Rubbings are how a chart travels. Lay thin vine-cloth on the slab, rub with ash, and the lines come out dark on pale. Slabs are heavy. Rubbings are light.

lines.text: Good charts need a good eye. Mine's not bad. Can you draw, shore-foot? A pillar, a bridge, a sea?

replies.text: A little's plenty. We all start at the ring and the dash. Bring a slab sometime and I'll teach the rest.
Then you read. Reading's half the trade. Sit here and I'll show you what each mark means.

lines.text: What would you chart first, if you could? Something near or something far?

replies.text: Near! A home-lover. Near's the hardest. You can't hide your errors from the neighbours.
Far! A wanderer. Far is easy. Nobody can check.

lines.text: I sign every chart with a tiny strider in the corner. Not my name. My name's forgettable. The strider is what people remember. It's a trick, and it works.
Between you and me, I always leave one small error in a chart. A pillar half a step off, a shallow marked as deep. Not to be spiteful. To catch the copiers.
When I was small I scratched the whole Mooring on the floor of our hut with a nail. My mother said I was ruining the floor. My father said I was reading it. They argued all the way to the hearth.
I've a slab for you: the Mooring and the sea round it, the best I've done. Keep it where it's warm. When you can't find your way, look at it and know somewhere knows you.
*shiver* Scratch, scratch. My hands are numb. The chart will come out crooked, and it'll be your fault, and I'll blame the cold.
Don't ask me to draw. I can barely hold the point. Ask when I'm warm and I'll draw you a masterpiece.

topics.ask: Tell me about the old charts.
lines: The oldest are kept under the Chartmaker's floor, wrapped in vine-cloth and hung from chains. The charts are old. The chains are older.
The oldest chart I've seen shows a sea that isn't ours. The pillars are wrong, the falls are wrong. I think the sea moved, and the Moorings moved with it, and we've been walking away from something.
A dead Mooring is marked with an empty ring, never rubbed out. Whoever scratched it knew a hearth once stood there, and a hearth deserves its place on the slab.
Some old charts have a second line beside the first, thinner and pale. That's a correction by a later hand. Reading an old chart is like reading an argument between the dead.
In the corner of a very old chart there's a tiny Ferrier falling off a tiny barge, and beside it a word: pays double. I laugh every time. Chartmakers and Ferriers have always teased each other.
Half the old slabs are black at one end, where the Wither's fire licked them. Basalt keeps, but it remembers. We don't clean the black. It's part of the chart now.
Reading an old chart is a skill. You must know what the Chartmaker meant, not what she scratched. Deep, in her time, meant very deep. Words wear down like quartz points.
Even the dead pillars are charted: stumps in the sea where bridges once stood. A barge can run aground on a stump nobody remembered. The chart remembers. That's the whole use of an old chart.
There's a rumour of a chart that shows the whole Nether, every sea and shore and people. There's no such thing. It's too big, too hot, and full of folk who'd redraw it. We love an impossible chart.

lines.text: Would you like to see one? The oldest I own? It's not much to look at. It's just lines.

replies.text: *unwraps it carefully* There. See that wavering line? That's a coast that's gone now. Someone walked it once, and wrote it down.
Another time, then. They keep. That's rather the point of them.

lines.text: Do you think the sea remembers the Moorings that were here? Or only we do?

replies.text: Then it's our job, isn't it? Remember loudly, and write it down.
Maybe it does. That might be why it's so restless, I suppose.

lines.text: There's a chart set into the hearth wall, bricked in with the stones. Nobody knows who put it there. Lay your hand on it and it's warmer than the stone around it. A Chartmaker's mystery.
Now and then I trace the oldest charts with a fingertip to keep the lines from sleeping. Basalt needs touching. Hearthkeepers say basalt has no feelings. Hearthkeepers have never been alone with one.
Every Chartmaker has one chart nobody may copy. Mine shows a place I found by accident, far out, where the lava lies dead calm and the roof glitters. I go there when I'm low.
I'd like to make you a chart of every place you've been. We'd do it together: you tell me, I scratch. At the end you'd hold a slab nobody else could read. That's what a chart is for.
*shiver* The oldest chart is in my hut, and my hut is cold. That's all I'll say about it.
Old charts. Dead Moorings. Brr. Cold subject, cold me. Come back when the hearth is bright.

lines: They trust their striders. They trust the haze song. They trust their own feet. Charts come fourth on the list, and only after a very long argument.
A Ferrier will always say the chart is wrong. I always say the Ferrier is lost. The truth is that the sea moves and we're both right, and neither of us will say so.
Ferriers are secret about shallows. Every one keeps a private map of where the sea floor rises. I've begged. I've bribed. I once sat beside one and watched her hands. I got a pillar and a headache.
My best work is a Ferrier's chart: the crossings, the haze songs, the places to rest. Ferriers scorn it, then copy it. Within a year every Ferrier has one tucked in a belt.
A Ferrier once put me down on a pillar for criticism. A pillar! In the middle of the sea! I waited a long while and was fetched. She said it was a joke. It was a joke. It was also a pillar.
A Ferrier read my chart wrong once and came home forty strides from where she meant to be. She said my chart was bad. It was her reading. We still argue at the hearth, nine fares later.
Ferriers won't admit it, but they check their charts at the dock before casting off. I've seen them. A quick glance, a shrug, a nod. I pretend I don't.
Some Ferriers want charts with no lines, only feelings. Draw me the sea as it feels, one said. I drew a big circle and wrote hot. It was a good chart, honestly.
A chart is a promise that the sea will be where I said. A Ferrier's feet are a promise that she'll go where she said. When the two promises agree we cheer. When they disagree we haggle.

lines.text: If you had to cross the sea, who would you trust: a Ferrier, a chart, or a strider?

replies.text: The strider! The oldest answer, and the right one. A strider has never once been wrong about the way home.
The chart! Well. Bless you. That's the first time anyone has said so. Take a chip.

lines.text: A Ferrier told me the best chart is the one you throw away at the end of the crossing. What do you make of that?

replies.text: Wise, and annoying. She's been throwing mine away for years.
Wasteful! Exactly. I made her pay for it.

lines.text: The good Ferriers take my charts and ask what's missing. The bad ones take my charts and ask what I want. I give the good ones extra.
I leave a private mark in every Ferrier's chart, a tiny pillar only they'd recognise. When they find it they smile and never say. It's a handshake that doesn't burn.
Once I misdrew a shoal and nearly stranded a Ferrier. She forgave me, but she carries that chart everywhere, as a warning. I haven't made that mistake since.
Whatever Ferriers say, it was a Ferrier who taught me my trade. She won't have me say so. Her name's on my first slab, scratched small where only I'd find it. Swear not to tell.
Ferriers. Hmph. Ask me when I'm warm and I'll insult them properly.
*shiver* Fine. They trust charts when they're cold, same as me. When you're cold, everyone trusts a lined slab.

lines: A Ferrier! No, wait, a Hearthkeeper! No, wait. A Lava-angler, because of the cream. No. All of them. I can be all of them if I'm quick.
I want to be a Ferrier because Ferriers get to shout walk on at the strider. I practise. Walk on! Walk on! See? I'm ready.
Hearthkeepers get to touch the hearth whenever they like! Nobody tells them not too near. I want a job where nobody says not too near.
Chainwrights make noise. Loud noise! Bang, bang, bang! I'd like a job with bangs. Mother says I'd be good at it. She says it with a face.
Quartzcutters go to the cold place and come back grey and brave. I'd like to be grey and brave. But not grey for long. Just long enough for people to say whoa.
Chartmakers draw. I draw! I drew the whole hearth on my hut wall and my father said that was a chart. I said it was just a hearth. He said that's what a chart is.
My grandmother wanted to be a Ferrier. She's a Chainwright. She says you don't pick the job. The job picks you, with a look. I hope it gives me a good look.
I want to be so good that people say there goes the best one when I walk by. Even if I'm only the best at being hot. I'm already the best at that.
Being big means your link on the post goes dark and cool. Mine's still the little bright one. When it's dark, everyone will say that's a proper link.

lines.text: Which job would you pick for me? Pick quick, I'll change my mind in a breath.

replies.text: Ferrier! Yes! Walk on! ...Wait, I changed. Hearthkeeper. No. Ferrier. You're right.
Chartmaker! I'd draw you, and you'd be very small and very pale. I'd give you a crest so you'd look right.

lines.text: Is it all right to want a job that's nobody's job? Like Strider-whisperer? Or Gap-hopper? Or Warm-spot-finder?

replies.text: Really? Then I'm going to be all three. Warm-spot-finder first.
It will be! Someone had to invent all the others.

lines.text: Don't tell, but I don't want to pick. When you pick, it's forever. I want to be a bit of everything. Is that allowed, or does everybody pick?
I asked the Ferrier if I could ride the barge when I'm big. She said only if I can haggle. So I practise on the strider. She isn't very good at it. I win every time.
You're the first I've told: I'd like to be a Hearthkeeper, but I'm scared of the carrying. Hands go black. I'd be good at it, though, wouldn't I? You think so too? Good.
When I'm big and have a hut, there'll be a seat by my hearth with your name scratched on it. The best seat. I'll have lots of quartz points. I'll be a Chartmaker too.
*brrr* I'll be a Hearthkeeper. Then I can sit in the hearth all the time. Right in the middle. Nobody will mind.
I'm n-not going to be a Quartzcutter. Not ever. N-never. Well. Maybe. When it's warm.

lines: I carry coal! Little lumps, one in each hand, from the pile to the hearth. I'm not supposed to run. I run a bit. It's good for the coal.
I'm in charge of the hot stones for guests. Seven for a very cold one, three for a chilly one. I count them out loud so nobody gets cheated.
I polish chains! You rub them with ash until you can see yourself in them. Then you see you've got ash on your nose. Then you rub that off. Then you see ash again.
I feed the striders. They eat out of my hand. Not my hand, the fungus on my hand. They pretend it's the hand. Then they sniff me like I'm a snack.
I hold the lantern when the Chainwright works. It's the most important job in the world. I'm not allowed to look away. I look away sometimes. The sparks are so pretty.
I'm the best at sitting on the warm spot so it stays warm for the grown-ups. I'm paid in cream. Sometimes in a pat on the crest.
Helping is hard when you're small. Everything's too tall. The hearth, the doors, the posts. I help with the low things. The low things matter, grown-ups say, in a voice.
Sometimes they let me say the haze song at the hearth. I get the words wrong. Everybody smiles. I think that's what I'm for: getting the words wrong in a way they like.
When {neighbour} has a quarrel, I go and sit in the middle. Nobody can stay cross with a child between them. It's an old trick. Even the Hearthkeeper uses me for it.

lines.text: Do you help your family, shore-foot? Do you carry things? I'd carry things for you if you had things.

replies.text: Good! Helping's what keeps the heat in. Whoever helps stays warm.
*gasp* Rather not! That's allowed? I'd get a talking-to. A long one.

lines.text: What's the best thing about helping? Do you know? Shall I tell you?

replies.text: You get to be part of the chain. A link! A little one. The smallest link. But a chain needs smalls too.
Cream's very good. But no. It's being a link.

lines.text: I helped the Ferrier tie the barge, and she said good knot, and I think about it all the time. Good knot. It's the nicest thing anyone's said to me.
I'm allowed to watch the Chainwright now. From the doorway. Not inside. If I'm quiet, I can wipe the hammer. Wiping the hammer is a very serious job.
I snuck a warm stone to the old Quartzcutter, the one who always goes grey. He kept it under his sash and didn't tell. We're friends now. Don't tell the grown-ups.
I saved you a job, the best one. It's carrying a hot stone to my hut when I'm cold. I haven't told anyone it's you, because you're not hot, but you can carry.
*brrr* I'm helping by standing near the hearth. Somebody has to keep it company. And it's warm. Don't tell.
I tried to carry the coal but I dropped it. The coal wasn't cold. I was. I got scared.

topics.ask: What do you pretend to be?
lines: Ferrier! I tie a rope to a bucket and drag it round the pen walk, shouting walk on. The bucket doesn't, but it's very polite.
Hearthkeeper: I sit in the middle of the gap and say nobody may touch the hearth but me. Everyone has to ask. Then I say yes. Then they thank me. It's the best game.
Lava-angler is the quietest game. You hold a bit of chain with a stone on the end and wait. The first one to wiggle loses. I've never lost. I go as still as a pillar.
Chainwright is the loudest game. We tap two stones together and shout bang! Mother says it isn't a game. She says it's practice for headaches.
Quartzcutter we only play near the hearth. You pretend to be freezing and everyone brings you a warm stone. The best game, because the pretending works too well.
Chartmaker: you draw on the ground with a stick. The whole Mooring! Then somebody steps on it and you start again. The stepping-on is part of the game.
We have a game where one of us is a sky-mourner, and drifts about crying, and the rest hide. Whoever gets cried on is grey. It's scary because it's true. We play it all the time.
Gap-hopping is for any job, my brother says. A Ferrier hops gaps. So does an angler. So does a Chainwright, only louder. Nobody hops like a Chartmaker, though. They count the hops.
When a grown-up joins our game it goes very quiet, then very loud. They're bad at pretending. They pretend with their whole face. We love it.

lines.text: Want to play Ferrier? I'm the Ferrier. You're the shore-foot. You pay in fungus. Do you have fungus?

replies.text: Oh, fresh! Thank you. That's not how you're meant to play, but I love it.
Haggle! Good! That's the whole game. Three quarters, and you owe me a story.

lines.text: Can I tell you the rule of every game? There's only one. Ready? The hearth wins.

replies.text: Because the hearth is where everyone is trying to get back to. So it always wins. That's the rule.
It is fair! The hearth is the only fair thing. Grown-ups agree.

lines.text: I invented a game! It's called Link. You hang from a rail with one hand and someone hangs from you, and so on. The last one mustn't let go. Everybody lets go. It ends in a splash.
I put you in my games. I'm the Ferrier and you're the friend who gets a free fare. I always say for you, no fare. The other kids say that's not how it works. I say it is now.

My best game is Mooring. We build the whole Mooring out of stones and sticks on the pen walk. I'm the Hearthkeeper, he's the Chainwright, she's the Ferrier. You're the guest. Guests get the best seat.
In my game you're a famous Ferrier who crosses the whole sea in one go. I made you a barge of rocks. It's the best barge. It has a name: the Shore-foot's Own.
*brrr* I'm playing Hearthkeeper. I'm keeping the hearth. By sitting in it. Go on, ask me nicely.
I can't play. My legs are cold. We can play sitting-down Ferrier, though. You hold the reins. I count.

lines: Everyone and no one. I'm not an apprentice yet. I'm a watcher. Watchers stand by and learn what not to touch. I'm learning very fast.
The Ferrier says I can start on the pen walk with the calves. When I can lead a calf round without it sitting down, I'm ready to lead a barge. The calves sit down a lot.
The Hearthkeeper tests us with a hot stone. You hold it as long as you can. If you drop it, you carry it back. I carry it back every time. I like carrying it back.
The Chainwright gave me my first link to forge: a tiny one, with a bend. She said it's yours, don't hang it anywhere. I hid it in my hip cloth. It's the heaviest thing I own.
The Chartmaker lets us scratch a chart of our own hut. You have to put everything in. The warm spot, the sleeping spot, the spot I'm not supposed to know about. Everyone has one.
I'm too small for the cliffs. The Quartzcutter says I can go in my tenth year. I'm counting. I'm on nine and a bit. Don't tell my mother I want to go. She'd say I'm cold already.
The best teachers hum when they work. You can tell what they're thinking by the hum. Low means careful. High means good. Silent means run.
The first lesson is how to be cold. Not how to dodge it, how to be it, a little, so you don't panic. We stand at the edge of the deck, count slow, and go back. The count gets longer.
We learn the haze song a line at a time. The first line is just {chain}. The second says where the Mooring is. The third says how to get home. I know two.

lines.text: Did you have a teacher, shore-foot? Mine hits me with a look. Not a stick. A look.

replies.text: Was it a good one? Mine's the best. Mine says again and means well done.
By yourself? That sounds lonely. I'd miss the looks.

lines.text: Do you think I'll be good? At whatever I pick? Honest, please. Not nice.

replies.text: Honest and nice at once! That's the best kind. Now I have to be good so you weren't wrong.
Practise and see! That's what my teacher says. Is everybody secretly my teacher?

lines.text: We have a game with our teachers. They say the old words, we say them back, and whoever laughs first loses. I always lose. Teacher says it's fine to lose. I'm very fine at it.
My teacher's seams are dim. She's old. She still shows me how to hammer: one two, one two. When she shows me, they shine, just for a breath. I think that's what teaching is for.
Teacher told me you can't learn a thing till you've been bad at it twenty times. I'm on fourteen. Six more and I'll be good. I'm saving the last ones for you to see.
I asked my teacher for a second teacher, and she said yes, if it's you. You don't have to teach me anything. Just stand there and be a friend. I'll learn from the standing.
*brrr* My teacher says I can't learn when I'm grey. So I'm learning to be warm. It's the hardest lesson.
I can't hold the stone. My fingers are numb. Teacher says that's the lesson. I don't like the lesson.
We greet with 'warm to you', and the answer is 'and to your chain'. A stranger may answer 'and to my feet'. We'll allow it. Once.

lines: Never cross a bridge in silence. Hum, cough, sing, anything. The folk at the far end need to know a weight is coming, and the bridge likes company.
Never step over a hearth-stone. Walk round it, however far. Stepping over says the fire is beneath you, and nothing on this sea is beneath the fire.

lines.text: Borrow a coal and bring it back with a pinch added. The pinch is the thanks. A coal returned exact is a coal returned cold, and folk remember.

replies.text: Then you'll never want for a seat. A pinch costs nothing and buys a whole welcome.
Not here it isn't. Here a coal is a loan, and a loan has manners. Think it over by the fire.

lines: Leave any deck and you leave its lantern lit, whoever's deck it is. A dark deck behind you is a promise broken, and the Mooring counts those.

lines.text: Refuse the first hot stone and you've insulted the house. Take it, hold it, even if you glow like a vent, and pass it on after. Kindly.

replies.text: Gladly! Good manners already. Nobody has to teach you the hard parts.
It isn't about being warm. It's about being offered. Take it, hold it, hand it back. Manners are the heat we make.

lines: A borrowed chain comes home polished, even if it was lent for a breath. When {neighbour} returns mine gleaming, I know they've broken something.
Find a bad link and you strike it three times on the nearest post so the whole Mooring hears. Hide a bad link and you've hung every one of us from it.
We never haggle over three things: a hot stone, a seat for the cold, and a coal for a child. Haggle over those and you lose your own seat.
Don't name a strider calf until it has stood on its own legs. Name it early and it sits down for life. The one in our pen is called Eventually.

lines.text: A gift is handed over warm side first, if it has one. The giver turns away while it's opened, so nobody has to look pleased on purpose.
My trade has its own custom: when two Ferriers pass on the wade out or home they clink chains across the gap and trade news before price. Whoever clinks last pays for the gossip.

lines: We never say a cooled person's name in anger. In sorrow, yes. In praise, yes. In a haggle, yes. They would want us to win with it.

lines.text: Our huts have no doors, only gaps, so we cough at the gap and wait for a cough back. Shore-feet knock, I'm told. Do you knock where you come from?

replies.text: Knock and wait! Civilised. We cough and wait. Same idea, less bruising.
Walk in! To a hut with a magma seam in the floor? Cough first. Always cough first.

lines: Pour nothing wet into the sea. Ash, yes. Words, yes. Wet, never. Ash is how we apologise to the sea, and we apologise to it often.
Point at the hearth with your chin, never a finger. A finger says the fire is yours. The fire has never been anyone's, and it knows it.

lines.text: For kin the hot stone is left in the doorway before they ask. That's the whole of being kin. You get it first, and the asking is a formality.
If I ever hand you the end of a chain, hold it and don't pull. That's trust in our tongue: someone holds your end and doesn't pull.
In {village} a spare hot stone hangs on every bridge post for anyone who goes grey mid-crossing. Take one, leave one. Everybody leaves one. Nearly.
The Hearthkeeper's custom is the oldest: nobody speaks while the fire is fed. Even a sneeze waits. We have swallowed sneezes for generations.
A Chainwright lends the chain, the anvil and the apprentice, and never the hammer. It knows one hand and sulks in any other.
Strangers only get the customs that can't be got wrong. The rest you learn by sitting here and being corrected. Kindly. Mostly.
Out here there's nobody to keep customs for, so I keep them for the sea: lantern lit, hum on the bridge, pinch on the coal. The sea notices.
*shiver* Customs. Warm to you. Done. Next question, preferably one with a coal in it.
The custom is to leave a cold Magmari alone. You've broken it. I'll forgive you for a coal. A big one.
Custom says be polite. Custom has never been cold. *teeth chatter* Ask me after I thaw.
The greatest is the Long Stoking. When the High Swell comes, every family feeds the hearth one coal for each person they miss, and says the name over it as it burns.

replies.text: The kindest we have. Also the one we get through fastest. I've never understood why.
That's a question for kin, and for a warmer sitting. I'll tell you it's a short name, and I say it slowly.

lines.text: The High Swell is the great rising of the sea, once every swell. Every bridge rings at once, and we run out with spoons to ring them harder. It's the best noise there is.
The Square-Up is the festival I dread. Every debt on the Mooring is clinked square or forgiven, whatever its size, and nobody may haggle for a whole sitting. Folk go pale. Paler.

replies.text: Kind, and terrible. Half of us spend a whole swell building up debts so we'll have something to forgive. Don't tell the Hearthkeeper.
A debt carried too long goes hard and cold like shore stone, and sooner or later someone gets hit with it.

lines: At the Dimming every lantern is turned low and we sit in the near-dark and say the chain-names of the burned Moorings, one by one. Nobody laughs. Nobody leaves early.
A first crossing is a feast too. The Mooring waits on the pier with a hot stone for the new Ferrier. If the fare was fair, the stone is hers. If not, she holds it anyway.

lines.text: At the Haggle-Fair the Moorings meet on a sea of bridges, and the best haggler wins a ring of chain to wear. It's never the same Mooring twice, so every Mooring says the judges are bought.

replies.ask: May I haggle at the Fair?
replies.text: A shore-foot at the Fair! We'd haggle over the price of your seat first. You'd lose. Then you'd be one of us.
As honest as a haggle gets, which is not very. Everyone leaves sure they were robbed fairly. That's the prize.

lines: When a calf first stands, the Mooring scratches its name on a pebble and hangs it on its tether. The pebbles pile up behind the pen in a heap of names. Some calves have three.
Any good thing can be a small feast: a first link forged, a first haggle won, a calf that finally stands. All you need is a hot stone, a speech and someone to pretend to listen.
Every feast has the same shape. The hearth is fed first, then the eldest, then the guests, and then the haggling begins. A feast without haggling is only a meal, we say.

lines.text: At the Long Stoking the youngest feeds the first coal, with the eldest's hand over theirs. The hearth flares. It always flares. Hearthkeepers say it's draught. It isn't draught.

lines: I miss the High Swell when I'm away from it. The whole sea hums and every strider in the pen tries to sing along. You haven't heard anything until you've heard a strider sing.

lines.text: A Ferrier never crosses at a High Swell. The barge stays tied while we ring the dock chain with the rest. It's the one time the sea gets to cross itself.
The Long Stoking is my busiest sitting: forty coals, forty names, and I may not drop one. I practise with pebbles for a whole swell first. Hands steady, mouth shut.
For the High Swell I forge a fresh ring-link for every bridge post, so each post has something new to ring against. It's the one feast where the banging is welcome.
At the Square-Up I give the sea back something: a link, a lantern-piece, a tooth, whatever the deep gave me that swell. Then we're square. I rest easier.
I cut a clear quartz for every Long Stoking and set it by the hearth. It doesn't burn. It only catches the flames, so there's something to look at while we remember.
At the Dimming I chart nothing. I sit in the near-dark with my quartz point in my lap and my hands still. The burned Moorings are the only charts I never finish.
I forgave {neighbour} a debt I'd carried since my first crossing, and felt strangely bare for a whole sitting after. A debt is company. Nobody warns you.
Come to the next Stoking, friend, and I'll set a coal in your hand. Bring a name to say over it. You needn't say whose. You only have to say it aloud and let it burn.
Festivals? We have a few. Stay long enough and you may see one. Strangers watch from the pier with a hot stone and keep quiet, and we think better of them for it.
{village} keeps the Swell loudest of all the Moorings. Our bridges are the oldest, so they ring deepest, and the old ones on the deck go quiet and misty-eyed at the sound.
I keep the Swell alone out here. I stand on a pillar and strike a length of chain on it, and the sea rings back. It isn't the same. It's close enough to ache.
*shiver* Festivals are for the warm. I'm not warm. Ask me when I am and I'll list every last one.
The best festival is the one where I sit by the hearth and nobody asks me for anything. Hold it with me. *teeth chatter*
Right now I'm celebrating Sitting Very Close To The Fire. Guests must be quiet. You're a guest.

lines: A rust-red moss grows on the warm side of the pillars. We scrape it, dry it on hot stones and crumble it into everything. It tastes of smoke and warm iron. Better than it sounds.

lines.text: Smoulder is our drink: charcoal chips steeped in warm cream until it's dark and thick as slag. Served in quartz cups so it can't burn through. It tastes the way a hearth feels.

replies.text: From a spoon, with someone standing by. It's stronger than it looks. Stronger than you look.
Sensible. Ask for it lukewarm. We'll set it near the hearth and call it cold. Everyone wins.

lines.text: Sugar grows in tiny crystals on the lips of the vents. The little ones scrape it with their nails and the Chainwrights hoard it. Nobody admits to the hoarding.

replies.text: A sliver, to see how you take it. Ask for a second and I'll know you're a Chainwright at heart.

lines: Ash-loaves are moss ground fine, pressed flat and baked in the embers until black. They look like a punishment and taste better than that. One loaf lasts a whole crossing.
A meal must be too hot for a shore-foot and just right for us. If you can hold the bowl bare-handed, it's a snack.
Dark smoulder with a pinch of blaze powder is for the half-frozen. One cup and your seams light up like a Ferrier's lantern. Two cups and you start to sing.

lines.text: When the hearth runs low we fast, all of us, until it's fed again. Nobody eats from a cold hearth. If the fire is hungry, so are we.

replies.text: It keeps the hearth fed first and the belly second. We've never let it go out, so it works.
A little. Hunger is the price of a bright fire. Cheap, honestly.

lines: From shore traders we buy dried things: strips of smoked something, hard nuts, once a grey loaf so tough it cracked a tooth. It hangs on the wall now. Nobody's brave enough to try again.

lines.text: A Ferrier eats standing, one hand on the tether: cream off a stick, moss in the cheek. Never sit to eat on the sea. The sea notices, and tips the barge.
I cook on the hearth's rim with slabs, stones and a long iron paddle, all by feel and by hum. A good meal hums when it's ready. A bad one clears its throat.
Cube cream tastes best straight off the hook, still warm and wobbling a little. I know. I know. Don't tell the cubes.
Chainwrights eat at the anvil: cream on a hot stone beside the forge, scooped with the flat of a hammer. Greasy, sooty and glorious.
On the shore I eat cold moss-bread. Cold food! It's a crime against the stomach, and I pay for it in grumbling all the way up the cliff.
I eat while I draw, which is why half my charts have little rings on them. Smoulder cups. You can tell exactly when I was happy.
Shore-feet eat cold bread and call it a meal. I once watched one bite an apple, raw, in the open air. My seams dimmed for them.
