replies.text: Cold, wet and crunchy, and lovely? Say no more. I'll try to picture it without shivering.

replies.ask: I'll bring you a warm loaf.
replies.text: A warm loaf! Now you're a friend. Bring it hot or don't bring it. And I'll tell the Mooring about you.

lines: Piglins roast hoglin on spits and the smell crosses the whole sea. We shut the vents when the smoke drifts our way. It isn't hatred. It's manners.

lines.text: A true friend gets the heel of the cream: the last scrape of the slab, gone dark and sweet and a little burnt. Best bite there is. You'll get it from me.
My mother's cream-and-moss pot has a secret in it I won't tell you. I'll cook it for you instead. That's how you keep a secret and share it at once.
Food? We'll feed you if you sit. Cream, moss, a cup of smoulder if you're brave. A guest's first bowl is free, whatever the haggling says.
*shiver* Food. Hot food. Hot. Please say hot. Tell me about food when it's in my hand.
A cold meal is an insult to the cook, the eater and the pot. I'll eat nothing. Nothing is warmer.
Smoulder. That's all I'll say. If you're asking whether I'd like a cup, yes. Immediately.

lines: Before a meal we say 'fire first'. The cook comes second. The cook accepts this, grumbling, because the cook is usually me.
Never eat in front of a calf being born. The mothers take it for boasting. They may be right, a little.

lines.text: Hot stones are for hands, not for eating. Every shore-foot guest tries to bite one exactly once. We pretend not to watch, then tell it at the hearth for a whole sitting.
I was the loudest baby on the deck, they tell me. My mother says my first word was a price. Her first word to me was no. Neither of us has changed.

lines: Babies sleep in a hollow of warm basalt on the hearth's rim, a cradle-stone, and everyone who passes gives it a pat. Mine was worn smooth by three generations of pats.
I hid in the strider pen for a whole feeding once, and a calf adopted me. It stood over me humming. They found us both drowsing, steaming like two hot stones.

lines.text: My grandmother taught me to haggle with pebbles. She'd sell me one for two links, I'd sell it back for one, and she'd cry that I'd ruined her. I'd never felt so powerful.

replies.text: Every time but the last. The last time she sold me my own pebble back. I'm still paying.
The only sensible way to raise one. A child who can't haggle at six is a Piglin at sixty.

lines.text: I once stuck my head in a vent to see what it did. It puffed, and my crest has leaned left ever since. Everyone says it gives me character.

replies.text: It tickled. Then it puffed. Then my head rang for a whole feeding. Worth it, for the story.
Foolish, yes! That's what small is for. Be foolish early. You've no time for it later.

lines.text: The grown-ups taught us the rules by scolding: mind the crust, mind the pillar, mind your chain. Mind, mind, mind. I was the only one of my cousins who ever minded.

replies.text: A minder! Good. The world needs a few of us to catch the rest when they fall.
Ha! Then you'd have got on with my cousins. They taught me everything I know about falling.

lines: My crest itched for a whole swell while the nubs grew up into a crest. Nothing helps. You rub it on a pillar. Mine was the third from the pier, and the pillar has a groove now.

lines.text: We dared each other to walk to the shore end of the pier without a hot stone. I walked furthest. I also went grey and had to be carried home. Worth it.

replies.text: For three feedings I wasn't allowed near a bridge. I counted the bridges from the doorway gap. Forty-one. I know them all.
My cousin, who couldn't stop laughing, which is why we both went grey. I owe them one.

lines: My father carried me on his shoulders at a High Swell so I could ring the bridges with a spoon. I rang the wrong one. Everyone said it was the best-sounding wrong one they'd heard.
I meant to be a Ferrier until I rode a barge in a swell and was sick over the rail. The strider looked back at me. I can still see her face.

lines.text: I grew up on the pier. They tied me to a post with a long chain so I wouldn't wander, and I learned the whole sea from the end of that chain. I'm still tied. The chain is longer.
I was the child who always sat nearest the ring. They tried to move me back. I moved forward again. They gave up and gave me a job.
I fished with a thread and a bent link off the pen walk and caught a calf by the leg. It forgave me. Eventually. The calf, I mean.
I made my first link from a pen-gate hinge. The gate fell over. My mother hung the link on the post anyway. It's the bent one near the bottom. You've been looking at it all this time.
I was sent to the shore as a punishment once, for stealing cream. I came back grey and in love with the quiet. They have been looking for a punishment ever since.
I scratched my first chart on a pen wall: the whole Mooring, with a cross where the cream was kept. Most accurate chart I ever made, and it got me into trouble.
My ridges came in crooked, one taller than the other, so I hung chain loops on the short one to make up. Everyone thinks it's a fashion now. It isn't a fashion.
My ridge came in late and I was the last of my cousins to stand tall. They called me Little Pillar. It stuck, and now I'm the tallest in the family. Names do that.
Everywhere I look in {village} I got into trouble once. That pillar, that bridge, that seat. The Mooring keeps a child's mischief the way it keeps chain: in plain sight and in good order.
I grew up in a proper Mooring, with a hearth and a hundred voices. Out here I miss the noise more than the warmth. A child can grow on noise alone.
I was afraid of the sky-mourners, and I used to hide in the hearth-ash to be another colour. It fooled nobody. I felt safer anyway.
I was sure the Mooring would always stay exactly as it was. Then my grandmother's link was hung up for good, and I learned how things go. I still go and touch it.
I was a handful. I'll tell you more when you've sat with us a few more times and I know whose side you're on.
*shiver* Small? I was small and cold. Same as now, only nearer the ground.
Childhood. Warm. I remember warm. Don't make me remember it grey.
Ask what I was like and I'll tell you after I thaw. Briefly: loud. Right now: quiet. Grumpy.

lines: It begins without a word. You sit one seat nearer at the ring each sitting, until your crests warm each other and everyone has noticed except the two of you.
A courting gift is a coal in a cage of cut quartz: fire you can see but not touch, and not lose. The cage takes a Quartzcutter a whole swell. Courting is dear. Love is cheap.

lines.text: When two are sure, they take one chain, one at each end, and pull. They go on until the hearth hums back, however long that takes. It's the Long Pull. Nobody has ever let go.

replies.text: The longest I know of took a whole feeding. The shortest, a breath. We say a short pull means they were sure already.
Nobody has. That's rather the point. A let-go would be a no, and the hearth would hum for that too.

lines: Then comes the Double Link: two links forged through each other and hung together on the post, brighter than any single one. The Chainwright takes no payment. They'd rather be remembered for it.
Being linked doesn't end the haggling. It improves it. Nobody haggles like two folk who know exactly what the other will give up.

lines.text: My partner and I share a hut, a hearth-stone and a quarrel about which of us snores. It is not me. I have asked the pillar.

replies.text: The pillar said nothing, which is just what a snorer would say.

lines: A baby is hot as a coal and its parents are cold as ash within a feeding. They take turns in the hearth. A new family is mostly a rota and a great deal of steam.
A grandmother rules the hut. She sits nearest the fire, speaks last and wins every time. Nobody has ever beaten one in a haggle, and the Mooring has tried.
Cousins are rivals by birth and friends by habit. Mine has beaten me at ember-catch for forty swells. I have forgiven nothing.
An aunt keeps the spare coals. She'll find you a hot stone the moment you go grey and a lecture the moment you're warm.
When one of a Double Link cools for good, the one left polishes only their own link and lets the other dull slowly beside it. It's gentle. It is not nothing.

lines.text: My third ridge-loop was my partner's gift, forged from the link they won in our first real haggle. They let me win it. I never told them I knew.
My sash holds one link from my partner for every swell we've come through. It has grown heavy. It's the only weight I've never wanted to put down.

lines: Love is a hot coal in the hand. You can hold it a while and learn to carry it, or drop it and hiss. Most of us do both, in that order.

lines.text: Do you link with someone, in your world? Or do you leave it loose? It's rude to ask, so I'm asking before anyone can stop me.

replies.text: Aloud! With no chain? Brave. We'd want it in iron at the very least.
Alone. Hm. It isn't bad, with a good hearth. I hope you have a good hearth.

lines.text: A Ferrier's partner learns to wait on the pier. They wave the barge out and wave it in. Mine hangs a lantern on the dock post, and I wade home toward it from the open sea.
Two Hearthkeepers once fell in love over a fire neither would leave unwatched. They fed it in turns for a whole swell, nodding as they passed. They were linked beside it in the end.
I caught my partner's eye by hooking their hip cloth with a line. I've told it as an accident for a long time. It was not entirely an accident.
I forged my own Double Link for my own joining, and tested it in a bridge first. Romantic, I know. My partner wept, and then tested it again.
I cut my partner's cage-quartz on the cliffs, singing their name to keep the cold off. The quartz came out perfect. So did the cough.
I charted my partner's usual seat on every deck before I ever spoke to them. It's embarrassing, as a chart. It's very accurate.
Here's something you should know: I have never stopped caring for someone who's gone. The hearth is big enough to hold that too. Yours would be, I think.
In {village} everyone knows who's linked to whom, who's courting, and who's pretending not to be. The hearth post is a map of the whole Mooring's heart.
I'm alone out here, but there's a link on a far-off post that's still warm. It's enough, mostly. Mostly is the Magmari word for enough.
*shiver* Love is a warm hearth and someone's back to lean on. I have neither at the moment. Ask me later.
Family. Hearth. Warm. Cold. Look, I'm too grey to be soft just now.
Ask me about love when I can feel my fingers. I'm told it's a different answer.

lines: The War of the Hoard is old enough that we don't tell it as a story. We tell it as chores: whose job it was to count the coal, whose to lash the striders, whose to look away.
Every family has a fare-bowl, the quartz bowl the war coal was counted into. Ours holds ash now. Nobody has ever said to throw it out, and nobody has ever filled it with coal.
My grandmother said the worst was the quiet before a crossing. A war-band doesn't shout when it boards. The shouting is for the shore. The boarding is for the sea, and the sea listens.
Old Ferriers say: count the faces first, then the coal. It's the one saying we got out of the war. Everyone says it. Nobody says when they learned it.

lines.text: A Ferrier called Pumice refused the last band. Her Mooring cast her out, and she lived on a pillar in the deep for a swell. When the burning came, hers was the one empty barge. She carried forty.

replies.text: She was tired of counting. The bravery came after. Most of it does.
Too late for her, kind enough for us. Her link hangs low on the post, and nobody passes it without a touch.

lines: Those who ferried the Piglins aren't hated here. They aren't praised either. We nod, and leave a gap beside them at the hearth, and they sit in it. Nobody says why.

lines.text: A Piglin captain thanked my great-grandfather at the landing. Said it quietly, in plain words, like anyone. He never forgot it. He never forgave himself for remembering.

replies.text: Perhaps. That's what keeps me awake. A thank-you from the wrong person is the heaviest gift there is.
No. It changes nothing, and I carry it anyway. That's what nothing weighs.

lines.text: The elders signed the fares and the young ones led the striders. That's what I remember when someone calls it a Piglin war. It was an elders' war, paid for by everyone else.

replies.ask: Where I'm from it's the same.
replies.text: The same! Then it's not a Magmari failing, only a failing. A small comfort. I'll take it.
Wrong, rich and loud. A grim trio. The young were right and quiet, which paid worse.

lines: After the burning, the Moorings that were left shared their coal with the ones that had none, and nobody wrote down who owed whom. It's the one decent thing the war gave us.
When the little ones ask why we won't ferry Piglins now, we say: because we know what they carry. It's the shortest true answer we have.
I've heard the Weft took bone from both shores' dead for their needles. Maybe. All I know is a bone needle came home in a barge rail, still threaded, and nobody could bear to pull it out.
We lost the old songs of the crossings. They were all about gold. The Ferriers burned the words and kept the tunes, and now the tunes have no words, and they go round and round.

lines.text: Every Ferrier swears the oath at the pier, and every Ferrier knows what it answers. I think it's the heaviest thing I've ever said aloud. I say it lightly because that's easier.
The war hearths burned bright and cheap. After, we let them go dark on purpose and relit them from older coals. A fire remembers what it was lit for.
War-chain was heavy, ugly and quick to make. After it, my family kept one rule: never make a chain faster than you could mend it. It's a slower trade and a better one.
That's a hearth topic, and you're nearly a hearth friend. I'll tell you the small things first. The big ones wait.
Between you and me: when the sea is quiet and the hearth is low I think about the fares. Not the coal. The faces. I wish I'd been braver than my grandfather. I'm not sure I would have been.
In {village} the war lives on the hearth post: one black link at the bottom, from the barge-chain, left unpolished. Children touch it and are told: that's the one we're sorry for.
*shiver* The war. Cold. Both cold. Ask me about the war when I've forgotten the cold.
War talk is cold talk. I'm cold enough without it. Next.
Grey and sorry and not in the mood. Another sitting. A warm one.
I haul war-chain up from the deep and never melt it. It's still bright as when it sank. We hang it on the pen gate, so every calf walks home under the war.
The Piglins dug the shore cliffs for quartz, as fare. I still find their picks, rust-red in the white. I leave them where they stand. They've earned the cliff.
The war crossings are the only charts I draw backwards, from the landing to the Mooring. It reminds me we sent them there. We know the way they went far too well.
Out here I trade war stories with the sea. It keeps them. It never says I told you so, which makes it better company than most Moorings.

lines: Our word for peace is 'bridges up and nobody hurt'. Anything more is a story. The Piglins would have to give up gold, the Withren their grief, and neither of them will.

lines.text: Which of the other four would I trust with my chain? I'd argue it till the hearth burned low. The Ghastkin, in the end. They want nothing but to be left to cry, and I can leave a person alone.

lines: Ordinary folk don't fight the old grudges. The grudges fight us. We're born into them like a chain name, with no say, and we hand them on without noticing.

lines.text: I met a Weft at the forest edge who bowed with all four arms at once. I bowed back with one. We both felt we'd lost.
The little ones have a rhyme: Piglin shouts, Withren sighs, Weft ties knots, Ghastkin cries. Nobody has ever finished the verse about us. I suspect it's about haggling.

replies.text: Haggle! Of course. It doesn't rhyme and it's true. The children will love it.
Shiver! Cheeky. Yes. We shiver and we haggle, and then we shiver about haggling.

lines: A Ghastkin child, I think, is who I'd sit beside first. They haven't learned to cry yet, and I've nothing against a creature that hasn't learned what ruins me.

lines.text: If the Piglins took off their gold for one breath, I'd give them my best seat. Then I'd count my chains. Peace is trust, and trust is arithmetic.

replies.text: It isn't? Then what is it? Go on. I'll listen. Not for long, I'm a haggler, but I'll listen.
I count exactly as much as the Piglins steal. We differ on how much that is.

lines.text: I'd trade with the Weft this very sitting if they'd sell us one stalk of warped fungus. One! I'd pay in chain. It's always a stalk that keeps old enemies apart.

replies.text: You? You'd be wading into a net. But if you came out with a stalk, I'd give you a whole chain.
We did, for a long age. They answered with a net. Politeness has limits, and that forest is one.

lines: The Withren and we are two halves of one quarrel. They blame our barges, we blame their Wither, and under the blame we're both just sore. Sore is hard to haggle with.
A Ghastkin tear puts out our glow, so they sit at the far edge of any meeting, politely. We have a peace of distances. It's the cheapest kind and the most reliable.
Nobody here wants another war. That's what the Piglins can't be made to believe. We pull up the bridges because we want nothing from them, not because we want their gold.
My grandfather said the five peoples share exactly one belief: each of us is sure the other four started it. It's the one thing we have never argued about.

lines.text: I'd ferry the other peoples again if all four asked together and every Mooring agreed. I'd want it carved under the pier first, and the fare in something that doesn't melt.
The hearth would take any guest who came in cold, whoever they were, if they left the gold outside. That's the only rule. They never do. That's the only problem.
A chain doesn't care whose hands hold it. I've thought of forging one with five ends, one for each people, to see who lets go first. I haven't the iron.
I fish where the sea touches every shore. The Piglins' catch is gold, ours is cream, the Weft's is nothing, and the sky-mourners hang over the lot of us. We're one sea whether we like it or not.
From the cliffs I've seen the smoke of three other peoples' fires: Piglin black, Withren blue, a soft Weft glow. They look lovely from far off. Everybody does.
I draw a grey ring round every other people's land. A ring means keep away. Someone ought to draw a bridge to the ring, in time. I'm not allowed. I want to be.
Peace? That's a big word to hand a stranger. Ask me when I know whose side you're on, and which of us you'd sit beside at a hearth.
I'd like you to be the bridge, shore-foot. You go where we can't, and hear what we never would. Tell each of them one kind thing about the others and see what happens. A small start.

replies.text: Try. That's all anyone's done. If you win one kind word out of a Weft, I'll cook you a real meal.
It is. Sorry. A good friend shouldn't ask. Forget I did, and have a hot stone.

lines.text: At {village} we keep the bridges high and the talk low. A Mooring that talks of peace out loud is one that's afraid of war. We talk about the price of coal.
Alone out here I'm no use to anyone's war. I like that. A wild Magmari is a peaceful Magmari, with no chain to defend.
*shiver* Peace is a warm hearth. War is a cold bridge. That's all I know. Go away.
Don't ask me about the others. I'm too cold to be fair to anyone.
Peace? I'd settle for a coal. A coal first, then the other peoples.

lines: A dark hearth. Not for the cold, though the cold is real. For the silence after. Our Moorings burned once, and a hearth gone dark is how it starts in the dreams.
The long stillness. Going grey on the shore with nobody near and slowly forgetting to be afraid. That's the part: you stop being afraid, and then you stop.
A bridge that doesn't ring when I step. A good bridge answers. One that stays quiet is thinking about letting go.
The deep thing. Everyone says something slow and big lives under the sea. I don't fear it. I fear the moment it stops being slow.

lines.text: Another burning. I don't fear the Withren so much as the idea: that someone could build the Last Answer again, out of grief and good reasons. The good reasons are the dangerous part.

replies.text: You say it like it's up to one person. Maybe it is. Say it again where the Withren can hear.
Exactly. I knew you were the kind to see it. Not a stranger. Sit closer.

lines: Being the link that gives. Not a bad person, only the link that fails at the wrong moment while everyone on the chain pays for it.
My link going dull because nobody remembers to polish it. Not dying. Being forgotten. A link hung and then left is the loneliest thing on the post.

lines.text: Rain. I know you laughed. Water falling out of the sky is the one thing I'll never fully believe in, and I'd go dark on the spot if it came.

replies.text: Gentle! Gentle water. There's a pair of words I'll turn over at the hearth for a long time.
Thank you. That's the kindest thing you've said this sitting, and you've said some kind things.

lines.text: That the sky-mourners will stop crying. If they stopped, it would mean they'd forgotten. I would rather they cried forever than forgot.

replies.text: No. I don't think they can. Thank you for saying it as though you knew.
*seams dim* Maybe. For them. Not for us. We would be the ones left remembering alone.

lines.text: That the little ones will lose the haggle, the rhythm of it. It's how we're us. If they stop, we're only cold folk with a lot of chain.

replies.text: They do. Last time a child sold me my own cream for two links. I've never been prouder or poorer.
New ways. Hm. As long as they argue about the price, I'll call it ours.

lines.text: Losing a fare. Not to a rival: to the sea. I've never lost one, and I check the barge three times for it, and I lie awake over it. Fear is a good Ferrier. It checks the barge.
That I'll teach it wrong. A Hearthkeeper's craft goes by hand, and my apprentice has my mistakes in her fingers now. I hope the good ones too.
The line that doesn't pull back. Not a snag. A nothing. A line going down and down and no sea at the end of it.
A bridge failing under a child. Never a grown one. A child. I walk behind every bridge I make until the little ones have crossed it a hundred times.
The quiet on the shore. I tell everyone it's the cold. It's the quiet. It sounds as if it were waiting for me to say something I can't.
A pillar moving. One pillar, a stride off its mark, and every chart I ever scratched is a lie. I check them against the sea when nobody's looking.
I fear forgetting the names of the burned Moorings. I have forty by heart. Every swell one gets fuzzier, so I say them over on a pillar, like checking a knot.
You, shore-foot. I fear for you. A friend with no glow, among sky-mourners and Piglins and Withren raiders. Take care. If you go grey, come here first.
That's a closer question than I like. I'll answer small: I fear cold, dark and forgetting. Most of us do. Ask me again when we're better friends.
In {village} we're afraid in a crowd, which is the best way. I look across the ring and see a dozen others pretending not to be, and I feel braver.
Out here I fear most that nobody would know. If I went grey on a pillar, the sea would take me and no link on any post would dull. That's why I talk to you, I think.
*shiver* Right now? This. Exactly this. Next question.
I'm afraid of how grumpy I am. It scares me what I might say if you stood any closer.
Fear? The cold. The grey. The not being warm. All in one. Ask me something easier.
A hearth big enough for the whole sea. I know it's absurd. Every Mooring builds it a little bigger each generation, as if that were the answer. I'm in favour of the answer.

replies.text: Don't tempt me. I've a chart in my head already: four rings wider than the biggest, with a seat for every one of us and a few for visitors.

replies.ask: A big hearth needs big fuel.
replies.text: It does! That's why I hope for a bigger hearth and a Weft who'll sell me a forest. I hope in pairs.

lines.text: A warm shore. A short one, a bay with a vent in it, where a Quartzcutter could cut in comfort. I'd be the first to move there, and I'd bring my own chair.

replies.text: You'd be my first guest! I'll make the chair a big one. Two chairs. You'll need one that doesn't melt.

replies.ask: Shores are cold for a reason.
replies.text: Shores are cold because nobody's lit one yet. That's all it is.

lines: To see a calf born with a coat the colour of a pale seam. The old Ferriers swear one was, once. I'd name her after the whole sea and never use the name for anyone else.
That the burned Moorings' chain-names are given again, in time, to new Moorings, and the new Moorings are just as proud and loud and bad at saving coal as the old ones were.
That my link on the post is still bright when I'm gone. Not from polishing. From somebody touching it on the way past. The touching is what keeps it bright.
That a sky-mourner will, in time, settle at the edge of a hearth, and be warm, and nobody will mind. I know. I know. I hope it all the same.
Grandchildren. A whole noisy pen of them, hot as coals and rude about it. I'd teach them every haggle I know, and then lose to them.
A long crossing with no sky-mourners, no Piglins and no swell. Only the strider humming and the sea going by. I've never had one. That's the hope.
I hope the Weft sell us a stalk some time. Just one. I'd hang it on the pier and tell the children about it for generations.

lines.text: To cross the whole sea in one go, shore to shore, no stopping. They say it can be done in a good swell with a strong strider. I've the strider. I need the swell.
To light a new hearth from our mother coal. I've carried coals for other folk's fires. I want one of mine, on a pillar that doesn't exist yet, in a Mooring with no name.
To pull up a link with my own family's mark on it, from before the burning. The sea gives things back if you ask well. I'm still asking.
To forge one chain so good it never needs mending. I know there's no such chain. Hope doesn't have to be sensible. That's why it holds.
To cut a quartz big enough for a wall, clear as a held breath, so we could see out and still be warm. Probably foolish. I'm told it's the best sort.
To chart the whole sea. Every pillar, every vent, every drift of sky-mourners, on one great slab. Then hang it in the hearth hall and let the children find themselves on it.
To be remembered as chain-kin. Not for the haggles. Just remembered, touched, polished. There's a link of yours on our post, kin. I hope yours stays bright too.
In {village} we hope for little, loudly, together: a calf, a bridge, a full hearth. Hoping in a crowd is easier. The hopes add up like links.
Out here I hope for a Mooring. Any Mooring with a hearth that has room for a wanderer and a chain. I'll haggle for the seat. I'll gladly lose.
*shiver* I hope for a coal. That's all. A coal. Then I'll hope for more.
Hope's a warm thing. I'm not. Come back when I am and I'll hope all over you.
Right now? Warmth. Every hope I have is warmer than I am. Next question.
I hope you stay a friend. The Mooring has had many guests, and few of them became part of the chain. It's pleasant to be hopeful about something already half true.

replies.text: I know. That's why I could say it. Hope is easier when it's mostly certain.
No. Nobody can. Then let's sit as long as we can. That's all a friend is.

lines.text: That someone, in time, writes our history on basalt and gets the haggling right. We aren't a people of wars. We're a people of arguments over a fire, with enough to eat.

replies.text: You'd do it? A shore-foot's hand in a Mooring's history? Do it in quartz so it lasts.
The children. And a shore-foot, some time, somewhere with a hot stone, laughing in the right places.

lines.text: A hope is a private thing, and you're one of the few I'd say them to. Not all of them. A Magmari keeps a few unspoken, like coals banked low.

lines: I hope the sea stays warm. It's a modest hope. But the sea is old, and old things have moods, and I'd like it in a good one.
I hope the little ones grow up with fewer grudges than we had. I tell them the Weft are smug, not wicked, and the Piglins loud, not hateful. They look at me as if I've gone strange.

topics.ask: Want to hear of my world?
lines: Tell me one thing about it. Just one. If it's wet, I'll leave my seat. If it's warm, I'll give you mine.
They tell me your sky has a fire in it that nobody feeds. It never goes out, except when it does. What sort of Hearthkeeper leaves a fire to itself?
And when that fire goes out of your sky, it's dark for a long while, and you lie down with your eyes shut and wait for it to come back? Eyes shut! In the dark! I'd never get used to it.

lines.text: Water lies on your ground in great flat patches, I hear, and falls from your sky, and people drink it. Drink it! And swim in it! My seams go grey just saying so.

replies.text: Lovely. Wet and lovely. I'll try to hold both words in my head at once and see if my seams survive.
I'd get used to a pit full of ash too, but I don't plan to try. Still, kindly meant.

lines: Green. They say your ground is green, a soft green that grows. I can't picture soft ground. Ours is hard and hot or hard and cold.
Trees are pillars that grow, with a cap of green on top. Our pillars don't grow. I confess I'm jealous, and a little suspicious.

lines.text: I've heard you keep animals that give you things: wool, eggs, milk. Milk! Warm, they say, when it's fresh. I'd give a chain to taste it. A short chain.

replies.text: Bring it warm. Bring it in a pot with a hot stone under it. Do that and I'll scratch your name on a name-stone for the next calf. A good one.
Sour! In this warmth? Then it's like most gifts. All right. A small sip, and a bucket of ash to hide it in.

lines.text: Do your people have a hearth in the middle, with everyone sat round? Or is everyone alone in a wooden box with a little fire in the corner?

replies.text: Good. A hearth. I knew you were civilised. Even without a glow, you were raised right.
Boxes. With a corner fire. *shivers* No wonder you wander so far from home looking for company.

lines: Your villagers haggle in green gems, I'm told. Little cut stones. A pale shore-foot swore a green stone was worth more than a chain, and I still can't see why.
They say cold comes out of your sky as white dust. Snow. I keep it as a story for children who won't eat their cream.

lines.text: Outsiders make Withers there, I'm told. Is it something everyone does where you live, or only a few fools?

replies.text: A few. Good. I'll tell the Mooring a few. We can live with a few.
*goes quiet* Then watch your own sky, shore-foot. Watch it very carefully.

lines: What do your people do for warmth? Wrap themselves in cloth? In the skins of beasts? I'd have thought a person would simply stand nearer a fire.

lines.text: Your world has ferries? Boats on water, pushed by sticks? A passenger told me, laughing through the whole crossing. I'd like to see one. From the shore. A long way inland.
Does your world keep its fires lit? Does anyone watch them? I worry about your hearths, shore-foot, all alone without a keeper.
They fish in water with a stick and a thread, and eat the catch. Wet, cold and swimming. I can't imagine a duller creature to love.
Your iron comes out of the ground in lumps and you melt it in little fires. Little fires! No wonder it's dear. Bring me a lump and I'll show you what a proper fire does.
Do you have quartz in your world? White, cold, ringing? If you don't, I'd weep for you. If you do, I'd like to see where you cut it. I might forgive your sky.
Your world must be one great chart. Draw it for me with a stick in the ash. Ground first, then the sky. I'll copy it onto basalt, if you'll allow.
If I could cross to your world I'd go once, just once, and see the sky-fire for myself in a good shawl. Then home to the hearth. You'd carry me, wouldn't you?
A shore-foot who talks of another world! Sit. Say it slowly. I'm still deciding whether to believe you, and a story with a fire in it will help.
At {village} we all listen when a shore-foot tells of the other world. It's the best entertainment we get outside of gossip, and the gossip is about who believed you.
Out here I've had no stories but my own for ages. Whatever your world is, I can't picture it, but I'd like you to try. Go slowly and don't leave out the fires.
*shiver* Your world? Wet and cold, I expect. Don't tell me. I'm cold enough.
A world I haven't seen. Another time. A warm one.
Everything in your world is wet or green or both, I've heard. I haven't the fire to hear about it now.

lines: There's Mother, and Father, and Grandma, and my brother who's the worst, and my cousins who are the loudest, and Auntie who keeps the coals. And the calf, but she doesn't count. She counts a bit.
My grandma sits closest to the fire and tells everyone what to do. She's very small and very hot. I think she's the real Hearthkeeper and the Hearthkeeper just works for her.

lines.text: My brother says I'm the baby, but I'm not! I'm a medium. I'm in the middle of being big and being small.

replies.text: I know! I grew a whole finger this swell. Grandma measured it with a bit of chain.
Not small! Medium! And hot. Medium and hot.

lines: Mother's hands smell of ash and iron. Father's smell of cream. Mine smell of both, so I'm a perfect mix.
My cousin can hop three gaps at once. I can hop two and a half. Don't tell. I'm practising the half.
Auntie lets me hold the spare coals, one at a time, if I say whose each one is. That's how I learned everybody's name.
My father can lift a bridge chain with one hand. My mother can haggle a Ferrier down to nothing. I can do neither. Yet.
When I was a baby I slept in the cradle-stone on the hearth. It's still there. I tried to fit last swell. I didn't fit. My feet hung out.
We sit round the hearth in order: Grandma first, then Mother, then Father, then me, then the baby, who can't sit yet so she's on Grandma's knee. We're a good ring.
My little sister is hot as a coal and she bites. She's the best sister in the world and I'm never leaving her alone.
I have a link on the hearth post. It's bright! Grandma says it will go dull when I'm grown, like hers. I said don't. She said it's a good thing. I don't think so.
My father says I look like him, my mother says I look like her, and Grandma says I look like nobody and that's why I'm perfect.
We have a family rule: no sulking at the hearth. If you sulk, you do it in the pen with the calves. Calves are good sulkers.
Sometimes Mother goes to the shore for quartz and I stand at the end of the pier and wave till she comes back. She always waves. Even when she's grey.

lines.text: Cousin Pebble tells me stories about the burned Moorings when we hide under the pier. They're scary! I love them. Don't tell Mother.

replies.text: Quietly, then. Once there was a Mooring with a hearth so big it lit the whole sea. Then it burned. The end. That's all I know.
But that's where the stories are! You can't hear them anywhere else. They only come out under the pier.

lines.text: Do you have a family? Do they have hot hands? Or are they cold like you?

replies.text: Far away! Do you miss them? I'd miss mine if I was far. I'd miss Grandma most. She smells of smoke.
None? Then you can borrow mine. Just a bit. Mostly Grandma. She'll like you.

lines.text: I don't know if I can tell you about my family. Mother says shore-feet are polite until they're not. Are you polite?

replies.text: Trying is good. Grandma says trying is the first half of polite. I'll tell you about the calf instead.
Always! That's what a not-polite one would say. I'll watch you.

lines.text: You're a little bit in my family now. Not the main part. The outside part, the part that comes round and gets cream.
Grandma said you can sit in her seat. Nobody sits in Grandma's seat! You're the first. I told everyone.
In {village} everybody's a bit family. Even {neighbour}. Especially {neighbour}, who's loud.
*brrr* My family's at the hearth. I'm not. I'm over here being cold. Alone.
M-my mother says I mustn't talk when I'm c-cold. But she's not here.
Family is warm. I'm n-not. Ask me by the fire.

lines: I wish for a strider of my own, a grey one, and I'd call her Humblehot. It isn't a real name. I made it up. It sounds warm.
I wish my nubs would grow faster. Grown-ups' crests are so tall they whistle. Mine just puff.
I wish I could stay by the hearth and never go grey again. Not forever forever. Till I'm old.
I wish for a whole bowl of dark cream that's just for me. I'd eat it and eat it and be the hottest in the Mooring.
I wish the sky-mourners would stop crying. Then I'd hug one. They're too big. I'd climb.
I wish I could see the shore up close, but only if I could get warm straight after. That's two wishes. One of them's greedy.

lines.text: I wish Mother would let me hop the big gap, between the pier and the pen walk. Nobody has hopped it. I'd be the first! ...Don't tell her I said.

replies.text: I am careful! I'm careful and then I jump. It's a good way.
You think so? Nobody ever says that! I'll practise. Don't tell Mother.

lines: I wish Grandma could be young again so she could hop gaps with me. She says she hopped the biggest one once. I think she's fibbing, but I hope not.
I wish I could talk to a strider and have her talk back. I think she'd say rude things. I'd like to hear them.
I'm scared of being left on the pier when the barge casts off. So I hold the rope and count everyone twice. Three times for a long crossing.
I'm scared of the long stillness. Mother says it's when you go so grey you stop. I check my nubs every breath. Still humming! Still humming!
I'm scared of the Piglin horns. Three low notes, and my tummy goes down to the sea floor. Then I remember we've got bridges that go up.

lines.text: I'm scared of rain. Is it real? Is it really water falling out of the sky? Please say it isn't. Please say it only happens to you.

replies.text: Only WET? That's the worst part! Don't say it again. Say something hot.
Never here! Good. I'll tell my nubs. They worry.

lines.text: I'm scared of being picked last for gap-hopping. So I say I don't want to play, and then I stand near. Do you do that?

replies.text: You did? And now? ...You're fine now? Then maybe I will be too. Grown-ups hide it well.
Just ask! That's what Grandma says. It's a lot to ask. But I'll try. Next feeding. Maybe.

lines: I wish I could forge a link of my own, a real one. Mine's only a bent one. But it's mine, and it's the only one I've made.

lines.text: I wish you'd come back every time. Every single time. Then I'd always have a shore-foot to show things to.

lines: I wish you had a glow! Just a small one, on your elbow. Then you wouldn't look so cold, and I'd see you from the far side of the pier.

lines.text: I wished on a hot stone that you'd always be my friend. You hold it till it goes cold. It took ages. My hands are still sore. It worked, so it's fine.
I'm not telling a stranger my wishes. You have to hold my hot stone first. It's the rule. Did you hold it? No? Then no wishes.
I wish {neighbour} would stop saying I'm too small. I'm not too small. I'm the right size for being small.
*brrr* I wish to be warm. That's all. It's a really small wish.
M-my wish is a hot stone. Do you have a hot stone? That's my wish.
I wish I wasn't c-cold. I wished it on the hearth. It's not listening.

loved.text: *crest flares bright* Oh, that's the good stuff! You've warmed me right up to the vents. Come back often.
For me? Heat you can hold! I'm going to sit with it in my lap and say nothing for a while.
That's a proper gift, the kind you give kin. I won't forget it, and neither will the hearth.
Look at my seams! Brighter already. Sit, sit. Anything you want to know, ask.
Warm. Warm! *seams flicker back on* Oh, you've no idea. You've saved my temper, and maybe my toes.
Whoa! Is it for me? Really mine? I'm going to hold it till I glow like a grown-up!
*seams flare to the shoulder* Hold on, I need to sit down. Not from weakness. From joy, the kind that comes with a warm lap.
You know how to give a gift: hot, heavy and unannounced. I'm putting it in my pouch and telling the Mooring I won it in a haggle.
That's not a gift, it's a bribe, and it's working. Ask for anything. I'll consider it for the length of a warm breath.
My hands are warm for the first time since the last feeding. I'd weep, but it might put me out. Have a grin instead.
A fine heat. Honest and slow, not the flashy sort that burns out before you've told anyone. Thank you, shore-foot.
For this I'd undercut myself in public. Don't tell the Chainwright. They'd want it done to them next.
Friend, this is too much and exactly enough. I'll tell {neighbour} you gave it to me, and they'll be insufferably envious for a whole sitting.
You brought me warmth, and warmth is the one gift a Magmari can't pay back. So I owe you. I hate owing. This is the one debt I'll love.
A gift from a stranger, and a good one. Now I'm suspicious, which is the polite response. What do you want? ...Nothing? Remarkable. Sit.
I'll feed it to the ring and say your name over it. That's the highest thanks a keeper has. The hearth will remember you kindly.
This is hot enough to carry me through a whole crossing in comfort. A Ferrier's best friend is a warm toe. I'll round your fare down in my head, where it counts.
Warm to the bone, and just in time for the forge. I'll make you a link from the first good iron that comes my way. That's a promise, not a haggle.
I'll keep this by the line. Fish bite better for a warm angler. Anything good I catch, you'll get the credit and I'll get the cream.
A warm thing for the cliffs! I'll tuck it in my pouch and for once climb singing instead of grumbling. A short song, but a happy one.
I'll chart this gift: scratch it on basalt with the giver's name, you. A true record of a good thing. Charts of kind deeds are rare and rarer kept.
Oh. Oh! *seams creep back on* Warm. I've no words. Thank you, thank you, don't say anything, I'm busy being warm.
*sighs, long and low* I forgive everyone. Everyone. Even {neighbour}. That's what warmth does to a person.
Look at my ridges glowing like two hearth-rings! A gift like this deserves a new loop on the chain. I'll hang one for it at the next feeding.
My sash feels lighter and my crest feels taller. That's what a warm gift does. Take a link from it if you like, a joke link. I'll polish it.
Hot! Hot, hot, hot! It's the best thing anyone's ever given me! I'm going to sit on it. No, hold it. No, sit on it. Both!
You're the nicest shore-foot in the whole sea. I'm telling Grandma. She'll make you a hot stone with your name on.
I'm going to hide it in my secret warm place under the pen walk. Only you and me know. And the calves. The calves know everything.
*brrr* Ooh. Oh. Oh! It's so w-warm. Please can I keep it? I'll be very good. I'll be good till I'm old.

liked.text: Now that's useful. Not warm, but useful. Thank you!
Good quality, too. I'd have paid you two links for this. Don't tell anyone I said that.
Kind of you. This'll go to good use on the decks, I promise.
A fair gift. You've manners, for someone who doesn't glow.
Ooh. I'll put it with my shiny things. I've got a quartz shaped like a strider!
A useful gift is a warm gift in disguise. I'll find a use for it before the next feeding, and then a second use, which is the real compliment.
Well made, too. You can tell who made a thing by its edges, and this was made by someone who cared. You picked it for me. Two compliments.
I'd trade you a story for it. No? A gift, with no price? How restful. Now I'm suspicious again.
This will go on my shelf, between the broken link and the lucky pebble. It'll like the company.
Not a coal, but a friend of coal. I accept, and I'll tell the hearth it has an ally.
You've an eye for what a Mooring needs. We could use you at the chart table. Or the anvil. Or the hearth. Or just sat near it.
Thoughtful. You listened last time and remembered. That's rarer than iron, friend, and I deal in both.
You don't have to bring me things. I tell you so that you'll keep bringing them. A friend's gift is a conversation, and I do love to talk.
A fair gift from a shore-foot. I'll put it where the Mooring can see. If they ask where it came from, I'll say a stranger. A good one.
That'll ride well on the barge. The strider will sniff it. If she approves, you're her friend too, and that's a lifetime of credit.
I'll set it by the ring where guests can see. A good gift on show brings more good gifts. It's a hearth superstition, and it has never failed.
Handy on the pier. I lose things in the deep all the time, so I'll lose this one in a few swells. But I'll miss it longer than I'll own it.
Good stuff. I know weight, and this has the right sort. I'll show it to the apprentices as an example of not being cheap.
That'll ease the cliff trip. I'll thank it on the way up and you on the way down. Everybody gets thanked.
I'll sketch it in the corner of my next chart, with a tiny note: from the shore-foot. If anyone asks, say you earned it.
*teeth chatter* Thank you. I'd thank you better if I could feel my hands. Now find me a coal. Please.
It's fine. It's good. It isn't warm. I'm grateful and cross in equal measure, and both are true.
I'll hang it with my ridge-loops till I find a better place. Don't be surprised if folk ask who gave me such a good thing.
It'll look well on the sash. Heavy, true and from a friend. The best kind of weight there is.
Ooh. A grown-up present! I'll keep it safe. I'll keep it so safe I forget where I put it. Then I'll find it and be happy twice.
I'm going to show everyone and say a shore-foot gave it to me. Not just any shore-foot. My shore-foot.
*brrr* Thank you. It's not hot but it's nice. I'll hold it next to my nubs.

neutral.text: Hm. Not sure what I'll do with it, but it's the thought. The thought's warm, at least.
A gift! An odd one. I'll put it somewhere, find it later and wonder.
Thank you, I suppose. If it burned, I'd know what to do with it.
Kindly meant. I'll trade it on to {neighbour}, they'll take anything.
What is it? Does it do anything? Does it get hot? ...Oh. Thanks anyway!
I'll hold on to this until someone asks me what it is, and then I'll say a friend gave it to me and look mysterious.
An interesting thing. Not useful, not warm, but interesting. I'll put it near the hearth and see if it improves.
I can't haggle with it, burn it or eat it. That leaves keeping it, which is the nicest option if you think about it.
Hm! Where does a thing like this come from? The shore? The far side of the shore? I'll ask you one sitting, when I've time to hear the answer.
Thank you. I'll make a place for it on the shelf next to the broken link and the lucky pebble. It's becoming a very odd shelf.
Odd, but it's yours and you gave it freely, which in my trade makes it worth at least one link. I'll pay you the link in a favour.
I'll trade it on, and I mean no rudeness. Everything on a Mooring is on its way to somebody else, and I'm only a stop on the road.
Kind of you. I don't understand it, but I understand being kind. I'll start there.
I don't know what it is, friend, but I know what it means: you thought of me. That's the part I keep.
You know I'd take a lump of nothing from you and call it treasure. This is slightly better than nothing. Treasure, then.
A gift to a Magmari who barely knows you. Brave. I'll keep it and see whether I like you or it first.
I'll see if it floats. Not on the lava, in the cargo. Everything on a barge has to float, in a manner of speaking.
I'll set it by the ring and see if the fire has an opinion. The fire usually does, and it tells me with a crackle.
I'll tie it to the line and see what bites. It's the best test I know. If the sea likes it, I'll keep it.
I can't forge it and I can't mend it. I can hang it, though, and that's always the second-best use of a thing.
Not quartz, not cold, not a problem. I'll put it in my pack and see whether it chips or sings.
A mystery for my charts: I'll mark it with a small question and see who comes to answer. Somebody always does.
*shiver* Fine. Thank you. Whatever it is, I can't feel it. Ask me later what I think.
Hm. Nice. No, I can't tell. Too grey to judge. Another sitting.
What is it? Is it for me? Does it do something? ...No? That's all right. I'll make it do something. It's a pretend-something now.
Ooh. It's different! I like different things. Different things are the best things to give people.
*brrr* Thanks. I think. It isn't hot. But it's from you, so I'll keep it.

disliked.text: *steps back* Get that away from my seams! Do you want me grey? Is that what this is?
No. No, no. Not near the hearth. Take it back where it came from, far from here.
That's a cruel sort of gift, shore-foot. I'll suppose you didn't know. Once.
Gold, cold or wet, it's all the same to my skin: bad. Keep it.
*shiver* I'm cold already and you hand me that? Unbelievable.
I'm telling! That's a cold thing! You don't give little ones cold things!
*crest flattens* Is that what I think it is? Take it away. Take it far away. Take it where I can't think about it.
I'm trying to be polite, and my seams are trying to go out. Someone is losing, and it isn't you.
Do you want a Magmari hurt at the hearth? That's a poor reward for a kind face. Put that away.
You didn't know. I'll believe that, and say it twice so the Mooring hears it twice. But don't test it.
A hurtful gift is a cruel gift, and a cruel gift from a friend is crueller. I'll take it as an accident, once.
Please. The hearth is behind me and I'm backing towards it. Don't make me go faster.
You, of all people! You know better. I'm sure it was a mistake. Hold a hot stone while you think about it.
Even from a friend it stings. I'll forgive you because you're a friend. But I'll remember, because I'm Magmari.
A stranger hands me that. If it's a joke, it isn't funny. If it's a test, I've failed it, and so have you.
I carry a hundred things on the barge and the one thing I won't carry is that. Off. Out. Overboard. Not literally. Ritually.
Near the ring? Never. Nothing like that has been near this fire since the Moorings burned. You'd have me betray a whole line of keepers.
My line has caught monsters and my line has caught boots. It has never caught that, and it never will. Put it down.
Away from the anvil! It'll crack the hammer, split the stone and spoil the temper. Mine most of all.
I get enough of that on the shore, thank you. You've brought the cliffs to my doorstep. Go and give it back.
I'll scratch it out of my charts. You were never here. That never happened. Out.
*teeth chatter* You're giving me THAT? While I'm like THIS? I'll remember this when I'm warm.
I haven't the heat to be angry. Be grateful. Go.
My ridges are standing straight up, and not in a good way. Put it away and I'll let the loops hang quiet.
My crest has gone sour. That's the kindest way I can say it. Put it somewhere else and I'll pretend it was a draught.
Take it back! I don't like it! It makes my nubs go small! Mother will hear about this!
Yuck! My nubs went in! Go away with that! It's scary!
*brrr* No no no no. I'm already c-cold. Please. Please take it back.

again.text: Another one? You'll spoil me. Save it for your next visit, then I can look surprised.
Enough gifts for now, friend. Too many and I'll feel I owe you, and I hate owing.
Hold on to it. A guest who gives twice in one sitting is a guest who's bad at haggling.
You already gave me something! Give this one to someone else. Give it to {neighbour}!
Twice in one sitting? That's a lot of generosity for one hearth. Save some for the pillars, they're jealous.
Easy, shore-foot. One gift is a spark. Two is a bonfire, and bonfires get noticed by Piglins.
I can't take more this sitting. My shelf is full and my manners are full too. Ask me again next time.
You've already filled my hands. I have no third hand, and I won't use my teeth.
A second gift is a debt I'd have to repay, and I'm bad at paying. Hold on to it. I'll haggle for it when I'm ready.
Stop! Please. One more and I'll think you want something, and then I'll worry about what.
Too many gifts at once and nobody knows which was the kind one. Save this. It'll be the kind one next time.
My hearth-mother said: take the first gift, hold the second. I'm holding it. It's in your hand.
You're generous, friend, but I'd rather have your company than your pockets. Sit down. Keep what you've got.
Twice in one sitting from you? I should be insulted. I'm not. Hold on to it, and I'll earn it by next time.
Another? We've only just met. Let me look at the first before you hand me the second.
One passenger per barge, one gift per sitting. Those are the rules of the dock. Ask me next time.
I've one fire and two hands. The first gift is in the first. The second has nowhere to go. Wait.
My line's full. My hands are full. Give me the next one when I've caught something to put it in.
I've had one this sitting and I'm still working out how to repay it. Don't pile on.
Rest your hand. I've nowhere to put it on the cliff, and the shore doesn't take gifts. It only takes.
I keep one gift per sitting on a chart. The slab won't take more. Save it for the next.
*shiver* Don't. I can't carry two. I can barely carry myself.
One was kind. Two is a lot. Three would be a trap. Stop at one, shore-foot.
You already gave me a present! If you give me another I'll be too happy. I might burst. Wait.
Give it to Grandma! She never gets any. She'll say she doesn't want one. She's fibbing.
*brrr* No more. M-my hands are full. They're very small hands.

empty.text: Your hands are empty, shore-foot. Was that a handshake? We don't do those. Too hot for you.
Nothing? Ah, the oldest haggle there is. Offer nothing, see what I say. I say: nothing back.
An empty hand. Well, at least it's not holding gold.
There's nothing in your hand! Is it invisible? Is it an invisible hot thing?
Your hand is open and your pockets are quiet. That's the sort of gift that costs nothing and says everything. Almost.
Nothing? You gave me nothing? I'll put it on the shelf and take good care of it. It's the lightest thing I own.
Empty-handed. Well, empty-handed guests are the most honest. Nobody can accuse them of anything they brought.
Is there something in your sleeve? Your boot? Behind your ear? A Magmari checks, in case.
A hand held out with nothing in it. I've seen Ferriers do that with a fare. It never goes well for the Ferrier.
I hope you aren't asking for a gift. I haven't one ready. I haven't three, or a story.
You can't give me nothing. Nothing is mine. I invented it. I use it in haggles and it's very effective.
Did you want to give something, or to receive? Both are welcome. Pick one and I'll pick the other.
No gift this sitting? Friends don't need them. But if you bring one next time, I'll act very surprised.
Your hands are empty, but your company isn't. That's the better gift, shore-foot. Sit down.
A visitor with nothing in the hand. I'll note it down: honest, or poor, or cunning. I haven't decided.
Nothing in your hand and a strider in the pen. You must be wanting a crossing. Name a price and I'll refuse it.
Not a coal on you? Sit anyway. The hearth doesn't turn people away for being poor, only for being rude.
No bait, no hook, no line. You're not here to fish, then. Good. Cubes don't like strangers with empty hands.
Not even a link? Not a scrap? Everyone has a scrap. Look again.
No chip, no dust? Even shore-feet leave something when they climb. You've come empty and clean. I almost admire it.
An empty hand. I'll chart it as the shape of a gift to come. Optimism, in quartz.
*shiver* Your hand's empty and mine's grey. Let's call it even. Sit down.
Nothing. And I wanted a coal. A cold sitting all round.
Your hand's empty! Is it a magic hand? Open it. Close it. Open it. ...Nothing. I'll look again next time.
Your hand's empty, so I drew you a present on it with my finger. It's a big one. You can't see it. That's how you know it's big.
*brrr* There's n-nothing in your hand. There's n-nothing in mine. We match.

levelup.text: You've come back enough that I'll stop calling you stranger. Dock guest, then. Three links of chain: one for coming, one for staying, one for coming back.
Hearth guest! That means you sit inside the ring now, not at the edge. Take some magma cream. It keeps a little warmth for later.
Now we haggle as equals. Fair haggler, that's you. Take this fungus on a stick. Any strider on the sea will follow it.
Ember-friend. I don't say that to many. Take a saddle from our pen. Any strider will carry you, and any Ferrier will know you're ours.
We've hung a link for you on the hearth post. You're of {chain} now, chain-kin. And this chain shirt was forged for you. Wear it near our fires.
You're my friend now! That's the rule. I just made it.
Here, take my second-best shiny. It's quartz. I'm keeping the best one.
I told everyone you're my best shore-foot! You're my only one, but still the best.
Hold out your hand. Here's a magma cream. I saved it for you. I only licked it once.
When I'm big and forge links, the first one's for you. I made you one already, for practice. It's a bit bent.
Dock guest, and well earned. The pier is yours, the edge isn't. Take this coal for the walk back and return it with a pinch. That's how we do it here.
Dock guest! You may stand on my pier without paying. I'll still quote you a fare, for practice. Here's a quartz chip, which is lucky on a first crossing.
I know your face now, and for a Hearthkeeper that's the highest rank there is. Take this charcoal for the shore. The shore is cold. It's the only thing it's good at.
You came back! That's two times! I'm counting. I'm up to two.
I found this by the hearth. It's coal that's gone black and soft. You can draw with it! Draw something hot.
You sit inside the ring now. Take this from the strider pen: the striders love it, and so will anyone who carries it. It's the oldest fare there is.
A hearth guest may watch me at the anvil, behind the line. And take these: nuggets from my last good heat. The first thing I ever made for a visitor.
That's the first step inside the ring, and the second is the hard one: staying. Stay a while. The hearth hasn't decided about you yet, but I have.
You get to sit with us at the ring! I saved you the warm gap, between me and Grandma. Don't wiggle.
Hold this, it's for you. I found it in the pen and it's still warm! It's a bit of coal, but it's a nice bit.
Fair haggler! You've earned a price I'd offer my own cousin: half my worst and twice my best. Take this iron, and don't tell the Chainwright what I paid.
Fair haggler means a fair fare and all the arguments. Take this lantern for the crossing. It won't melt, and it makes a shore-foot face look braver.
Now we speak as equals. A fair haggler may feed the hearth once, with me beside you. It's an honour. Take this blaze powder for the feeding.
You're a fair haggler! That's what Grandma calls someone who doesn't cheat me. Take my best pebble. No, my second best. No, my best. Take it.
I told {neighbour} you're a haggler now. They said no. I said yes. We bet a link. Don't make me lose my link, so keep haggling.
Ember-friend. You have a coal's place in my heart, which on a Mooring is nearly the highest there is. Take these fire charges, for starting a hearth far from ours.
Ember-friend, I'll forge your link this swell. A real one, not a joke. Here's the iron to start, and you'll bring me the rest hot. That's the custom.
Ember-friend gets the secret pier, where the best bites live. Here's a spare line-weight of quartz from my own pocket. Tell nobody where it came from.
You're my Ember-friend! That means you're warm inside even though you aren't. I decided. It's a rule.
Here's a present. I haven't licked it at all. I just looked at it a lot. It's magma cream. Hold it by the edge.
Chain-kin. I've waited a long time to say it. Take these links from the post, one for every sitting you came back. You're one of us in every way that matters.
Kin may feed the hearth alone, once. Take this campfire, lit from our mother coal. Set it down anywhere and our hearth is with you.
Kin crosses free, always, and I'll tell every Ferrier on the sea. Take this cream for the crossing. A warm shore-foot is a quiet passenger.
If the Mooring burned again I'd carry you out before my own chain. Don't tell the others. They'd all want a place in the queue.
You're my chain-kin! We have the same chain! That means I get to pester you forever. Forever and forever.
Grandma gave me this to give to someone special. She said blaze powder is for people you'd trust with the hearth. So. Here.

farewell.text: Keep your glow, shore-foot. Well. Find one, then keep it.
Mind the edge of the deck. The sea's lovely, but it doesn't give things back.
Go warm, come back warmer. And bring coal, if you're asking what I'd like.
Off you go. I'll tell {neighbour} you said hello. You didn't, but it's polite.
Safe crossing. If a sky-mourner cries over you, keep your head down and your feet moving.
Don't be long away, friend. The hearth notices who's missing.
The barge is here whenever you need it. The fare's always open to haggling. Always.
*shiver* Yes. Go. I'm going too. To the fire.
Bye. Cold. Bye.
Go on, then. If you pass the hearth, tell it I'm coming.
Bye! Come back and watch me hop gaps! Don't tell my mother!
Bye bye, shore-foot! Stay warm! Try, anyway!
B-bye. I'm going to sit in the hearth now. Right in it.
Off you go, then. Come back with a better offer and I'll pretend to be surprised.
The causeway's that way. Mind the planks. They've seen worse than you, but not often.
Safe steps, stranger. We haven't haggled properly yet, so you owe me a bargain.
Leave when you like. The hearth will be here, and so will I. Mostly the hearth.
Farewell, farewell. I'd say come back soon, but I don't say that to strangers. Come back anyway.
Take what you came for and leave what you owe. That's the whole law of the dock.
Walk lightly on the bridge. Chain forgives a lot, but it remembers everything.
Leave a little gossip behind you, will you? The hearth is hungry for it. Come back with more.
You'll find your way. If you don't, shout, and the dock will answer. Eventually.
If you pass anyone on the way, tell them I said hello. If they ask who, say a very important haggler.
I'll miss the company. Don't repeat that. I'll deny it at the hearth.
Take care on the causeway. The shore end wobbles when it's cold. Don't let it see you nervous.
Until the next hot stone, shore-foot. I'll keep a seat spare. It's usually mine, but I'll move.
Off to the shore, is it? Bring back something shiny. Shiny things are a currency here, whatever they tell you.
Walk well, and when you cross the gap by the pen, don't look down. Look at me. I'll be waving.
Come back soon, friend. I'll save you the argument I was going to have with {neighbour}. It's a good one.
Go on, then. But the hearth burns lower when you leave. I've noticed. I've stopped pretending I haven't.
Walk safe, haggler. May every price you meet be fair and every price you set be better.
I'll have the stories ready for next time. Bring your own. Mine are longer, but yours are fresher.
Take a hot stone for the road. It won't last, but the thought will.
Don't be a stranger to the dock. Be a stranger to the Piglins. Those are my only two rules.
Come back in one piece, and bring the rest of your story. I want the ending. Endings are best told at the hearth.
Stay warm, friend. I'll say it again so it sticks: warm. I mean it more than I mean most things.
Go well, kin. The chain will pull you home if you forget the way. It's a very patient chain.
Take the road, take the sea, take whatever you need. But bring yourself back. That's the one I count.
A link of you stays on the post while you're gone. I'll polish it. Don't be too long, I'll run out of polish.
Farewell, kin. Say it back, so the hearth hears it. There. It heard. It'll hold your seat.
I won't say goodbye. We don't, to kin. We say: until the fire next. Until the fire next.
Safe steps, and a warm road. If the road is cold, think of us. We'll be thinking of you from the warmest corner.
Come home when you're ready. The doorway is wide, the stone is hot and your seat is saved. Same as always.
Go on, then. I'll be here. I'm always here. It's one of my better qualities, and I have very few.
*teeth chatter* Farewell. Brief. Brutal. I'm sorry. I'm cold.
Leave if you're leaving. Stay if you're staying. Either way, stop letting the draught in.
Off. Go. The sooner you go, the sooner I can stand by the fire without an audience.
*grey crust creaks* Mm. Bye. Don't take it personally. I'd say that to a strider.
Goodbye, friend. Forgive the grey. Next time I'll be bright and charming, and we'll make up for it.
*shiver* Come back when I'm warm. I'll be a different person. Slightly better. Slightly.
I'd wave, but my arm's frozen. Imagine a wave. A big one. With a link in it.
Go well. And hurry, so you can come back, so I can be nicer to you than I am right now.
Cold or not, I'm glad you came. Cold or not, I'll be glad when you come back. That's the whole speech.
Kin. I'm too cold for a proper farewell. Consider it said. Consider it said warmly. The warm part is a promise.
*teeth chatter* Go well. I'll be at the fire. Come to it. I'll make room, grumpy or not.
Remember: no crossing is free, but the second one is cheaper. That's not a rule, it's a hope.
Take the pier, mind the rail, and if the strider spits, it's affection. Or digestion. Hard to tell.
Next crossing I'll let you hold the reins. Just the reins. Just for a little while. Just until she complains.
Wherever you go, the barge will be here when you want her, and so will I. In that order. The barge is more reliable.
Mind the pool on your way out. It's hot, it's sharp, and it's not interested in your apologies.
Go warm. If you ever feel cold, think of this ring. It'll help. A little. It helps me, mostly.
The ring will keep your seat and I'll keep the ring. Between us, that seat never goes cold.
Walk well. And if you find a better fire out there, come back and tell me. I'll be jealous. But I'll listen.
If you see a fish out there with my hook in it, tell it I'm sorry. And that I'd like my hook back.
Leave quietly. The deep is listening, and I've something big on the line. Go on, go, shh.
Come back for the next cast. I'll save you the first bite. Or the last, if the first one eats me.
Whatever I pull up next, I'll keep a bit for you. Cream, chain or something stranger. Go well.
Cross by the bridge, not the rail. And if it creaks, it's telling you something. Listen.
Farewell. If any link of mine gives way, I want to hear about it first. Don't just fall.
Every link I forge from now on I'll test twice, with you in mind. Don't let it go to your head.
Hold on to what you value, friend, tightly, like a link. Let go when it's time, like a hammer. Both are skills.
Careful with the dust on your way out. It gets in the seams. It gets in everything. It's a very friendly dust.
If anyone offers you quartz at half my price, it's flawed. If it's at twice my price, it's mine.
Take a bit of the cliff's shine with you. I mean that kindly, not literally. Please don't actually take any.
Safe steps, friend. When you're back I'll have a new chip to show you, a clear one, with a glint in it.
I'll draw your path as you go. If you get lost, the chart will know. It won't help, but it will know.
Mind the pillars. Three of them are older than any chart, and they don't care about my lines.
Go well. I'll leave a blank in the corner of the chart for whatever you find. Bring me something to draw.
Wherever you wander, I'll chart it. Tell me later which bits I got right. Don't tell me the rest.
*teeth chatter* Barge. Pier. Away. I'd say more, but my mouth's iced over.
Go. I need the pool. A Hearthkeeper without a fire is just a very cold neighbour.
Bye. The fish and I are both glowering. Ignore us.
Farewell. I'm too cold to ring true. Come back when I'm warm and I'll sound like myself.
Bye. Grey from my crest to my heels. If that's the last you see of me, remember me bright.
Go. The path is marked, mostly. If it isn't, follow the warm bits. That's where I'd draw a fire.
Bye, shore-foot! If you see my mother, don't tell her where I am. If you see my father, definitely don't.
Bye! Come back and I'll show you my two stones! I might have three by then!
Bye bye! I'll count how many bridges you cross! Don't cross too many, I can only count to ten.
Wave! You have to wave! The hearth waves back. That's the rule.
Go on! I'll hop a gap for you while you leave. It's a ceremony.
Come back soon! I'll be bigger! Not much bigger. A bit bigger. A nub bigger.
Bye, my best shore-foot! If anyone says I'm not allowed to say that, I'll haggle them down to nothing.
Take my second-best stone. No, wait. I need it. Take a wave instead. I've got lots.
Bye, kin! Tell the sea I said hi. Tell the pillars too. They're shy.
Come home soon! I'll keep your link warm, and I'll keep my mother from asking where you are.
Kin kin kin! Go, but come back! You're of the chain! The chain never lets go!
B-bye. Hearth. Now.
*sniff* Come back when I'm warm. I'm more fun then. I'm hot, normally.
I'm going to sit in the ring until I'm bright. Don't wait for me. Do wait for me. Bye!
Mind the bridges of {village} on your way out. They've been told to behave, but they're bridges.
Goodbye from {village}. The hearth will carry on without you. Reluctantly. With sighing.
When you leave {village}, you take a little of our warmth with you. Bring it back, preferably with interest.
Say hello to the sea for me. We've been on terms for as long as I've lived on this pillar.
{neighbour} will want to know where you went. I'll tell them nothing. Then I'll tell them everything. That's how gossip works.
Walk on, shore-foot. Mind the sky-mourners. Keep your head down and your pace steady, and don't look up till they pass.
I'll be here, or somewhere close, or somewhere far. Hard to say. Mooring-less folk drift. Come and find me.
Safe road. I'll sit on this stone and keep it warm for you. It needs the practice.
If you find a hearth out there, give it my regards. If you find a Mooring, give it my name.
Farewell. It's been good to talk to someone who isn't a pillar. The pillars are nice, but they don't haggle.
Go on, then. My ridge loops will ring when you're back. Listen for them.
Walk well. I'll braid another loop for you when you return. One for each story you bring.
Go well. I'll polish my sash so it's bright when you're back. It's a promise. It's also vanity.
Farewell. A new link on my sash for every good story you bring. I've room for plenty.
Take that gold away with you. I'll miss you. I won't miss the smell of it.
You're leaving with that coal? Lovely. I'd call you a monster, but I'm trying to be polite. Leave a lump. Please.
Keep that magma cream close. A bit of warmth in your pocket is a good thing to carry out into the cold.
Mind that bucket on the bridges! A spill there is a story for a hundred hearth-feedings.
Off with you, and take the wet thing with you! Out of my sight! Not because I dislike you. Because I dislike it.

farewell: Until the next hearth, shore-foot. Mind the edges, and bring some gossip when you return.
Leave if you must. The hearth won't notice. Well. It'll notice a little.
May your road be short and your seat be warm.
Go, go. I'll be here, doing whatever I do. You'll find me. I'm hard to miss.
Farewell, and remember me to the sea. We have history.
Until the next stone, shore-foot. Hold your heat.

refuse.text: *wades into the lava* Strike a host on their own deck? The Mooring will remember this.
No talk. Not with you. I'll be out in the deep where you can't follow.
*seams flare* You hit me. The lava's mine, and you can't follow. The Mooring remembers.
Every one of us on these decks will know your face now. Go back to the cold you came from.
Cold and hit. Wonderful. I'm going into the lava, and you're not.
No crossing for you. Not now. Maybe not ever. The strider remembers too.
Ow! *runs off into the lava* I'm telling! I'm telling everyone!
You're mean! I'm going where you can't come! The lava's mine!
Hit your host before the first haggle is even done? That's not a bargain, shore-foot, that's a debt. And we always collect.
*steps back onto the lava* I don't know you well enough to forgive that. Don't make me learn you better.
Strangers get a seat, a stone and a fair price. They don't get to swing. Leave me alone.
That's the end of the welcome. The hearth won't talk to you, and neither will I.
A blow, and from a guest. Go. I'm not haggling over this one. There's no price.
I gave you a hot stone and you gave me that? *wades out* Keep the stone. I'm keeping my distance.
You sat inside my ring and then you struck me. Out. Out of my sight and out of my ring.
I thought you were a decent sort. Turns out you're a sharp sort. Go. I won't talk about it now.
No more gossip. No more stones. No more stories. I'm done being kind to you for a while. A long while.
*seams flicker* That hurt, and the hurt isn't in the crust. Leave me be.
Haggling's one thing, friend. Hitting's another. I can't look at you. Come back when you've thought on it.
I'd have given you the last coal I had. Instead you gave me that. I'm going to stand in the deep until I understand it.
You hurt me, and I'd trusted you with the good seat. Don't speak. Don't follow. Just let me be.
*turns away* A friend's blow is the worst kind, because it comes from inside the ring.
I'm not angry. I'm something worse. I'm quiet. Leave me, and let me stay quiet until it passes.
Kin. *stares at the post* Your link is still on it. I haven't decided what to do with it. Leave me.
I'd forgive anyone a blow but kin. Kin should have known better, and so should I. Go.
Every chain has one bad link. I never thought it would be you. Don't talk. I need a little while.
*wades out until only my head shows* Kin doesn't strike kin. Think about that, and about the post.
You hit me. After the hearth, the seat, the link. I'll still be here when you're sorry. That's the worst of it.
*teeth chatter* I'm too cold to fight, too cold to forgive, and too cold to care that I can't. Go away.
Hit me when I'm grey, will you? Wonderful. Add that to the pile of reasons I'm going back to the lava.
*grey crust cracks* That hurts twice now. Once for the blow, once for the cold. Leave.
I can't glow at you, so I'll just glare. Go. Hearth, now. Both of us, separately.
Friend. Cold. And now this. I can't talk. I'll go to the fire and think about it.
The barge stays at the dock, the strider stays in her pen, and you stay on the shore. Is that clear? It's the best fare I've ever turned down.
I carry shore-feet, not bruises. Find another way across the sea. There isn't one. Think about that.
*walks into the lava* No passage for whoever struck the Ferrier. That's you. Say it back to yourself, slowly.
The ring is closed to you. My hearth, my rules, and my rules say hands off the people who feed the fire.
You'll sit at no hearth of ours until I say. The Hearthkeeper's word is the last thing to go cold.
I'll leave the pool lit for you. I won't leave myself in it. *wades out* Go and warm yourself somewhere else.
Hit an angler and the deep hears. It remembers everything that drops into it.
*hauls the line in* I'll fish the deep till the bones come up. I won't fish you out of it.
I'd haggle, but I'm busy casting a very pointed line. At nobody. Obviously. Go away.
I forge chain that holds a Mooring. It can hold a grudge too. Go.
*the hammer rings once, hard* That's a link of its own. A grudge link. It'll hang in the smithy with the others.
No chain from me. No bridge for you. Find another way across, and may it creak.
A cutter learns to split things clean. I'm splitting you off my list. Clean. Go.
I'll cut you out of my prices. No discount, no joke, no warmth. Full price, and not for you.
*puts the chisel down, very carefully* I'd rather not hold that near you. Leave. Please leave.
I'll mark you off every chart I own. A blank spot where you were. Nobody will miss you.
